the_shining_age.title: The Shining Age
the_shining_age.text:
The Shining Age
Before time, Virelia was a place of divine order. There were as many gods as there were domains to maintain, and they directed the natural order by hand, lovingly carving each leaf and grain of sand into its proper shape.
Some relished the mortal races. They took delight in the attention, the adoration, the small intricate stories mortals could not help but conjure.
Some saw no real difference between a man and a stone, and preferred tending to other projects: designing new physics, tending to a garden or perfecting a gust of wind to flutter around leaves in a manner that matches their exact taste.
This was an era of beauty and miracles, where mountains were raised in symmetrical ranges and rivers softly trickled where they were commanded. The Gods walked the earth and had turned it into their heaven.
As a reflection of the gods’ law, the immemorial Remosan Empire ruled over the vast majority of the continent. It was an extraordinary period of abundance coupled with immense hubris, when Gyre-Stones were built to regulate the weather, and imperial highways healed themselves over night.
War still happened, but it carried a different sentiment from what the word means now. Soldiers fell in battle and rose again the next morning, dusted off by the local god and sent home with a story to tell.
The weapons they used, ones that modern Virelia knows only as legend, were left scattered across the fields after the day's fighting, to be picked up and put away back into the toybox.
There were no Rifts, there was nothing yet that could break, unless someone willed it.

the_sundering.title: The Sundering
the_sundering.text:
The Sundering
There was no war in heaven. No warning either. One moment the gods were there, and the next they weren't. Eighteen centuries ago, give or take, the shrines went quiet, and the processions arrived at empty altars. Whatever the gods had been to the people who worshipped them, was now gone.
What followed took a little longer to arrive. Systems broke, in different ways, for different reasons we mostly still don't understand. The center of the continent fell inward into what's now called the Mire. Above Lastrago, the sky tore open in an event that came to be called the Mazur.
Thirekhet had come down into Molakar to cool the desert into a sanctuary and got perhaps a third of the way through. Neither the ice nor the desert has given ground against the other in eighteen centuries.
Divine magic was the worst of it. It had been a tool, only useful the way a plough is, because something larger was pulling it. With the gods gone it went feral, and the survivors, who did not yet understand it had gone haywire, kept trying to use it.
The results were on the scale you'd expect.

the_age_of_silence.title: The Age of Silence
the_age_of_silence.text:
The Age of Silence
When the gods vanished, the people in charge of the Remosan Empire set themselves to fixing things, and they were the wrong people for the job. They were the innocent children of the Shining Age. They had never seen a wound that didn't close or a spell that failed.
War, to them, was a kind of strenuous theater. Death was a story you told at dinner. The idea that an action could have a consequence which then stayed was not something their education had prepared them for.
And so they reached for the tools. The damage of the Sundering was severe but not yet total. The Imperial Highways still ran from coast to coast and healed themselves overnight. Grain still moved between provinces.
The Gyre-Stones still stood across the empire, each holding its patch of the world steady. What was missing was the maintenance the gods had been quietly performing, and the empire's generals and archmages set themselves to replicate it.
They had the old records and the leftover instruments, sometimes even vague memories of how these were once used. They had no idea what they were doing. They didn't even have the framework for understanding that their ignorance was dangerous.
The trouble was that they didn't agree on what needed restoring, or how. The Shining Age had as many priesthoods as it had gods, each with its own methods and records, and while the gods were present the differences hadn't mattered. After the Sundering they mattered enormously.
Every surviving tradition believed it held the correct approach to a job none of their patrons had ever done alone, and none of them were willing to give an inch to the others.
The Age of Silence lasted longer than anyone expected. The damage scaled with the tools. The gods had left behind an entire apparatus of creation: forges, instruments, weapons, arcane infrastructure built to operate on a divine scale.
Mortals now held all of it, understood very little of it, and had no way to test their ideas at anything less than full power. Mages reached for ruinous and experimental schools of magic, and were quick to weaponize them.
The results irradiated whole populations and twisted entire villages into the crystalline Varn. Elsewhere the Kelarra Peaks tore loose from the continent and rose into the upper air, and are still there.
When human soldiers proved too fragile for terrain that no longer behaved, the imperial bio-forges began producing the Orrak, designed from the start to survive what men could not.
As famine and arcane radiation hollowed the labor base, the administration turned to the Graith: given the empire's last clear instructions, set to maintain the infrastructure no living workforce could.
None of it worked. Even the names of the priesthoods and the specifics of their disagreements have not survived. Many of the Soft Zones and Rifts on the modern map are the work of what later ages called the Witch Wars.
They are artillery craters from when humanity broke the world trying to force it back into shape. By the end, the empire was still there in name, but it had used itself up. What came next happened because it no longer had the authority to hold the provinces together.

the_fracture_wars.title: The Fracture Wars
the_fracture_wars.text:
The Fracture Wars
There’s no specific date I can point at where The Age of Silence ended. What matters is at some point people ran out of things to try, and Remosa’s provinces began, quietly and then far less quietly, to defy their leadership. The first deserters are nameless now.
Probably in provinces that no longer exist as distinct places.
What most historians cite as the true beginning of the Fracture Wars is Trefgann's Synod of Secession, some two hundred years ago, when the mayors and guild-masters of Remosa’s largest province, which also held the empire's former capital, formally slammed their gates against the empire.
The Synod was not the first rebellion, but it was the first one that was organized enough to matter.
After Trefgann, the pattern repeated in Haldrith, Rivhalde, and Southfield. The era of grand armies was no longer. Those who replaced them were smaller, meaner, and fought over every last habitable scrap of land.
Remosa did not accept any of this. Three times across the years that followed the empire gathered what it had left and marched on Trefgann, each invasion smaller than the last and each one repulsed. The third was fifty years ago.
Failed the way the others had, and at roughly the same border. Whether this counts as the end of the Fracture Wars is a question only the people who weren't doing the fighting bothered to ask. For everyone else, war was weather.
No one could remember the world without it, and no one expected it to ever end.

the_fractured_era.title: The Fractured Era (The Current Day)
the_fractured_era.text:
The Fractured Era (The Current Day)
The last failed Remosan invasion of Trefgann was fifty years ago, and the Empire could no longer afford to organize a fourth. That is as close as we have come to peace.
No treaty was signed and no borders were formalized, but the grand armies are gone, even though everything they were meant to protect us from is still here.
Rivhalde, Southfield, Haldrith, Trefgann and a handful of other regions hold their own ground, more or less, against the wildlands between. Less in most cases. Rifts still open in market squares on ordinary afternoons. Bandits take the roads the militia cannot afford to patrol.
Rogue arcane weather drifts in from unstable areas and occasionally kills a village nobody had the manpower to warn. Trefgann still expects a Fourth March within the lifetime of its current children and trains accordingly. Is this peace? Either way, it is what it is.
Magic. Goddamned magic. The apparatus the Age of Silence left behind has been rotting for most of two millennia, and most people have decided they want nothing to do with what remains of it. They have reasons.
A wall that mostly repairs itself is of no comfort when it occasionally throws a brick at your house. A road that mends overnight will, twice a generation, mend itself through a cart and the family in it.
The few divine-era objects that still work reliably are guarded by people who understand them far less than they pretend to, and the ones that work unreliably kill more men than they have ever saved.
Religion has shifted from worship to archaeology. A handful of clerics still name their gods, either because their families never stopped praying or because the names survived in scholarship, but no living priesthood carries an unbroken tradition.
Most clerics don't bother with the names at all. They channel what is theorized to be Divine Residue, tapping into leftover echoes of the vanished Gods like scavengers. The average person is atheistic, not as a philosophical position but as a practical one. The gods are no more.
This is something a child learns early, alongside which neighbors to avoid.
In the absence of an empire, governance has settled into a multitude of pragmatic (and less pragmatic) arrangements: city-states, trade consortiums, industrial guilds, monastic orders, each ruling its own island and answerable to nothing larger than its own survival.
Authority is measured in what a ruler can secure for his people: food, safe roads, protection against whatever drifts in from the wild. No one rules further than they can reach.
Factions trade because they must, cooperate where their interests align, and guard their borders against rivals and the encroaching wild with equal vigilance. Contracts, coin, and the constant threat of collapse hold local order together.
No one is under the illusion that they have built anything that will outlast them.

the_regions_of_virelia.title: The Regions of Virelia
the_regions_of_virelia.text:
The Regions of Virelia
Twelve regions, and not one country between them.
While the land is intact, although bruised, the continent’s regions stand mostly alone.
The ground between holdings has gone hostile enough that steady trade and diplomacy are more aspiration than practice, and what a caravan brings home from the next region over has often been paid for in more than coin.
Where the land stopped being the immediate problem, often the neighbors picked up the slack. The central regions function anyway, after their own fashion. The edges are a more complicated story, and they each have their fair share of problems.
In some places the struggle is justified by resources which cannot be found elsewhere. In some, the locals are bullheaded madmen if you ask me.
The regions are not, for all this, uniformly grim. People marry, build, and quarrel over inheritances in places the empire would have written off as uninhabitable. Whatever the Sundering took, it was not our small communities or the quarrels inside them.

knotsreach.title: Knotsreach
knotsreach.text:
Knotsreach
Ma, Don't use the map Dad bought, it's useless past the ridge. When you reach the split rock, turn left, but only if the left path is still there. If it isn’t, sit down and have lunch until you notice it. It usually comes back. After that, walk until the wind feels warm on your neck, then stop. Do not follow the deer trail, even if it looks faster. Just wait there and shout my name. I’ll come get you. It’s not far, just... tricky.
Letter found in a mud-stained envelope near the border
The Garden of Forking Paths
A lush rugged highland that makes for a great place to lose things, and a terrible one for anything else but. Deep forests, jagged hills, with an alien, uncomfortable beauty to it all. The terrain is shifting, unstable. It is as deadly as it is unreliable.
All on account of what the locals have lovingly (?) named Wendy, and everyone else calls by its name: the Wending. Voices of insects fill the area, and anything that can hold a pine needle, does indeed.
The trees look just a bit off from a distance, but take a closer look and you'll see them fold inwards violently. Same goes for everything else here. Rivers flow uphill before correcting into loops that lead nowhere. Roads coil back on themselves.
Fog swirls unnaturally, and the ground moves under your boots without you noticing. None of the neighboring regions dare cross this place, and navigating it is impossible for the rigid-minded.
Survival requires one of two things: a scholarly, almost mathematical grasp of the shifting patterns, or an extremely sharp intuition. Those who rely only on their eyes and strict logic will find themselves walking in circles until they starve.
The Next Best Thing
During the Witch Wars, a large Rift opened in this highland and disgorged something the imperials could not kill. No record of it survives, unfortunately. What did survive is what they did in response.
Lacking the means to kill the creature or close the Rift, they settled for something adjacent to competence: to scramble the terrain around it into a labyrinth no hostile force could cross. The spell worked. It also kept working.
What was meant to warp the ground around the creature wrapped around the imperials themselves and spread outward, until the whole highland had been folded into its own geometry. A miscalculation, in retrospect.
The Rift, if it is still there, sits somewhere near the center, under terrain nobody has managed to reach in eighteen centuries. The locals call the phenomenon Wendy, and maintain that the land is a living thing, resisting any attempt to solve it.
The Wending
Research into the Wending has been all the rage in recent centuries, since, if solved, the region could become a much-needed connective route between Tavernash, Remosa, and Haldrith.
I won't entertain the ceaseless babbling of the scientists, but to my understanding, current research suggests it is a mixture of perception distortion and genuine physical displacement.
Though nobody has managed to observe it directly, the evidence for the latter lies in how nature adapts to it. The previously described trees and rivers, for a start, and the ground underneath them, which makes no sense if you bothered digging in it.
There's a particular type of lichen here that I grew fond of. It locks down against the rock when the ground around it destabilizes, pulling inward and shifting to a gentle ember color until conditions settle.
People use it to navigate, or perhaps better to say, they use it to discern when it's time to stop navigating.
And this pretty much sums up what it's like traveling within Knotsreach a humbling experience which most people would only choose to go through once. One must rely on what's in front of him at the time, and nothing else, and even that can't be taken for granted.
People either stick to their lighthouse-like homes, stay on the go with their carriage houses, or try to blend in with the tangle in hopes that they'll remain hidden. Escapees, druids, or an extreme variant of solitudinarians. You can find them all here, meaning, the population is small.
Nature’s Arsenal
In contrast to the land's freneticism, most wildlife in Knotsreach shows surprising laziness. They stalk, hibernate, lie in wait, dig in. Anything that lets them sit in place and wait for long periods of time.
Birds mostly avoid the place, which has allowed rodents and small insects to proliferate. Maybe that is why they never adapted the same way, and continue to scuttle about aimlessly.
Mimics are extremely common, dressed up as fallen trees or butt-tempting rocks. Following the same principle, kamadans, cloakers and shambling mounds also use the region as a hunting ground. Displacer Beasts have earned a special mention.
They don't hunt in packs anywhere else, but here they've learned to. Lurking in the canopy, using illusion and numbers in equal measure to prey on anything and everything. You can't escape them, and you can't tell which ones are real.
Many think it's the worst thing in Knotsreach, and I don't beg to differ.
The prey is less impressive, but still worth mentioning. Everyone has to feed on something, after all. For example, there's a burrowing rodent the locals call a knuckle, about the size of an apple, dark brown, and not particularly bright.
They burrow underneath rocks to avoid predators, mainly kamadans. This is theorized to be the reason "rock mimics" have become so abundant.
The knuckles haven't caught up yet, and so young mimics feed on them until they reach adulthood, when they can feed on sloth bears and the occasional human.
Beyond Luznica?
There isn't enough to govern, and so nobody bothers to. A refreshing concept, to be honest.
Luznica is the only major settlement, though that might count as cheating as it sits on the outskirts of the Wending, and serves as a hub for the type of people who think Knotsreach is fascinating rather than dangerous. Not fascinating enough to live inside it, mind you.
That spot is saved for the truly lost. First conceptually, and then quite literally.
I'll be frank, describing whatever goes on in Knotsreachean society is a challenge, since society is doing some heavy lifting in that sentence. I think I'd serve you better by describing a particular native. Take Odilile Neembranch. She's a halfling merchant.
People more generous than I would describe her as a "free spirit". I'd say she's a random hermit who wanders randomly from place to place, and will probably die just as randomly. Odilile came to Knotsreach some twenty years ago on a supply run and never left.
Time might tell if this is by choice or not. One way or another, she, exhaustingly, describes the region as beautiful without a trace of irony. She hunts whatever comes across her, and trades leftovers for necessities and anything that's pickled.
Her carriage is pulled by Papaya, her pet bear, and she seems to have decided that it serves as better company than anyone else she might have to share a road with. She survives off the path while attempting to move from one household's beacon to another's. Trades, and moves on.
It could be seen as a sad existence, but she'd wave it away with "it's all about the road" or some other cliché.
Rumors
But Why Are They Warm: Random objects made of clay have been washing down a river from the deep interior. Smooth, well made. They started appearing three months ago. The scholars in Luznica are thrilled, and want the source investigated.
Evolution: New beacons began appearing in the deep reaches. A known trader followed one and was found half eaten later, no beacon in sight. One more died similarly a week later. Locals are worried. Someone, or something, is exploiting the system.
The Untying: A group of Luznican scholars have come to believe that the shifting pattern can be broken mathematically if it was only slightly expanded eastward. They are attempting to recreate a weaker version of the original spell to expand the Wending and “complete the equation”.
Heartache: A couple that has lived in the region for decades have decided they’ve had enough of each other. They insist one of them must leave, but they keep accidentally returning to the same place.
In the meanwhile, the husband lives in a shed in the yard, but they insist this cannot continue. Their daughter is worried for her father’s safety in such an undefended structure.
Gold Rush: A rich Haldrithian merchant wishes to create a “Knotsreach zoo” in Luznica, and looks to hire help to capture native species. Most locals resist, thinking this is either stupidity or a dangerous intrusion of nature.
The argument is becoming heated, and sabotage is apparently no longer off the table.

People either stick to their lighthouse-like homes, stay on the go with their carriage houses, or try to blend in with the tangle in hopes that they'll remain hidden. Escapees, druids, or an extreme variant of solitudinarians. You can find them all here, meaning, the population is small.
Nature’s Arsenal

In contrast to the land's freneticism, most wildlife in Knotsreach shows surprising laziness. They stalk, hibernate, lie in wait, dig in. Anything that lets them sit in place and wait for long periods of time.
Birds mostly avoid the place, which has allowed rodents and small insects to proliferate. Maybe that is why they never adapted the same way, and continue to scuttle about aimlessly.

Mimics are extremely common, dressed up as fallen trees or butt-tempting rocks. Following the same principle, kamadans, cloakers and shambling mounds also use the region as a hunting ground. Displacer Beasts have earned a special mention.

They don't hunt in packs anywhere else, but here they've learned to. Lurking in the canopy, using illusion and numbers in equal measure to prey on anything and everything. You can't escape them, and you can't tell which ones are real.
Many think it's the worst thing in Knotsreach, and I don't beg to differ.

The prey is less impressive, but still worth mentioning. Everyone has to feed on something, after all. For example, there's a burrowing rodent the locals call a knuckle, about the size of an apple, dark brown, and not particularly bright.
They burrow underneath rocks to avoid predators, mainly kamadans. This is theorized to be the reason "rock mimics" have become so abundant.
The knuckles haven't caught up yet, and so young mimics feed on them until they reach adulthood, when they can feed on sloth bears and the occasional human.
Beyond Luznica?
There isn't enough to govern, and so nobody bothers to. A refreshing concept, to be honest.

Luznica is the only major settlement, though that might count as cheating as it sits on the outskirts of the Wending, and serves as a hub for the type of people who think Knotsreach is fascinating rather than dangerous. Not fascinating enough to live inside it, mind you.
That spot is saved for the truly lost. First conceptually, and then quite literally.

I'll be frank, describing whatever goes on in Knotsreachean society is a challenge, since society is doing some heavy lifting in that sentence. I think I'd serve you better by describing a particular native. Take Odilile Neembranch. She's a halfling merchant.

People more generous than I would describe her as a "free spirit". I'd say she's a random hermit who wanders randomly from place to place, and will probably die just as randomly. Odilile came to Knotsreach some twenty years ago on a supply run and never left.

Time might tell if this is by choice or not. One way or another, she, exhaustingly, describes the region as beautiful without a trace of irony. She hunts whatever comes across her, and trades leftovers for necessities and anything that's pickled.

Her carriage is pulled by Papaya, her pet bear, and she seems to have decided that it serves as better company than anyone else she might have to share a road with. She survives off the path while attempting to move from one household's beacon to another's. Trades, and moves on.
It could be seen as a sad existence, but she'd wave it away with "it's all about the road" or some other cliché.
Rumors

But Why Are They Warm: Random objects made of clay have been washing down a river from the deep interior. Smooth, well made. They started appearing three months ago. The scholars in Luznica are thrilled, and want the source investigated.

Evolution: New beacons began appearing in the deep reaches. A known trader followed one and was found half eaten later, no beacon in sight. One more died similarly a week later. Locals are worried. Someone, or something, is exploiting the system.

The Untying: A group of Luznican scholars have come to believe that the shifting pattern can be broken mathematically if it was only slightly expanded eastward. They are attempting to recreate a weaker version of the original spell to expand the Wending and “complete the equation”.
Heartache: A couple that has lived in the region for decades have decided they’ve had enough of each other. They insist one of them must leave, but they keep accidentally returning to the same place.
In the meanwhile, the husband lives in a shed in the yard, but they insist this cannot continue. Their daughter is worried for her father’s safety in such an undefended structure.

Gold Rush: A rich Haldrithian merchant wishes to create a “Knotsreach zoo” in Luznica, and looks to hire help to capture native species. Most locals resist, thinking this is either stupidity or a dangerous intrusion of nature.
The argument is becoming heated, and sabotage is apparently no longer off the table.

molakar.title: Molakar
molakar.text:
Molakar
"Come on, Lenny. I know you're tired, but even that shell won't protect you from that hail storm. Up-up, boy! We have to reach Ravelstead before the weather changes on us again. You get us there, I get you a carrot. Deal?"
Jek, Strider-Rider, muttering to his mount
The 1800 Years’ War
Ah, the ancient sands of Molakar, scarred only by deep crystalline valleys known as Veins. The sand runs the color of old bone and glitters where the grains half-turned to glass, sharp enough to cut through boot leather. By noon the sand can blister skin at a touch.
By early morning it has cooled to a brittle crust.
Settlements sit in close proximity to the Veins for both water and work. Most are half-dug into the desert floor, with thick walls to handle the temperature swing and strong winds.
The clans work in the four usable hours at either end of the day and shelter through the rest, which is most of life out here. The downtime is used for cards, repair work, arguments about water rations, and some more arguments about anything else really.
Veins are another matter. Two kilometers across at their widest, hundreds of meters deep, their walls fluted ice the color of aquamarine. Every block cut from those walls is worth more than the lives of the men sent to cut it.
Meltwater runs down the west faces when the sun catches them, pools on the floor, and freezes back into the wall overnight. Where cold air meets the heat above, the edge throws up a permanent curtain of steam that hides it from anyone standing more than a few paces off.
The boundary between the two is called the Cannonade by the Molakari. A band of unstable air perhaps fifty meters wide where the desert and the Vein argue in hurricanes and gusts. Crossing it on foot in the wrong minute has killed more travelers than bandits and thirst combined.
The worst of it can lift an entire caravan and set it down half a kilometer away, usually in pieces.
A God’s Job
The records mention a god named Thirekhet, one of "stillness and endlessness," who took the region for his playground and set about turning it into something other than sand.
He began at the foundations: Cooling the stone, hardening the groundwater into crystal, probably working outward from wherever he had chosen to stand. He got perhaps a third of the way through before he vanished with the rest. That’s the charitable summary.
While apparently not endless himself, his work has been. The Veins preserve what falls into them, wreak havoc on the local weather, and stand as proof that an artist's work outlasts the artist.
The Clanholds
Authority in Molakar rests with the Clanholds: ten extended families who between them run the ice trade. Anyone is free to walk out into the desert and try to cut ice, but newcomers typically come back empty-handed or not at all.
The clans work the trade through competing methods and are openly hostile toward rival traditions.
Ishkane rely on inherited knowledge: route patterns, Cannonade timing, how to read a Vein wall. Training begins before a child can walk and continues for fifteen years. Crews are small, disciplined, and almost entirely blood. Losses are low but so is the output.
Clans like Toruna run on scale. Larger crews, cheaper equipment, hired labor from outside the family on wages that make the risk worthwhile. Losses run high and occasionally catastrophic, but the volume covers the methods. To the traditionalists, this is a mockery of the craft.
Aylagu and Serimai have risen to prominence in the last two generations, and they have risen loudly. They invest in enchanted gear: cold-resistant armor, cable harnesses, reinforced caravan shells that can take a Cannonade.
The cost of a single expedition is tenfold the older methods, and the money is spent with the confidence of a worthwhile investment. Where it comes from is not entirely clear. Their crews extract remains preserved in the depths of the Veins, and the older clans call them grave-robbers.
They are also, to the traditionalists, uncultured, vulgar, and incapable of understanding why that would matter.
The Slow Road
Long-distance travel across Molakar happens on the backs of Strider-Tortoises. A strider lost to a Cannonade is a year's setback for its clan. They are heavy, slow, and built for this exact landscape. Their shells hold heat through the cold hours and shed it through the hot ones.
Their legs are long enough to keep their bodies three meters above sand that would blister anything standing on it. They move at roughly twelve kilometers a day and refuse to move faster.
A caravan's pace is a strider's pace, which is to say the rhythm of Molakari life is slower than anywhere else on the continent.
The Whole Arm
Anything cold-aligned amplifies within hundreds of meters of the Veins. A cooling cantrip meant for a waterskin can frost an arm to the elbow. Fire is the opposite. It does not work at all.
A related phenomenon is the Cold-Touched: Molakari Karex, perhaps one in a generation, born with an immunity to cold. It is theorized the Veins act as a type of Rift, or Rift-adjacent concept, and their effects bleed into the surrounding desert.
Some Karex born under that influence carry the cold in them in addition to the usual unusual disorders. Even a rumor of one is cause enough for an all-out war between the clans, as has been proven on several past occasions.
Rumors
The Expanding Vein: A well-mapped Vein has begun to widen. The ice is creeping outward at a meter a day, and the nearest village will be under crystal within the season. The elders believe something has stirred deep in the ice and is trying to finish the god's work.
The Glass Tomb: A sandstorm has scoured a dune and exposed a perfect dome of blue crystal where nothing should be. It has no opening. Those who lay a hand on it report hearing a heartbeat, slow and slowing.
The clans cannot agree whether to break it open or bury it again before the rumor spreads.
The Empty Vein: An Ishkane crew returned from a Vein they had been working for three generations to find it cleaned out, the stable seams gone, and Aylagu sled-tracks leading away. Aylagu denies the route was theirs. The Ishkane have called for arbitration in Ravelstead.
Both clans are also quietly preparing for the arbitration to fail.

southfield.title: Southfield
southfield.text:
Southfield
"Brennan's ox, again! You can't tell me that crackpot raised such a beauty. Everyone knows he's at it with his sheep! You know I fucking heard him sneeze in the middle of the street the other day? The man is a savage."
Overheard at Flatford's annual fair
Far from the Madding Crowd
Southfield is a simple-minded region, one of hardy people, traditionalists, farmers mostly. Good potatoes, mediocre poetry, and old people glaring at strangers.
The weather is windy, on the cold side throughout most of the year, and fits the gloomy atmosphere that lurks throughout the region. The cottages are built low and thick. The sheep outnumber the people, and probably have more to say too.
For most of its post-Sundering history, Southfield was home to a region-wide rift that made noise leech on vitality. The exact nature of the phenomenon was never entirely understood, but the evidence was unquestionable. Where there was noise, life dwindled. Crops died.
Stillborns were more common. Cattle got sick. The rift has been waning for roughly a century, and in the last fifty years was declared to no longer affect the land at all. Despite this, the locals mostly maintain the habits they developed during that period.
Southfield is exceptionally quiet. Whether out of tradition or trauma depends on who you ask.
Death Whispered a Lullaby
The rift arrived within the first century after the Sundering. By the time anyone understood what was happening, it was already too late. At first people thought the region was cursed. Imagine realizing years later that all of this suffering, death and famine were preventable.
Once the pattern was understood, the adaptation was fast and total. Festivals stopped. Forges allowed to work only under an active Silence spell. Tools dampened with wool, and livestock was culled to breeds that made less noise.
The architecture changed within a generation: walls thickened, doors got heavier, roofs were lined with whatever would muffle the rain. People latched onto anything they could in an attempt to fight the rift. The communities that adapted survived. The ones that couldn't are no more.
Sign language emerged as the region's main form of communication: a vocabulary of gestures borrowed from shepherds and dock-hands, expanded over generations into something precise enough for day-to-day conversations. Written slates replaced negotiation in public spaces.
Within a few generations the silence stopped being a response to danger and became the ordinary texture of daily life.
The rift began to fade roughly a century ago. The first generation to notice treated the signs as luck. The second renewed research of the anomaly. Then about fifty years ago, a council of village elders formally declared the rift is no more.
The fact that it is so is not enough to convince most Southfielders that things can now change.
All Quiet on the Southern Front
When Southfield was considered cursed, the empire was quick to write the region off. They didn’t have the means to aid it while the fracture wars were taking place, and they were worried the rumors of a dying region would become ones about a dying empire.
Nobody wants to be in the same room with a plague victim, after all. With the empire gone, so went most commoners. Only the stubborn and the poor remained.
Decades later, when the rift was discovered and adapted to, the locals grew fearful of the empire’s return, and so they contacted the Compact.
Seeing an agricultural region with no imperial oversight and a population too small to resist, the Compact was quick to accept. They sent administrators, auditors, and soldiers, and quickly integrated themselves into Southfield’s political system.
The administrators filed reports that grew shorter each quarter. The region, despite its potential, was poor. Hard headed farmers and local oddities stemming from the rift required more adaptation than the Compact could muster.
Within a decade, they cut their losses and signed a protection agreement: Southfield pays a yearly tax. The Compact claims the region on paper. In exchange, the Compact does nothing at all, which is precisely what Southfield has always wanted from the people in charge of it.
The arrangement keeps the Lienhunters out and the imperial banners from coming back. It is, by Southfield's standards, the most successful negotiation in the region's history.
Farmers’ Market
Each village runs itself, and the conventions vary enough between them that a farmer from the interior would find the coastal settlements odd.
Once a year, the villages send representatives to a general council, held at a rotating location, where the agenda covers road maintenance, the Compact's tax allocation, and whatever local problems have grown large enough to require outside opinion.
The rest of the year, the villages have no obligation to each other and mostly act like it. This works until it doesn't and then works again after everyone has had time to cool down. I think the strongest law that holds Southfield together is probably just inertia.
This is, incidentally, one of the reasons the Compact's integration failed as thoroughly as it did. They arrived expecting a political structure to slot into and found a region that runs on local oddities and has no centre to govern from. An administrator can issue a decree.
The question is who, exactly, would carry it out.
Those Who Remain
The exodus during the cursed years gutted the region, and it never fully recovered. Humans make up most of it. Dwarves are the next largest group, and the culture suits them: quiet, practical, and uninterested in performance.
A scattering of Orraks settled after the Fracture Wars, mostly ones with no ties to Remosa worth preserving. Beyond that, not much. Myrrkin avoid the place entirely, for obvious reasons, and Halflings are not far behind them.
The region is too conservative and too gloomy to attract visitors, and too quiet to keep them.
Rumors
Have You Ever Seen The Rain: An onion farmer is worried that the rainfall this fall won’t be enough. He needs someone to clear out a group of bandits who settled by the nearby lake so he can divert the water.
Rudely enough, the bandits are singing drunk songs at night, and he is convinced the noise is souring his crop.
The Taxman: The Compact's annual tax collector has arrived three months early, accompanied by a surveyor and six Lienhunters. He claims the Protection Agreement entitles the Compact to a "periodic review of territorial assets."
The nearest village council is looking for hired muscle to escort the delegation through the region and ensure they leave on schedule. The Compact surveyor is quietly mapping things that have nothing to do with taxes.
The Harvest of the Living: Three weeks ago, a merchant was found dead on the Quiet Road between Netclam and Glaskatch. What unsettled the locals is not just the killing, but the fact that it was loud. Travelers kilometers away reported hearing screaming that lasted for hours.
The nearest village council is looking to find whoever is responsible and deal with them. A second body was found just last week.

myrskov.title: Myrskov
myrskov.text:
Myrskov
"There's a crow outside my house that's been doing Tansya's voice for a month. Wakes me at dawn telling me I'm late. She finds it hilarious."
Bram Jensik, resin-tapper at Brackwater Hold
The Overlapping Land
Spruce, hemlock, cedar, fir… Point is it's mostly just trees, slow rivers, and standing fog. Unremarkable if not for the fact that some time after the Sundering, the realm of Myrr collided with this part of Virelia and bent the local area's behavior in passing.
Unfortunately, the collision destroyed most of Myrr, and continues to do so. As for Myrskov, it has been subject to a quality which I can only describe as "intertwining". It is hard to detach the concept from the spiritual mumbo jumbo that wraps the whole thing, but I'll do my best.
Things in Myrskov seem to aspire to become a part of their surroundings. A village dog might pick up on local human habits. Speech, even. Riverside pebbles "sweat", and a newly dug road quickly dissolves into the surrounding forest.
People call this peculiar configuration "home" despite it all, which has to amount to something.
Settling In
The forest is healthy, in its way. Game is plentiful, the soil is rich, and the winters are no worse than Haldrith's. One might be tempted to think that building a life in here will be easy. They couldn't be more mistaken.
Build somewhere with no history, no "presence", and you'll quickly find that it's harder to form complete sentences and everything you've built slowly dissolves into the forest. The more common tactic is to expand what's already out there.
It's a struggle, but you'd have a higher chance than in fighting the forest head-on. Unless you're either up to the task, or willing to give in completely, of course.
For those who managed to stick around, awaits a glorious life full of goats, gardening, trapping, foraging and the occasional encounter of something truly bizarre. Spend a day in one of these villages and the intertwining becomes obvious.
A village always looks like they’re sharing a gene pool. The vegetables look like they’re from the same garden, no matter where you’ve picked them. There’s a dull uniformity to the whole mess. Tranquil, “natural”, or a tad too intimate. I suppose you can think of it as both.
The one genuine export that allows the whole thing to last is Barkmail. Strips taken from Hemlocks grown along the mountain border toward Kelarra, where the wood picks up the stone's properties. Dried over weeks, the result is a material lighter than wood and harder to split than oak.
Armorers buy the bulk for shields, utensils and furniture. The premium grades go to coopers in Tavernash, who age their wine in Barkmail casks and charge accordingly.
The Collision
Before the Sundering, Myrskov was a forest. Trees, fog, the usual. What happened next is a matter of theory.
The prevailing one holds that the gods had been keeping the rules of Virelia cleanly separate from those of every neighboring realm, and that when they left, that separation became blurry. Virelia's rules and Myrr's began to overlap.
Where they overlapped hardest, here, the two tore open against each other. The Myrrkin themselves do not agree on what exactly happened and who, if anyone, should be held responsible.
My only opinion on the matter is that the scholars who defend this theory use the word “membrane” a great deal.
Myrr was a place that responded to the people living in it. Atmosphere followed mood, emotion took shape in color and fauna. It was simply how the place ran, and everything in it had grown up working with it. Plants drew on the shared experience like Virelian plants draw on sunlight.
The Myrrkin flourished through it without noticing it was there. Fish in water, so to speak.
Virelia is built differently. Things here are what they are regardless of who is looking, mostly, anyway. When the two collided, Virelia's rigidity began bleeding into Myrr and has been killing it ever since. What leaked the other way is what Myrskov is living with.
Myrr, however, cannot become Virelia. Its ecology, its air, its ground, all of it was built around a shared experience. Where the Virelian rules reach, Myrr stops working. Forests collapse, rivers go still, whole valleys empty out.
The Myrrkin who reach Myrskov are leaving a home that is rapidly being made uninhabitable.
Remosa attempted to hold the region during the Fracture Wars and gave up within a decade. Walls may keep out the forest but not its effects, and a garrison that loses men to the woods faster than it can recruit them is not a garrison for long.
A Druid’s Job
Myrskov is governed by what is essentially an old argument between two groups. At least one of which is insufferable, but I'll let you be the judge.
The Druids consider themselves ambassadors of the forest, and are treated as such by the local communities, partly out of respect and partly because nobody else can do what they do.
When a grove starts pulling too hard on a nearby settlement, when the roots start threading through foundations and the walls begin sweating sap, a Druid is the one you want. Even though their methods are opaque and their priorities are obvious.
A Druid circle relocating a family because some shrub needs the space is the sort of thing that happens here with a regularity that has earned the ridicule of the rest of the continent.
They also mediate disputes between villages, which in Myrskov tend to involve questions that would make no sense anywhere else.
The Listeners are the other half of the arrangement, and the half more likely to take the stubborn villager's side.
They're traditionalists who walk the Chime Routes, old paths hung with iron bells and bone wind chimes that have been soaking in the forest long enough to register its shifts.
Reading them is a practiced skill, passed down by apprenticeship, one Listener picking a child and spending a decade until the child replaces the teacher and the cycle of exploitation continues. They carry news, small trade goods, warnings about which paths have gone sour.
Stay off their routes long enough and the forest starts thinking you’re a part of it. Past a certain point the Druids stop calling it a rescue and weapons are drawn. Ferals are dangerous, erratic. Think a pack of wolves with bows and well-planned traps.
Which is why the villagers welcome the Listeners with open arms, and pay the organization the closest thing the region has to a tax. The Halcyons, naturally, think the whole operation is quaint.
Their runners pass through Myrskov on continental routes and deliver mail faster than any Listener could. The Listeners tolerate the Halcyons the way a farmer tolerates a neighbor's dog that keeps barking in the night. As in, not really.
Some would say the Druids are out of touch, and they'd have a point. Some would think the Listeners are sentimental, and they'd have a point. When it's urgent they work together, usually badly.
The rest of the time they argue, and I suspect the region would collapse without either the cooperation or the arguing.
Meet The Neighbors
The fey have been multiplying here since the collision. By this point they're everywhere in Myrskov, the little buggers. Mimicking your voice back at you with the wrong emphasis, moving your tools when you're asleep, drawing faces on rocks.
Children grow up knowing the rules: don't accept, don't follow, don't argue. Some do anyway. Their king, Chopp, holds court next to an oak tree that serves as a consultant.
The Listeners maintain a working relationship with him, mostly because he controls which stretches of forest the fey leave alone and which ones they make unbearable. He is also the main reason the Remosan invasion of Myrskov some 210 years ago failed as catastrophically as it did.
The empire committed four legions and had spent significant resources to build Brackwater Hold as a permanent garrison at the region's center. Chopp didn't appreciate it, and so the campaign, later known as the Overgrown War, began.
Supply lines collapsed within the first year. Wagons arrived carrying the wrong cargo, no cargo, or pinecones packed neatly where food should have been. Soldiers on long patrols stopped coming back. The ones who did were changed, unable to remember their rank or why they'd come.
Severe insomnia spread through the army and did not lift. Men who hadn't slept in weeks stopped distinguishing their own thoughts from the sounds of the forest. The Druids and the forest did their share, no doubt. An angry druid in his natural habitat is a sight to behold.
"And the roots feasted on blood", as the local poem goes. But it was the fey who showed the civilized world how cruel a joke can be. The laughter from the foliage never stopped, not once, for three years. The empire threw four legions at the forest.
What came out was perhaps a quarter of that, and much of it had stopped being useful as soldiers. The empire withdrew, quietly, without a real fight ever taking place. Chopp seems to have forgotten about the whole ordeal since.
Rumors
The Tamer: A Rivhaldean researcher named Bratos set up camp outside Brackwater with three ferals in chains. He claims they can be rehabilitated, that the intertwining can be reversed with controlled reintroduction, and that his work will save lives.
Several families have recognized one of them as a trapper who went missing last spring, and the word "slavery" has started making the rounds. The families want him arrested, tried, and removed.
The problem, as it always is in Myrskov, is that there is nobody to do the arresting, no court to hold a trial, and no precedent for any of it. The Druids have declined to get involved. The Listeners are split.
Kidnapped: A Listener named Edea took a child from Othrelmark four months ago. By tradition, this is how it works, and the village accepts it as part of the arrangement. Othrelmark doesn't. The family says the child was taken without consent, and had stopped paying its levy.
The Listeners have never had to enforce collection before, and the argument over whether they should, or even can, has opened a rift in the organization.

segments.text: Myrskov
"There's a crow outside my house that's been doing Tansya's voice for a month. Wakes me at dawn telling me I'm late. She finds it hilarious."
Bram Jensik, resin-tapper at Brackwater Hold
The Overlapping Land

Spruce, hemlock, cedar, fir… Point is it's mostly just trees, slow rivers, and standing fog. Unremarkable if not for the fact that some time after the Sundering, the realm of Myrr collided with this part of Virelia and bent the local area's behavior in passing.

Unfortunately, the collision destroyed most of Myrr, and continues to do so. As for Myrskov, it has been subject to a quality which I can only describe as "intertwining". It is hard to detach the concept from the spiritual mumbo jumbo that wraps the whole thing, but I'll do my best.

Things in Myrskov seem to aspire to become a part of their surroundings. A village dog might pick up on local human habits. Speech, even. Riverside pebbles "sweat", and a newly dug road quickly dissolves into the surrounding forest.
People call this peculiar configuration "home" despite it all, which has to amount to something.
Settling In

The forest is healthy, in its way. Game is plentiful, the soil is rich, and the winters are no worse than Haldrith's. One might be tempted to think that building a life in here will be easy. They couldn't be more mistaken.

Build somewhere with no history, no "presence", and you'll quickly find that it's harder to form complete sentences and everything you've built slowly dissolves into the forest. The more common tactic is to expand what's already out there.
It's a struggle, but you'd have a higher chance than in fighting the forest head-on. Unless you're either up to the task, or willing to give in completely, of course.

lastrago.title: Lastrago
lastrago.text:
Lastrago
"Everything is wet. My boots are molding while I wear them. The paper in my ledger is turning to mush. I have to oil my sword three times a day or it rusts in the scabbard. I hate this place. The cinnamon, though…"
Sheylok Genn, merchant
When It Rains
Mold and mosquitoes. Thus declared whatever god created Lastrago as it is. Thick canopy, above it tower the Barktrail and the cities, all carried on stilts. And further up, the Mazurat, "Sky rivers". All this glory, filled to the brim with mold and mosquitoes.
A jungle of mad prophets calculating the elements day and night, and their flock, which happens to produce some of the best spices a tongue could come across. Such is Lastrago, with its roaring thunder and its somber rain.
Interestingly, if you buy into the Tavernashi claim that Kenosis is a philosophy and nothing else, Lastrago is probably the only place where religion has gained a foothold in Virelia. The Mazurat are their masters, and they can be oh so cruel.
An unprepared village can get wiped off the map in a single tempest. Ferocious waves of rain, and winds strong enough to break bone. I’d pray too.
Their only line of defense are their priests, the Mazuren. Part meteorologists and part oracles. They decide where a village is built, when a harvest is abandoned, which stretch of the Barktrail is safe to walk this season.
After which the spice farms follow: cinnamon, ginger, vanilla, medicinal herbs. Grown quickly and to colossal heights. All respectfully sit where the Mazuren allow and await their turn to be harvested.
Meanwhile the people sit on their pillows at their ridiculously small tables, drinking hot tea and eating the local spiced abominations they call food.
A Ripple in the Pond
We know the people of Shining Age Lastrago really liked the unpleasant part of the alphabet, all these "Tz" and "Ch" sounds. Unfortunately, they didn't leave us enough of it to work out their language. What pieces remain lie in the names of some settlements that survive to this day.
Then, following the Sundering, came the Mazurat. That much we know for sure. Apparently river-shaped storms are enough of a thing for everyone to write about in all the languages that were available at the time. I've read conflicting records of the event itself, the “Mazur”.
The Mazuren myth is especially vivid. "Sacred water from the tears of the gods who were forced away". I will spare you the details of the myth, point is it's probably bollocks. The foreign accounts are more useful.
If we filter the noise, they repeat roughly the same thing: the sky cracked, water poured, and since then it's all mold and mosquitoes.
After a long period of chaos, comes a Karex named Pakara with glowing eyes who's good at predicting the weather, and so a new religion is formed. One must wonder if we were always so unexacting towards the divine.
Anyway, they built their first temple in Azwighen, and given enough time, temples always turn into bureaucracy. The Mazuren established their rule in the next few centuries.
They built the (very impressive) Barktrail, the cities as they stand today, and a culture that quite literally worships the weather. Lucky for them, they weren’t tested on much more than that. The Fracture Wars never got here.
Trefgann separates them from Remosa's reach, and they've prospered for it.
Downstream
Imagine a deep, turbulent river, sweeping up anything in its path in an unrefined demonstration of power. Now, take that same river, and lift it off the ground. Constantly on the move, raining from above, twisting and curling like a snake on a warpath.
Imagine this, and you get a single Mazurat. Lastrago has about ten at any given time, each with its own kill count and name. On a calm day you can watch one crawl across the horizon trailing rain like a hem. On a bad day one drops.
The Lastragans call it a cascade. The word undersells it. A cascade strips canopy, soil, and anything built on either down to bare rock. A recount I came across goes: “Kichavvo had called for the evacuation two days prior. He said we were lucky to have one so early.
I’ve waited a week for things to quiet down before I came back, hoping to grab some of my things from the ruins. There was nothing. The entire village, gone. Trees snapped at the base, roots in the air, as if the Mazurat has made a deliberate choice to leave absolutely nothing behind.
Seventeen people who refused to leave are still buried there, under the mud.”
The canopy then closes over the cascade site within weeks. The water the Mazurat carries is heavy with minerals and compounds nobody has been able to identify or replicate. Where it hits, the soil turns obscenely fertile. Cinnamon bark grows as thick as a loaf of bread.
Vanilla reaches the canopy in a single season. The spice farmers know this, and follow the cascades with complete disregard to whatever might have been there prior.
They plant in the still-wet soil before the mud has settled, harvest what they can before the forest reclaims it, and move on. The whole economy runs on the aftermath of disasters the Mazuren spend their lives trying to predict.
Somewhat ironic, to have a nation officially organized around cleaning up after their modern gods’ mess.
Upstream
The Barktrail is a massive road on pylons of petrified wood and cut stone, rising above the canopy and connecting Azwighen to Tinzarit and out to Imellah. Apparently a devoted public with access to mathematics can accomplish quite the feats.
Probably better not to let the modern Remosan bureaucrats know that. It was routed through stretches historically safe from the Mazurat, and built to survive one anyway.
The two cities at either end follow the same logic: steep roofs, runoff funneled into aqueducts that roar beneath the walkways during storms. Everything angled, braced, channeled. A coordinated machine for surviving a waterfall. The farming villages, as always, weren't quite so lucky.
They build lighter, because a Mazuren can declare their home abandoned the moment the skies demand it.
The Mazuren rule is too ramified to summarize in a single paragraph, or an entire book for that matter. What I will say is that it relies on two pillars. The first are the Storm-Marked. Karex, taken from their families young, strapped to the temple spires for the next breaking cascade.
Most die up there. The survivors gain some sort of insight into the storms, and then it's a childhood of meteorology lessons followed by a life of tasting water and calculating charts. The highest of honors in Lastragan society.
A priest whose reading later fails is offered the same spire again. Or there's exile. The Mazuren call it the Second Drowning. Fittingly, as most don't survive.
The second are the archives. Both Azwighen and Tinzarit keep branching catacombs filled with rows of stone pools, each holding water from a recorded cascade. Priests take a sample and "taste" the conditions that produced it, cross-referencing against their current charts.
Basically wine tasting with no alcohol nor fun. The priesthood employs collectors for this. Reckless fanatics who run toward the Mazurat with a pot in their hand while everyone else runs the other way. Foolish, stupid, simple-minded, indispensable idiots.
The Locals
Lastragan "traders" mostly sit on their ass next to a pile of cinnamon and wait for the people who want it to come to them, which they reliably do. Caravans make the trip because cascade-grown spices grow nowhere else, and the Mazuren know this well enough to set terms nobody refuses.
The temples allocate the cascade sites, approve the harvest, take their cut, and bless whatever's left for export. Religion and commerce are the same apparatus here, as is the case anywhere else, really. The elves figured this out centuries ago and wanted no part of it.
Their villages in the deep canopy predate the Mazuren, and they've kept to themselves since. The Mazuren let them because pretending they don't exist is easier than searching, and no priest wants to deal with an outsider that might disagree with his methods.
A sensible arrangement, all things considered. Rare for Virelia.
The two temples don't always agree, and the Lastragans made this the local equivalent for entertainment. When Azwighen and Tinzarit issue contradicting forecasts for the same territory, the priests argue in front of the affected villages.
Samples are tasted, charts compared, and the farmers who will stake their harvest or their lives on the result sit and choose the more convincing priest. Two seasons ago a village split between the readings. Seven people died on Tinzarit’s side.
The surviving priests are still arguing methodology, which tells you everything about the priorities of everyone involved.
Rumors
Little April Shower: A cascade stripped an ancient pylon foundation bare, exposing inscriptions in a script nobody can read. A dwarf mason copied them before the pylon was rebuilt. A Rivhaldean scholar who saw the rubbings claims they're coordinates. To what is anyone's guess.
The Conquest of Bread: A Molakari trade caravan is stuck in Azwighen. The Mazuren have closed the Barktrail’s southern stretch for the season. The Molakari insist it's a play to extort a bribe. The Mazuren insist it's necessary. Meanwhile the cargo insists that it is spoiling.
The Messenger: An elf village that hasn't contacted Azwighen in decades has sent a runner asking for help. They won't say with what. The Mazuren aren't interested, and the runner was left to wait at the gate.
Voices From The Deep: A farmer's child fell through the canopy and was missing for three days. She came back speaking words nobody recognizes and insisting there are people living beneath the tree line.

Lastragan "traders" mostly sit on their ass next to a pile of cinnamon and wait for the people who want it to come to them, which they reliably do. Caravans make the trip because cascade-grown spices grow nowhere else, and the Mazuren know this well enough to set terms nobody refuses.

The temples allocate the cascade sites, approve the harvest, take their cut, and bless whatever's left for export. Religion and commerce are the same apparatus here, as is the case anywhere else, really. The elves figured this out centuries ago and wanted no part of it.

Their villages in the deep canopy predate the Mazuren, and they've kept to themselves since. The Mazuren let them because pretending they don't exist is easier than searching, and no priest wants to deal with an outsider that might disagree with his methods.
A sensible arrangement, all things considered. Rare for Virelia.

The two temples don't always agree, and the Lastragans made this the local equivalent for entertainment. When Azwighen and Tinzarit issue contradicting forecasts for the same territory, the priests argue in front of the affected villages.

Samples are tasted, charts compared, and the farmers who will stake their harvest or their lives on the result sit and choose the more convincing priest. Two seasons ago a village split between the readings. Seven people died on Tinzarit’s side.
The surviving priests are still arguing methodology, which tells you everything about the priorities of everyone involved.
Rumors

Little April Shower: A cascade stripped an ancient pylon foundation bare, exposing inscriptions in a script nobody can read. A dwarf mason copied them before the pylon was rebuilt. A Rivhaldean scholar who saw the rubbings claims they're coordinates. To what is anyone's guess.

The Conquest of Bread: A Molakari trade caravan is stuck in Azwighen. The Mazuren have closed the Barktrail’s southern stretch for the season. The Molakari insist it's a play to extort a bribe. The Mazuren insist it's necessary. Meanwhile the cargo insists that it is spoiling.

The Messenger: An elf village that hasn't contacted Azwighen in decades has sent a runner asking for help. They won't say with what. The Mazuren aren't interested, and the runner was left to wait at the gate.

Voices From The Deep: A farmer's child fell through the canopy and was missing for three days. She came back speaking words nobody recognizes and insisting there are people living beneath the tree line.

tintbent.title: Tintbent
tintbent.text:
Tintbent
Entry 204: The Turncoat Vine (Vitis Contravius) A parasitic creeper characterized by aggressive Contrast. To maximize energy absorption, the vine’s pigment shifts instantly to the exact inverse of the ambient light. If the sky burns Red, the vine turns Teal. If the sun shifts Yellow, the vine snaps to Indigo. Makes for fine tea!
Field Warning: Do not traverse dense patches during rapid light-storms. The strobing clash between sky and ground destroys depth perception and induces severe vertigo. Harvest only in total magical darkness. Excerpt from Flora of the Broken Spectrum, Vol IV.
A Sight for Sore Eyes
Imagine waking from a summer nap at high noon. Eyes unfocused, drenched in sweat, the world is a bleary haze of drawn-out colors and painfully bright sun. Add a pinch of nausea, and you'd have a rough idea of what it's like stepping into Tintbent for the first time.
"Tintbent", such an obtuse name. But what can you expect from a population of farming cave dwellers. The peninsula is riddled with caves. Old, water-carved. Communes have spent centuries refining and connecting them.
People who have chosen to live where they're clearly unwanted, all for the sake of either laziness or greed. Only to find out life in Tintbent isn't the rumored "two hours a day" kind of work nor especially profitable. Most leave, others stick with a local crew and learn the hard way.
They spend most of their time underground processing food, fishing, cultivating fungi, and sleeping. Not necessarily in that order. Occasionally they surface to work their excuses for a field. I'd call it an uphill battle, but people here have surrendered completely to the ecosystem.
They can only farm on its terms, and go for a walk when they're allowed to.
Deeper in, even the notion of a walk becomes optimistic. Light bends around solid objects and puts everything a few meters from where it sits. The surges come harder and more often, and will blister exposed skin in minutes. Despite that, nature is abundant here.
But more on that later, as it seems we’ve run out of page.
Solaris
Imperial archives from the Shining Age describe Shekrat as a perfectionist, which I find hard to believe given what the peninsula looks like now.
The records call it a constructed paradise: light painted in shapes for the viewer's pleasure, colors gently arranged in palettes, buildings of pure light that changed with the hour. The usual divine excess.
How much of this is empty flattery to what used to be a living god at the time is anyone's guess. What survives in the peninsula today suggests a deranged pixie over a meticulous artist.
One way or another, Shekrat vanished with the rest. The first generation probably only noticed the colors were slightly wrong. Our only surviving document is from the third, and it mentions the buildings of light collapsing violently and blinding everyone around them.
It is also, maddeningly, mostly concerned with a property dispute between two minor priesthoods. Anyway, we can assume what followed.
The region was built around Shekrat's infrastructure, and as his systems failed, people fled to soft zones through trial and error in what was probably a fatal learning curve. The few who made it burrowed, or built in beige and grey. Either way, they quickly learned the ropes.
Death by error does that to people. These rare communes that survive till this day have been on their own longer than most regions have been independent. A few of them sit on old Shekrat-era infrastructure that still works, at least partly.
Camouflages the houses, calms the light, that sort of thing. The ones that have these live a bit easier, and protect them dearly for it.
Science Fair
A traveler stepping into Tintbent walks through moss that shifts from gold to violet over an afternoon. Growth follows spectral surges rather than seasons, and the lingering light feeds the peninsula well past sunset, pumping far more energy than most plants can absorb.
Broad-leafed species cover themselves in thick waxy coats and curl inward before a surge hits, often before you know one is coming. The rest push out what they can't use as visible glow, as if to make sure night brings no relief.
On the outer ring, herd animals shimmer in sync, nearly invisible until they scatter. Aggressive territorial males and venomous species are painted grey, flat brown, white. Dull against the shimmer, and learned to avoid quickly.
Predators blend into the visual chaos and rely on body heat instead.
Further in is where only real fools are found. Fading pigments. Vestigial eyes. Creatures that don't react when you pass but tense at the sound of your footsteps. By the time the deep zones begin, sight has left the picture entirely. The fauna is pale, often eyeless.
Every step announces you to things that hunt by tremor and scent. No more color games, no panache. These are left for the plants alone to play.
What greets a traveler in the deep interior is a dense, loud forest, filled with echolocation screeches and bright colors that nothing alive can see. Beautiful, if eerie, or so I'm told.
The Raven Paradox
Describing the communes is a bit like describing good poetry books. They are rare, and each one kind of plays by its own rules. Most upper land settlements go grey: matte walls, no windows, sealed entrances.
Children here learn to gather before they learn to read, assuming they learn to read at all. They also put Haldrith to shame when it comes to practical invention, though don't dare try to tell that to a guilds-man.
Mithras uses mirrors to angle controlled light into cave mouths, and uses it underground for growing and crafting. The neighboring "settlements" think they're one bad surge from a mass funeral.
While the average Mithrasi probably thinks the grey communes are squatting in holes out of cowardice.
As if they don't have enough local trouble to handle, they also have imported one in the form of the Speculars.
They arrive on pilgrimage believing the anomaly is sacred, buy anything reflective, carve shrines into rock, and hold rituals during surges that locals consider somewhere between reckless and obscene. Some communes tolerate them for the money but most, understandably, want them gone.
I'd say it's all an impressive proof of mankind's resilience, but sadly, the communes are slowly going extinct. A tunnel collapses, a commune leader dies, or a stabilizer gives out... the reasons are varied. The reasons don't matter, since nobody alive can found new ones.
The barrier is too high and the peninsula has never been in the business of welcoming strangers. What survives is old, insular, and stubborn. I'd say it can't last, but they've been outlasting that prediction for longer than I've been alive, so what do I know.
Below
The relief of stepping underground is immediate. The light stops, the headache fades, and the temperature stabilizes. Most communes are small, fewer than a village worth of people sharing a network of carved and natural chambers, occasionally connected by underground rivers.
The peninsula only has about three settlements large enough to be called that. The rest are crews of a few dozen, spread across rough living spaces: sleeping alcoves, fungi gardens in the damp sections, fish pools fed by diverted river channels.
They usually work by light cantrip or in near darkness. Places like Mithras have their mirrors, or whatever other solution they came up with. Everyone knows everyone. There's no privacy and no strangers. It takes getting used to. Most visitors never do.
Past the inhabited sections the caves continue, unmaintained. Flooded passages, collapsed tunnels, gas pockets in the lower reaches. Occasionally a commune breaks through into spaces that were inhabited before, usually by creatures that don't appreciate visitors.
One more entry on the long list of reasons for Tintbent's declining population.
Rumors
A Light At The End of The Tunnel: A Specular cell has set up near a commune. They bring supplies and pay well for wax and bioluminescent stock. They're also carving mirrors into the bedrock, and the commune's elder wants them out. Some of the commune's traders don't.
The Speculars claim they're close to proving the anomaly is an opening, and that closing it would permanently fix the region.
The Blind Man: Livestock is turning up dead in the deep zones between two communes. Then a trader who should have known better. The kills are clean, precise, not animal work.
A search party has found someone living out there, blind and half-mad, navigating by sound, and he refuses to leave. Someone has to deal with him.
Exodus: A commune's Shekrat-era stabilizer is failing, and the zone it held calm for centuries is drifting hard. They need help to get to the nearby settlement across sixty kilometers of hard territory with children and livestock.
And the neighbors are not, by any account, pleased with the idea.
Unearthed: A major surge strips the soil in the deep zones and exposes Shekrat-era architecture on the surface, partially intact. Three communes, a Specular cell, and a trader caravan are all converging on it for different reasons. A fight seems unavoidable.
