kelarra_peaks.title: Kelarra Peaks
kelarra_peaks.text:
Kelarra Peaks
You know, I dropped a wrench yesterday. I watched it fall for a full minute before it disappeared into the clouds below. The air is so thin up here that you have to breathe slowly, deliberately, or you pass out. It forces you to be calm. I think that's what I needed. Please stop sending letters asking when I'm coming down. I’m not. Tell Ma I’m safe.
Letter from Kael, Novice at the Halos temple
The Three Altitudes
Kelarra is a region built in three altitudes. At the bottom is the grounded range. Mountains, valleys, foothills, the hazardous road that runs east toward Ezgarin and Remosa, and the city of Stoneveil at the hinge of it. Most Kelarrans live here and never go higher.
To an outsider, this is what Kelarra looks like: a hard, thinly populated mountain country with one proper city and a great many problems.
Above it lie the summits. There are few settlements here, mostly just waystations, Halcyon outposts, and the people who make their living guiding others up. Most who pass through here do so twice and as quickly as possible.
And lastly, above the mountains are the peaks which granted the region its name.
The floating archipelago, several hundred islands of stone hanging in the upper air, reached by glider from the launch ledges and connected to one another by a vocabulary of bridges, cable runs, and airways that only the proficient or the ignorant would dare cross.
The peaks are what foreigners mean when they say Kelarra. The grounded range is what Kelarrans mean, but nobody asks them anyway.
The Trouble With Gravity
There were probably mountains here before the Witch Wars, though nothing on the present scale. The fragments that survive suggest a modest highland range with goatherds, a few mining villages and not much else. What it was called unfortunately did not survive the passage of time.
We’re unsure of the exact events that occurred, but the agreed-upon shape of it, among the few scholars who care, is this: Emari, an imperial mage, cast a spell in an attempt to make the region more fertile.
The spell had touched something in the bedrock that should have been left alone, and the bedrock answered by lifting. The man got his farmland. By the end of that year the old range was gone.
In its place stood mountains of impossible height, still rising, with the upper portions already separating from the lower as the folds settled into extreme equilibrium. Whatever villages, wildlife and garrisons that were there went up along with the ground.
What kept the rise from continuing forever are the Stillpoints. Without them the peaks would have continued rising into the uninhabitable thin air centuries ago, and the question of Kelarra’s absurd civilization would not matter.
Dozens of them are scattered across the upper reaches, unmistakably divine-era work, holding each anchor point against the slow upward pull the locals call the Drift. Most islands don't sit on a Stillpoint of their own.
They are tethered to one by cable, or by long line and patient labor, or only by the periodic willingness of someone to glide out and haul them back. Nobody built them after the Sundering and nobody alive understands the principle they operate on.
They are also, fortunately, not very demanding. The Engineers who maintain them oil the gears, tighten the screws and shoo out the occasional bird. The maintenance work is mostly housekeeping.
The Drift wreaks havoc in the grounded range too. Gravity runs sideways for two miles at the Inverted Pass. A sphere of water hangs above the empty bed of Hollow Lake. At least one idiot breaks a limb every year by falling from the floating water.
Smaller anomalies, too many to list, dot the foothills. Places where the lifting did something locally strange. Locals route around them, and outsiders quickly learn to.
A Concept of Proof
Kelarra has been ruled for the last forty-two years by Vulluin, "the Steward," an elven monk, and a cunning bastard. Governing from his court in Stoneveil through his appointed right-hand man Wermund.
The Steward is the title of Kelarra's leader, whereby the holder is understood to advance the ideals of his own abbey for the duration of his tenure.
Vulluin arrived in the peaks some sixty years ago, joined the temple of White Garden, and managed to garner a following large enough to lead the region's largest abbey, and then Kelarra itself. A bit too quick of a rise if you ask me, but the Kelarrans certainly don’t.
Within a year of his investiture he declared the Measure: a yearly combat tournament, open only to masters of established abbeys, the winner of which leads Kelarra until he is defeated as well. He has won every Measure since.
Most Kelarrans take this as proof of his wisdom rather than as the design of a tournament that has never produced a different result. Stoneveil and the lower peaks live under his rule directly. The upper peaks are governed by the Steward in name and by no one in truth.
The Stillpoints are maintained with supplies the Stoneveil provides to the upper peaks to avoid catastrophe, and that is the extent of the relationship either party has any interest in developing.
Wermund handles the practical work: disputes, contracts, infrastructure, tax… anything too mundane for Vulluin’s wise-monk persona. He is the third governor of Vulluin's tenure and is generally considered competent. He serves at his master's pleasure, after all.
Altitude Sickness
The Drift's effects intensify with altitude. On the ground they are uncommon and localized, exceptions in a landscape that mostly behaves. In the peaks the proportions reverse.
Sound occasionally carries too far and arrives slightly out of order, so a conversation on the next peak can be overheard a beat after it ends or, less often, a beat before it begins. Echoes are common at the upper altitudes: visual mirages of people or events that got mixed up in time.
The locals have mostly gotten used to it. Occasionally someone gets confused and dies, but it's only one more cause of death out of many others in the frontier.
Castles in the Air
Stoneveil and the grounded villages build in stone with some wooden parts here and there. The peaks build with whatever the climb permits them to bring up, which is mostly timber, canvas, and resin, with metal reserved for foundations and the occasional critical structure.
The upper bands strip even further. Buildings are framed minimally and many hang below the rock rather than sitting on it, doing double duty as living space and counter-weight. Almost every upper-peak home has a launch porch, and entering one often means landing on it.
I Chose the Sky
Most people who come to Kelarra expect a spiritual experience. What they get is Stoneveil, a mountain city full of people who have watched a thousand of them arrive with the same expression and are, at this point, mainly interested in how much they're willing to spend.
The monks are no better, surprise surprise. A seeker arrives expecting a wise man on a rock and finds three competing monks who want to know if he can cook a meal and hold a staff.
Underneath all of that, the city continues its mundane existence. The born Kelarrans stock the stalls, complain about newcomers peeing in their gardens, and will happily tell you the city was a better place before the abbeys turned it into a staging ground.
Not that it stops anyone from coming. As if to demonstrate we all lack direction in equal measure, Stoneveil has drawn people of every race and kind. All looking for a secret ingredient that they've decided is missing from their lives. The Varn I'll give a pass.
They say the peaks are quiet, above the ambient arcana that spreads across the surface. Lacking crystals myself, I am compelled to accept their reasoning.
Higher up, the population thins to almost nothing, and what's left isn't interested in explaining itself. The settlements around the Stillpoints house a few dozen people who came for reasons they consider settled. Some wanted out. Some were put out.
I don't have much to report on them because they don't have much to say, which, coming from a continent of people who won't shut up about their reasons for being wherever they are, is almost refreshing.
When one of them dies the news drifts down eventually, and Stoneveil notes it the way you'd note a change in the weather.
Rumors
An Easy Fix: During a storm, the secondary cable of Oakhaven Peak snapped. The island is now listing heavily to the side, and the settlement’s Stillpoint is overheating.
The town needs a team to traverse the underside of the island and manually re-engage the emergency clamps before the whole town flips upside down.
The Drifting Monastery: A remote monastery, known for its extreme discipline, has gone silent. Upon checking, it has risen higher, into the altitude where the air is too thin to breathe. The locals are worried for the monks' lives.
The Salvage Run: The master of a minor lower-peak abbey needs someone to travel to a remote village and retrieve a student who left the abbey a year ago, supposedly the strongest practitioner the abbey has produced in a generation.
The master wants him back in time to enter this year's Measure. The student does not want to come back. The master has not said why the student left, and the village he's hiding in has its own reasons for protecting him.

The Stillpoints are maintained with supplies the Stoneveil provides to the upper peaks to avoid catastrophe, and that is the extent of the relationship either party has any interest in developing.

Wermund handles the practical work: disputes, contracts, infrastructure, tax… anything too mundane for Vulluin’s wise-monk persona. He is the third governor of Vulluin's tenure and is generally considered competent. He serves at his master's pleasure, after all.
Altitude Sickness
The Drift's effects intensify with altitude. On the ground they are uncommon and localized, exceptions in a landscape that mostly behaves. In the peaks the proportions reverse.

Sound occasionally carries too far and arrives slightly out of order, so a conversation on the next peak can be overheard a beat after it ends or, less often, a beat before it begins. Echoes are common at the upper altitudes: visual mirages of people or events that got mixed up in time.
The locals have mostly gotten used to it. Occasionally someone gets confused and dies, but it's only one more cause of death out of many others in the frontier.
Castles in the Air

Stoneveil and the grounded villages build in stone with some wooden parts here and there. The peaks build with whatever the climb permits them to bring up, which is mostly timber, canvas, and resin, with metal reserved for foundations and the occasional critical structure.

The upper bands strip even further. Buildings are framed minimally and many hang below the rock rather than sitting on it, doing double duty as living space and counter-weight. Almost every upper-peak home has a launch porch, and entering one often means landing on it.
I Chose the Sky

Most people who come to Kelarra expect a spiritual experience. What they get is Stoneveil, a mountain city full of people who have watched a thousand of them arrive with the same expression and are, at this point, mainly interested in how much they're willing to spend.
The monks are no better, surprise surprise. A seeker arrives expecting a wise man on a rock and finds three competing monks who want to know if he can cook a meal and hold a staff.

Underneath all of that, the city continues its mundane existence. The born Kelarrans stock the stalls, complain about newcomers peeing in their gardens, and will happily tell you the city was a better place before the abbeys turned it into a staging ground.

Not that it stops anyone from coming. As if to demonstrate we all lack direction in equal measure, Stoneveil has drawn people of every race and kind. All looking for a secret ingredient that they've decided is missing from their lives. The Varn I'll give a pass.
They say the peaks are quiet, above the ambient arcana that spreads across the surface. Lacking crystals myself, I am compelled to accept their reasoning.

Higher up, the population thins to almost nothing, and what's left isn't interested in explaining itself. The settlements around the Stillpoints house a few dozen people who came for reasons they consider settled. Some wanted out. Some were put out.

I don't have much to report on them because they don't have much to say, which, coming from a continent of people who won't shut up about their reasons for being wherever they are, is almost refreshing.
When one of them dies the news drifts down eventually, and Stoneveil notes it the way you'd note a change in the weather.
Rumors
An Easy Fix: During a storm, the secondary cable of Oakhaven Peak snapped. The island is now listing heavily to the side, and the settlement’s Stillpoint is overheating.
The town needs a team to traverse the underside of the island and manually re-engage the emergency clamps before the whole town flips upside down.

The Drifting Monastery: A remote monastery, known for its extreme discipline, has gone silent. Upon checking, it has risen higher, into the altitude where the air is too thin to breathe. The locals are worried for the monks' lives.

The Salvage Run: The master of a minor lower-peak abbey needs someone to travel to a remote village and retrieve a student who left the abbey a year ago, supposedly the strongest practitioner the abbey has produced in a generation.

The master wants him back in time to enter this year's Measure. The student does not want to come back. The master has not said why the student left, and the village he's hiding in has its own reasons for protecting him.

tavernash.title: Tavernash
tavernash.text:
Tavernash
“I have a rock here from Haldrith. Look at it. Jagged. Sharp. Unbalanced. Hold it. Feels good, doesn't it? It’s yours for 50 silver. Just don't let your father see you holding that.”
Franz Greenhaven, smuggler, talking to an absolved child
Nothing Ever Happens
Most would describe Tavernash as a dull, flat rock on top of the ocean, filled with people who are just as dull and flat. The wind is always soft, the sea barely moves, try laughing too hard and it will be swallowed by the peninsula's overbearing effect.
It's their sacred Gyre Stone, of course. A piece of imperial machinery at the peninsula's center, holding the world at an arm's length. Without it, Tavernash would be underwater, to little effect for the rest of the world. Aretzu centers this effect, which tapers off the further you go.
The coastal villages get a softer version, just enough to keep the weather quiet. By land, Tavernash connects to the continent only through Knotsreach, which is to say not at all. Most arrivals come by ship through Vranek Bay.
The Stone's calm extends a few kilometers out, making the voyage a short, yet exhausting journey filled with rowing. Exports are wine aged in Barkmail casks, kelp from the coast, and the occasional pilgrim back from the Ringwood.
Imports are few, and whatever does arrive is taxed and inspected at the docks with a thoroughness that would embarrass the Greywater Compact. They don't want to sully their precious land with the ugliness outside, after all.
The Doll’s House
There are conflicting records regarding pre-Sundering Tavernash. Some claim Nareth, the god who ruled it, was a god of calm. He's described as shy, curious and introspective.
One especially disturbing piece claims he was actually no more than a child, whose monarchic kingdom served merely as theatrical entertainment. He enjoyed watching the mortals celebrate their ceremonies and scheme their way up and down the ladder of nobility.
Either way, the Gyre-Stone was built to keep the wider world from interrupting his kingdom. After Nareth vanished, the priests who maintained it put it to the court plainly: hand over the throne, or the peninsula drowns.
The Tavren have been in power since, powerful and exceptionally long lived. The records of how they got there have vanished from every Tavernashi archive. Imperial ones, unfortunately for them, have not. Sacred continuity, the locals call it, and best not to try to tell them otherwise.
The Varieties of Religious Experience
The Kenosis, "The Great Emptying", teaches that emotion is a vice that binds the soul to the suffering of the material world. To be holy is to let the world pass through you, to exist beyond it.
In order to achieve this state, the nobility drinks "The Sacrament of Nareth", ceremonial tea brewed from Ringwood sap which dissolves anxiety, ambition, and rage. It's also quite vile. They call themselves the "Absolved".
They're calculated, slow to speak and move with the type of grace only one with no weight on his shoulders could carry.
Then of course, there are the commoners. The "Laden". Too busy for enlightenment and too necessary to be offered any. Fishermen, Kelp farmers, winemakers and any other profession that brings use to society.
They bear their role with pride, convinced their rulers sacrifice their humanity for a sacred spiritual duty. Whether the Absolved experience this as sacrifice is a question the Laden have learned not to ask.
Hallowed Be Thy Name
Valerian VI governs from Aretzu, if governing is the word for it. He takes his Sacrament, maintains the Stone, and signs what his advisors put in front of him, in roughly that order of importance.
The kingdom runs the way it ran the last three centuries, and will probably continue to until the day when it's Valerian VII's turn to walk the lakes in sequence, each with its own ceremony. Dawn, Vigil, Signet, Oath, Ascension, Feast, Crown, and lastly, Sword.
Unfortunate that spine isn't one.
Order is kept by the Tranquils, monks armed with tuning-fork staves who police discord. A brawl, a breakdown, a bad reaction to the Sacrament, all met with swift sedation and isolation. The fishing villages handle their own disputes. If it doesn't reach Aretzu, it isn't anyone’s problem.
Sorites Paradox
The Nareth Ringwood sits at the peninsula's southern tip, past the Stone's reach. The trees absorb sound, and the deeper you walk, the more you leave behind. The sap the Absolved drink comes from here, and the trees are far more effective in their raw form.
At the center of the perfectly round forest sits Silence, a stable Rift. Pilgrims come from across the continent to whisper their worst memories into the woods. Silence takes what's offered, and returns sweet nothingness. They exit leaving a piece of themselves behind.
Fragmentists, as they are, flock to the place. The crown considers them heretics, and the Tranquils handle the matter with the most enthusiasm the kingdom has ever shown for anything.
Rumors
The Defect: An Absolved noblewoman is looking for someone who can get her off the peninsula. She's been tapering off the Sacrament in secret and the feelings are coming back.
The Sap of life: A smuggler in the fishing villages is exporting a concentrated, black version of the Nareth Sacrament. It causes total memory erasure, and leaves a trail of empty people behind.
The Southern Coast: Laden fishermen are going missing near the Ringwood. The villages pooled what they could afford to hire outsiders. The missing fishermen are alive, sitting in the wood, unable to remember why they walked in.

haldrith.title: Haldrith
haldrith.text:
Haldrith
I have reviewed your report regarding the bedrock density in Sector 4. You claim the stone is too hard to drill on schedule. Let me remind you where you stand, and what your contractual obligation is. I do not care if you have to melt the granite or break every drill-bit in your inventory. We have a contract with the Karagrunds to open that tunnel by the solstice. Fix the gradient, Brotmoc, your excuses and geological conditions are of no interest to me.
Memorandum: Site 4 Delay, Mokash Hammerhand, Foreman of the Iron Guild
The Industrial Grind
I hate Haldrith, I admit. Considered leaving these pages blank, but the gap in the table of contents would bother me more than the writing.
And so here I am, writing about a bunch of bigoted dwarves, all numbed by a millennium of alternating between the land's chilly evening fog and the heat of their metalworks. I'm sure they wouldn't even appreciate it.
A tall person, daring to describe their ill-mannered crime-ridden crumbling excuse of a society.
They are capable of beauty, mind you. I have seen it. The ancient dwarven monuments of the Age of Silence, still standing in Remosa, waiting for a sculptor who will never come. Fallmere, fine polished rock, salted to gleam against Lake Remathis.
All of it, slowly replaced by short-sighted greed one only expects to meet in legends. They scrapped the old Quartz townhall to rebuild it in metal and stone. They're on the seventh version now. The 6th's windows had a 0.6cm angle, you see.
It's all run like a dick-swinging competition between guilds with more power than wisdom, and more aspirations than caution. A group of criminals, politicians and criminal politicians. And, as per usual, the people underneath get to answer to all of them in equal measure.
These days they mine, they forge, they file, they drink, they fuck, they sleep, and then they do it all again for the sake of it. I'm convinced none of them could tell you what they work towards, unless you count the end of their shift or a contract's expiration date.
Craftsmen demoted to statesmen. What a sad sight.
The Iron Stairs
Pre-Sundering Haldrith was the domain of Vrothnak, who was the creator of many of Remosa's built wonders: the Imperial Path, Tharlin's Crossing, Brenmath, the fountain of leaves... Quite the portfolio.
He was rather modest when it comes to his own lodgings, though, judging by the few ancient Remosan remnants that can still be found around Haldrith. Scattered, half-buried ruins. That's about it.
There is no written evidence for this, but my own intuition is that Vrothnak was a creator first and foremost. He liked building things and hated maintaining them. That would explain why so many of Remosa's wonders were self-repairing.
I think he was the type to go to his workshop, create art that goes beyond the abilities of men, only to go back home to a house that is essentially four walls and a bed. You know the type: bad temper, no social skills.
This would explain why all his marvels remain outside Haldrith's borders, the loose dwarven monarchic system that he apparently cared nothing for, and why everything worthwhile in Haldrith was either built after his time, or clearly not by him.
A tad too convenient an explanation, but I’ll take it. Anyway, away he goes, and the dwarven duchies were left to their own devices.
So there they were, a collection of duchies loyal to the Remosan Empire. No leadership, no legitimacy. It's a wonder they survived for so long, but I'm getting ahead of myself.
The dukes had soldiers and titles, but had slowly grown weaker and more despised while the empire bled itself dry in Trefgann.
The taxes kept arriving for a public that spent most of its time caring for somebody else's interests, all while the guilds had the mines, the forges, the working force, and a bubbling hatred of the nobility, with their empty ceremonies and pathetic idleness.
What followed, naturally, was a long, decentralized war of strikes, sabotage, backstabbing and valley-by-valley fighting that went on for the better part of a century. Different guilds backed different factions. Some dukes held on for decades. Others folded within a season.
You'd have to ask an expert on the matter for a clearer picture, as this mess of a historical period is quite honestly too much for me to make sense of.
The turning point, to my understanding, was House Brawneye. A major duchy that sided with the guilds early, armed their workers, and tipped the balance. They gave legitimacy to the rebellion, and shifted public opinion to the guilds' favor.
The official account holds that after power switched hands to the guilds, House Brawneye voluntarily dismantled its title to allow the new system to take root. Some historical records suggest "voluntarily" is doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
The Brawneyes were stripped, scattered, and a decent portion of the family were assassinated. Voluntarily, I'm sure.
The guilds had won, and celebrated by spending the next few decades infighting. Then, at long last, they realized fighting passive-aggressively is cheaper, and the Nonagon was established. A dignified climb from subjugation to self-rule, they'll tell you.
Over a great pile of corpses, I'll add.
A Balanced Diet
Only a Haldrithian would look at a fresh, perfect cod and say "I should grind that into mush and serve it alongside oatmeal and some diced veal." At least they named the dish "Foggy Sunset" so you know you're in for an experience.
And unless the owner has something to prove, then it's probably also served with diluted beer, if you're a tall person, that is.
You then get to bump your head against the ceiling on your way to the toilet which will not have a light since nobody ever considered the idea of a person with no darkvision. Truly, a tourist experience for the ages.
And all of it is built in metal and stone, chilled against the fog and the harsh winds that roam between the hills. Luckily, the scorn for pleasantries doesn't go as far as hearths.
If you plan on visiting despite all this, let me tell you about contracts. They talk about them constantly. Who lost one, whose guild underbid whose, whose got renewed at worse terms.
Over drinks, over work, over a fistfight, which, I should mention, tend to go harder than anywhere else on the continent. The guilds are to blame for most of it, and I'll get to them later.
But my point is that Haldrithian guilds, and by extension, their people, are a bit like that annoying teenager who's determined to paint a penis over every wall in town. Or in this case, their guild sigils.
Whoever paints the most sigils, fights the most rivals, produces the most horseshoes... For them the honor. And so it goes. Shift ends, tavern opens, shift begins.
Building To Break Apart
It started with the Hoof-Hatter. A gnomish invention that produces a horseshoe in under ten minutes. The Black Hands protested at first, but it would seem Hjorn was quickly convinced by the trend in numbers. Pride is the armor of the penniless, as they say.
The other guilds quickly followed, and after them a myriad of other devices. That was 38 years ago, and at the time the thing was treated as a clever curiosity to show off at council meetings. Now most simple stuff that comes out of Haldrithian forges has never been hammered by hand.
The whole arrangement was always going to land somewhere like this. The Nonagon system runs on production numbers, not the quality of craft, and certainly not artistic merit. Whoever produces the most at the cheapest price wins the contract, and contracts are Haldrith's official coin.
It's almost poetic, even more so for how futile the whole thing is. The craftsmen, proud, skillful. Traditionalists looking to honor a practice that predates speech. Standing against their own creations, which some gnomish ingenuity has grown beyond their creators.
The whole thing sent the region into a spiral in recent decades. At first it was the Karagrunds who pushed against it, with eruptions of violence unusual even by Haldrith's standards. Then Yrnar stepped away from the fight, to much dismay from his fellow guildsmen.
Now there are no clear sides to it all. All I can say for sure is that something is going to give. And here I thought that the dwarves and rock gnomes played together so well. Shame.
The Nonagon
Governance in Haldrith is handled by the Nonagon, a council of nine guilds that have clawed their way to the top. Or so the story goes, anyway.
Their authority is the only law in the region, and while supposedly they can be replaced, five of the founding nine haven't changed hands once in that time.
Interesting characters, the lot. Take Pebbleclink, for example. He took a developing field, enchantments, and spent a decade and a half building a system around it from scratch.
He then proceeded to navigate himself into a council seat against every prejudice the dwarves could throw at him. The Myrrkin finally got his acknowledgment when the leadership of his preceding guild vanished one day. The Nonagon nodded, documents were signed, and there you have it.
Haldrith in a nutshell. Thelinde is another one. An elf, no less. Used to run a brothel, and turned it into an empire. She's outlived every chair who's tried to remove her, which at this point has amounted to quite the body count.
A cunning vixen, built herself from scratch only to sit next to "Bregast the Younger." Fourth of his line. Each one drinks more and is more unhinged than the last. I guess sovereignty comes in many forms.
Anyway, three of the seats have changed several times since the Nonagon was founded 190 years ago. The rest hold on by doing what the system rewards, which is making yourself both too dangerous and too useful to remove. Chairs die in their sleep with some regularity.
Rising guilds get gutted overnight, and as long as nobody is caught, nobody bats an eye. Poison is common enough that any chair worth the title won't eat something that hasn't been prepared under watch.
There's a whole culture of duels and public contests where craftsmen pit their work against each other for standing. The thinking, if you can call it that, is that if you survived all of this, you probably deserve the seat. Guild chairs are respected, extremely so.
And should one forget that, they'll be quick to remind him why.
I'll try to explain how the domains work, since the system is unique to Haldrith alone as far as I'm aware. Each guild serves a function. Tunhall runs your drink. Hjornast delivers your grain. The Black Hands forged the lock on your door. Hammerheads maintain the street outside it.
In any given building, three or four guilds have a claim to a part of the owner's pocket, and the place only works because all of them provide for it. The theory is mutual dependency. The practice is that if Hjornast has a problem with you, your supply cart arrives late, or not at all.
Nothing in Haldrith happens without passing through someone else's domain, and they all keep count. Meticulously so.
The Haldrithians will tell you this ensures that power is earned rather than given. Most would describe it as foolish and ineffective, but the Haldrithians take deep pride in their flawed system, which "keeps the gears running while the machine is being tuned."
I'd argue the machine has been "tuned" for 190 years and counting, but what do I know. I'm tall.
What Falls Through
Haldrith has this bizarre unofficial system where a craftsman who wrecks a competitor's workshop is a criminal if he's caught and an entrepreneur if he isn't. A mining guild that bullies a smaller outfit off a claim is breaking the rules right up until nobody files a complaint.
You get the gist. Say you run an inn. You answer to Tunhall for the drink and the permits, Hjornast Wagons for the food (and some more permits), and the Hammerheads when the roof leaks (and some more permits). Each of them will lean on you to edge out the others.
Favor Tunhall's supplier over Hjornast's preferred vendor and your next delivery is short. Fix your own door instead of calling the Hammerheads and see how long it takes for an inspector to find a code violation. And this is all within the Nonagon.
Below them sits a whole ecosystem of smaller guilds fighting for scraps, and they play dirtier because they have less to lose. Not to mention, should you choose a cheaper, smaller guild for one of these services, you'd have to spend the rest of your life avoiding their competitors.
Then there's Pulp. "The Sacrament of Nareth", or what's left of it after it's been mixed with some crap, shipped through Stenvik's bay, and sold out of the back of whatever establishment Mokval's Legion isn't watching closely enough. In Tavernash, the Sacrament is ceremony.
Here it's merchandise, and an expensive one. The regular stuff takes the edge off. Dissolves the anger, the ambition, the parts of you that care about the contract you lost or the guild breathing down your neck. You can see why it sells. The black version is something else entirely.
Total erasure. Though temporary, the effect accumulates. Not a pretty picture. And if after all of this, you're still keen on visiting... Well, at least make sure you get proper ale from the same cask as the locals.
Rumors
Stamp of Approval: Counterfeit enchantment licenses have been circulating in Fallmere's lower districts. The work is good enough that most merchants can't tell the difference, which means enchanted goods are hitting the market without Index oversight or expiration dates.
Pebbleclink has been unusually quiet about it. Either he hasn't found the source, or he has, and the answer is inconvenient.
Fourteen: The Brassmen guild was dissolved overnight. The fourteen newly orphaned children are now Thelinde's Hearth's responsibility, funded under an old agreement that requires all nine seats to contribute.
The Hammerheads, who had a long-standing dispute with the Brassmen, refuse to pay their share. This can turn bloody quickly.
Holt Elderbark: Illegal elderbark lumber has started appearing in Stenvik’s markets. The supply chain runs through enough subcontractors across enough domains that no single guild has jurisdiction to investigate.
The forest is considered to be neutral ground under Nonagon’s agreement, and they want this dealt with.

What followed, naturally, was a long, decentralized war of strikes, sabotage, backstabbing and valley-by-valley fighting that went on for the better part of a century. Different guilds backed different factions. Some dukes held on for decades. Others folded within a season.
You'd have to ask an expert on the matter for a clearer picture, as this mess of a historical period is quite honestly too much for me to make sense of.

The turning point, to my understanding, was House Brawneye. A major duchy that sided with the guilds early, armed their workers, and tipped the balance. They gave legitimacy to the rebellion, and shifted public opinion to the guilds' favor.

The official account holds that after power switched hands to the guilds, House Brawneye voluntarily dismantled its title to allow the new system to take root. Some historical records suggest "voluntarily" is doing a great deal of work in that sentence.
The Brawneyes were stripped, scattered, and a decent portion of the family were assassinated. Voluntarily, I'm sure.

The guilds had won, and celebrated by spending the next few decades infighting. Then, at long last, they realized fighting passive-aggressively is cheaper, and the Nonagon was established. A dignified climb from subjugation to self-rule, they'll tell you.
Over a great pile of corpses, I'll add.
A Balanced Diet

Only a Haldrithian would look at a fresh, perfect cod and say "I should grind that into mush and serve it alongside oatmeal and some diced veal." At least they named the dish "Foggy Sunset" so you know you're in for an experience.
And unless the owner has something to prove, then it's probably also served with diluted beer, if you're a tall person, that is.

You then get to bump your head against the ceiling on your way to the toilet which will not have a light since nobody ever considered the idea of a person with no darkvision. Truly, a tourist experience for the ages.
And all of it is built in metal and stone, chilled against the fog and the harsh winds that roam between the hills. Luckily, the scorn for pleasantries doesn't go as far as hearths.
If you plan on visiting despite all this, let me tell you about contracts. They talk about them constantly. Who lost one, whose guild underbid whose, whose got renewed at worse terms.
Over drinks, over work, over a fistfight, which, I should mention, tend to go harder than anywhere else on the continent. The guilds are to blame for most of it, and I'll get to them later.

But my point is that Haldrithian guilds, and by extension, their people, are a bit like that annoying teenager who's determined to paint a penis over every wall in town. Or in this case, their guild sigils.
Whoever paints the most sigils, fights the most rivals, produces the most horseshoes... For them the honor. And so it goes. Shift ends, tavern opens, shift begins.
Building To Break Apart

It started with the Hoof-Hatter. A gnomish invention that produces a horseshoe in under ten minutes. The Black Hands protested at first, but it would seem Hjorn was quickly convinced by the trend in numbers. Pride is the armor of the penniless, as they say.

The other guilds quickly followed, and after them a myriad of other devices. That was 38 years ago, and at the time the thing was treated as a clever curiosity to show off at council meetings. Now most simple stuff that comes out of Haldrithian forges has never been hammered by hand.

The whole arrangement was always going to land somewhere like this. The Nonagon system runs on production numbers, not the quality of craft, and certainly not artistic merit. Whoever produces the most at the cheapest price wins the contract, and contracts are Haldrith's official coin.

It's almost poetic, even more so for how futile the whole thing is. The craftsmen, proud, skillful. Traditionalists looking to honor a practice that predates speech. Standing against their own creations, which some gnomish ingenuity has grown beyond their creators.

The whole thing sent the region into a spiral in recent decades. At first it was the Karagrunds who pushed against it, with eruptions of violence unusual even by Haldrith's standards. Then Yrnar stepped away from the fight, to much dismay from his fellow guildsmen.
Now there are no clear sides to it all. All I can say for sure is that something is going to give. And here I thought that the dwarves and rock gnomes played together so well. Shame.
The Nonagon
Governance in Haldrith is handled by the Nonagon, a council of nine guilds that have clawed their way to the top. Or so the story goes, anyway.
Their authority is the only law in the region, and while supposedly they can be replaced, five of the founding nine haven't changed hands once in that time.
Interesting characters, the lot. Take Pebbleclink, for example. He took a developing field, enchantments, and spent a decade and a half building a system around it from scratch.

He then proceeded to navigate himself into a council seat against every prejudice the dwarves could throw at him. The Myrrkin finally got his acknowledgment when the leadership of his preceding guild vanished one day. The Nonagon nodded, documents were signed, and there you have it.

Haldrith in a nutshell. Thelinde is another one. An elf, no less. Used to run a brothel, and turned it into an empire. She's outlived every chair who's tried to remove her, which at this point has amounted to quite the body count.

A cunning vixen, built herself from scratch only to sit next to "Bregast the Younger." Fourth of his line. Each one drinks more and is more unhinged than the last. I guess sovereignty comes in many forms.

Anyway, three of the seats have changed several times since the Nonagon was founded 190 years ago. The rest hold on by doing what the system rewards, which is making yourself both too dangerous and too useful to remove. Chairs die in their sleep with some regularity.

Rising guilds get gutted overnight, and as long as nobody is caught, nobody bats an eye. Poison is common enough that any chair worth the title won't eat something that hasn't been prepared under watch.

There's a whole culture of duels and public contests where craftsmen pit their work against each other for standing. The thinking, if you can call it that, is that if you survived all of this, you probably deserve the seat. Guild chairs are respected, extremely so.
And should one forget that, they'll be quick to remind him why.

I'll try to explain how the domains work, since the system is unique to Haldrith alone as far as I'm aware. Each guild serves a function. Tunhall runs your drink. Hjornast delivers your grain. The Black Hands forged the lock on your door. Hammerheads maintain the street outside it.

In any given building, three or four guilds have a claim to a part of the owner's pocket, and the place only works because all of them provide for it. The theory is mutual dependency. The practice is that if Hjornast has a problem with you, your supply cart arrives late, or not at all.
Nothing in Haldrith happens without passing through someone else's domain, and they all keep count. Meticulously so.

The Haldrithians will tell you this ensures that power is earned rather than given. Most would describe it as foolish and ineffective, but the Haldrithians take deep pride in their flawed system, which "keeps the gears running while the machine is being tuned."
I'd argue the machine has been "tuned" for 190 years and counting, but what do I know. I'm tall.
What Falls Through

Haldrith has this bizarre unofficial system where a craftsman who wrecks a competitor's workshop is a criminal if he's caught and an entrepreneur if he isn't. A mining guild that bullies a smaller outfit off a claim is breaking the rules right up until nobody files a complaint.

You get the gist. Say you run an inn. You answer to Tunhall for the drink and the permits, Hjornast Wagons for the food (and some more permits), and the Hammerheads when the roof leaks (and some more permits). Each of them will lean on you to edge out the others.

Favor Tunhall's supplier over Hjornast's preferred vendor and your next delivery is short. Fix your own door instead of calling the Hammerheads and see how long it takes for an inspector to find a code violation. And this is all within the Nonagon.

Below them sits a whole ecosystem of smaller guilds fighting for scraps, and they play dirtier because they have less to lose. Not to mention, should you choose a cheaper, smaller guild for one of these services, you'd have to spend the rest of your life avoiding their competitors.

Then there's Pulp. "The Sacrament of Nareth", or what's left of it after it's been mixed with some crap, shipped through Stenvik's bay, and sold out of the back of whatever establishment Mokval's Legion isn't watching closely enough. In Tavernash, the Sacrament is ceremony.

Here it's merchandise, and an expensive one. The regular stuff takes the edge off. Dissolves the anger, the ambition, the parts of you that care about the contract you lost or the guild breathing down your neck. You can see why it sells. The black version is something else entirely.

Total erasure. Though temporary, the effect accumulates. Not a pretty picture. And if after all of this, you're still keen on visiting... Well, at least make sure you get proper ale from the same cask as the locals.
Rumors

Stamp of Approval: Counterfeit enchantment licenses have been circulating in Fallmere's lower districts. The work is good enough that most merchants can't tell the difference, which means enchanted goods are hitting the market without Index oversight or expiration dates.
Pebbleclink has been unusually quiet about it. Either he hasn't found the source, or he has, and the answer is inconvenient.

Fourteen: The Brassmen guild was dissolved overnight. The fourteen newly orphaned children are now Thelinde's Hearth's responsibility, funded under an old agreement that requires all nine seats to contribute.
The Hammerheads, who had a long-standing dispute with the Brassmen, refuse to pay their share. This can turn bloody quickly.

Holt Elderbark: Illegal elderbark lumber has started appearing in Stenvik’s markets. The supply chain runs through enough subcontractors across enough domains that no single guild has jurisdiction to investigate.
The forest is considered to be neutral ground under Nonagon’s agreement, and they want this dealt with.

rivhalde.title: Rivhalde
rivhalde.text:
Rivhalde
"I’ve run the numbers on Rowanholt. Their buckwheat output is down 12% this quarter. If we deploy a Lienhunter squad to clear out the goblins, the cost of the operation exceeds the village's projected tax revenue for the next five years. Let it burn. We can repossess the land once the goblins move on."
Senior Auditor Richard, denying a request for aid
A Land of Milk And Honey
Wide plains run to the horizon, cut by slow rivers and rich with crops. The roads are well-maintained cobblestone lined with tollbooths at every crossroads. Gorgeous, really.
The Greywater Compact pays the Weave to keep Rifts shut and funds enough patrols to keep the roads clear, which makes Rivhalde the safest region on the continent by most measures and the most expensive by all of them.
The Compact runs the region the way a landlord runs a tenement: it is surveyed, weighed, and should it overstep, disciplined.
Half the continent eats Rivhaldean grain, and the Compact has had generations to leverage that advantage into brutal, efficient strength. They are the wealthiest, most organized power on the continent, and no current rival has the means to challenge them directly.
Luckily, they're so focused on making enemies of their own people that neighboring regions need not worry.
The locals keep enough of what they grow to get by. The rest goes to the Compact's ledger. A village that falls behind on its assessments will quickly meet a Lienhunter crew. One is allowed to rid himself of his assets should he choose to, after all.
What the Harvest Bought
Rivhalde fed the empire for centuries, until Remosa threw everything it had at retaking Trefgann, and left the region to fend for itself. What followed was ugly. Bandits raided the granaries. Deserters from three different armies settled in and took what they wanted.
The Rivhaldean administrators sent emissaries with plea after plea, and got nothing in return.
Bitter and abandoned, the merchant families who ran the river-ports and the grain stores pooled their coin, hired sellswords, and spent the better part of a decade clearing the roads and securing the harvests by force.
By the time it was done, the administrators were answering to them, not the other way around. At that point the empire had stopped being useful, and Rivhalde's merchants are not sentimental people. And so there was “freedom”.
It's Strictly Business
The Board of Signatories governs from Krumfeld. Its members are the heads of the Compact's founding merchant families, and they divide the region's revenue streams between them. Each family controls a suite of settlements, trade routes, or industries, and collects the tariffs accordingly.
The Board meets to set policy, coordinate prices, settle territorial disputes, and decide on the spending that goes toward keeping the roads patrolled and paying for The Weave’s services.
In Rivhalde, anything that generates revenue and doesn't threaten the Compact's hold is permitted and taxed. Necromancy, experimental research, slavery, sex work… every vice is just a licensing fee away from being legal.
The only things the Compact prosecutes with any real enthusiasm are unpaid tariffs and civil resistance.
Whatever does get enforced is done by publishing a contract for the scum of the earth to collect on. A Lienhunter crew rides out and handles it by whatever means necessary. They are well-paid bandits and opportunists. Good at their job, too.
The Compact has never maintained a standing army. It has never needed to.
Sabotage And Other Civic Duties
Despite some evidence to the contrary, it would seem that most people wish to be led by something more than a debt collector. And indeed, change is brewing underneath Rivhalde's semblance of calmness.
The crime-lord-led black market grows ever larger, and resistance cells who came to call themselves "Sabots" commit rare, yet effective, attacks.
The black market runs on Ghost Roads: smuggling routes through the Feskir Woodland and the coast that the Compact hasn't been able to shut down. Unlicensed goods, and people who have reasons to avoid the Compact’s eye go through them.
The operation has grown sophisticated enough to offer its own coinage and protection, effectively, a second Compact with lower rates and fewer Lienhunters. The Board finds this less amusing than everyone else does.
The Sabots are driven by stronger stuff than coin: resentment and ideology. And what a pairing it is. They are dangerous, and no less cruel than the Lienhunters. Debt archives have burned in three cities in the last decade, along with every worker in them.
Lienhunter crews regularly get ambushed on rural roads, and their bodies are consistently brutalized after the fact. Two Compact auditors were killed at their desks in Krumfeld just in the last year. The Board’s response is violent and extreme.
An active Sabot in the Compact’s hands is probably the worst thing one can become. Both sides of this coin deserve each other, if you ask me.
Rumors
A Well-Thought Harvest: A licensed necromancer farmer outside Elmstead has been working for three seasons with no problem. Everything is legal, every tariff paid. However, last season the neighboring farms started failing for different reasons.
The Compact won't directly touch a licensed operation, but they’re worried something fishy is afoot.
Ghosts, Ghosts Everywhere: Smugglers on a Ghost Road through the Feskir Woodland have found something in the trees that shouldn't be there. They can't report it without revealing their route, and they can't ignore it because it killed two of their people last week.
They need outside help from someone who won't ask how they came across it.
God on Trial: A town near the border has filed a contract dispute against the Board itself, claiming the Compact has failed to deliver on its obligations under the original protection agreement. The legal argument is surprisingly solid.
The Board seeks to hire outside help to make the problem disappear discreetly before anyone else gets the same idea.

remosa.title: Remosa
remosa.text:
Remosa
To: Citizen Marl, District 4
Re: Collapse of Outer Wall Section C-9 onto Residential Property
Regarding your complaint that a strategic masonry unit dislodged from the defensive perimeter and crushed your kitchen: Claim Denied. Under the Imperial Preservation Act, all defensive structures are classified as "Active Military Assets" regardless of their current structural integrity. Gravity is considered an act of nature, not state negligence. Furthermore, be advised that filing a second complaint will result in an audit of your household’s conscription eligibility.
We suggest you grind the brick into mortar and repair your roof yourself.
Stamped by Junior Adjudicator Sloan
The Rusting Shield
The Remosan Empire, much reduced. The nation that once ruled most of the continent now barely governs the region around the Mire, a roughly oval hole in reality at its center.
Even its original capital, Brenmath, was lost in the Synod of Secession two centuries ago and has been in Trefgann hands since. Three subsequent invasions, the most recent fifty years ago, failed to take it back.
The Council in Ezgarin still issues maps that include Brenmath, in an attempt to convince children that it’s theirs.
The region is in a long decline, but yes, it is also magnificent. The locals will tell you both at length if you aren't quick enough to stop them. The avenues of Ezgarin are paved in white stone that hummed once with self-repair enchantments and today mostly just hum for the sake of it.
The arches and statues are larger than anything else on the continent. The streetlights work in a third of the districts. The harvest tax was paid in spring and a Mire Commander's outrider may yet come back in autumn for another.
People take real pride in living somewhere that was once the seat of mortal civilization, and curse it constantly for not being that anymore.
The current empire's energy is spent on three things: maintaining what magic still functions, holding the Iron Perimeter against the Mire, and asserting through paperwork what it can no longer assert by force.
The Mire is the one that matters. If the Green Wall stopped drinking or the Iron Perimeter stopped watching, the hole would widen into Haldrith, Kelarra, and Rivhalde within a generation. The wall and the perimeter are funded entirely out of Remosan taxes.
No other region has ever contributed. The Remosans keep count.
The End
The Mire is an oval shaped crater where reality collapsed into itself during the Sundering. The empire at the time still had the means to construct the Green Wall around it. A dense forest of bio-engineered trees planted in the Sundering's immediate aftermath.
Grown specifically to stabilize and absorb whatever comes out of the Mire: gasses, monstrosities, ambient magic, damaged physics. If it kills, it's probably there. From the Wall, the interior is visible. Shapes, colors, and matter fold and reform faster than the eye can register.
Ground becomes sky, solidifies, collapses into something liquid, and then into something that has no word. Light behaves without pattern.
Gasses that don't exist outside the crater pour upward and fill the air above it in colors that shouldn't work together and don't stay long enough to name. There is no agreed description of it in any Remosan record I've come across.
Outside the forest's outer ring stands the Iron Perimeter, a military infrastructure of ancient machinery and soldiers whose only job is to make sure the end of the world stays contained within the trees.
And also, of course, to deal with the occasional slip with whatever ancient machinery they have. Perimeter soldiers rotate off the Wall every eight weeks. Ones who argue they can stay longer are the ones who need to leave most.
As they say, stare long enough into the abyss and the abyss stares back. There are also patrols that work the inner edge of the Green Wall, ostensibly to establish a buffer zone, and in practice to collect volatile ingredients that can't be found anywhere else.
All at the cost of Remosan lives, of course.
Hubris
The empire was rich and well established when the Sundering occurred. The Green Wall was planted within a generation. The Iron Perimeter quickly followed. Despite everything, some competence was still there to be found.
When human soldiers proved too fragile for terrain that no longer behaved, the Bio-Forges began producing the Orrak. When famine and radiation hollowed out the labor base, the Graith were activated to maintain the infrastructure no living workforce could.
Whatever goodwill this earned the empire, the Witch Wars erased. Their damages were a product Remosa exported to the entire continent.
By the time the provinces started rebelling, the empire had spent everything it had on holding the world together and further breaking it in equal measure. Trefgann's Synod of Secession, two centuries ago, took a third of the empire along with Brenmath, the empire's original capital.
Haldrith, Rivhalde, and Southfield followed within a generation. The empire gathered whatever bits and pieces it had left and marched east to take Brenmath back. And then again, and again fifty years ago. A shameful defeat, every single time. The empire still hasn't acknowledged the loss.
No One Writes to the Colonel
A new statue of General Aldren was unveiled in the Ezgarin Forum last year. The sewer pipe under the Forum has been awaiting repair for six. Meanwhile the Continuity Council governs from Ezgarin.
It is composed of old noble families and senior administrators who have inherited the empire's titles if not its territory.
They commission monuments, organize military parades, fund public speeches about Remosan heritage, and run a civic education program that teaches children the empire's borders as they were drawn two centuries ago.
The Mire Commanders manage the Iron Perimeter. They conscript citizens, seize supplies, and requisition whatever they need under standing emergency powers that were granted temporarily three centuries ago and never revoked. The Council sends formal requests for budget reports.
The Commanders send back requests for boots and lumber. Neither side bothers reading what the other sends.
Of Graith And Men
A third of Remosa is Orrak. The Bio-Forges made the first generation. The rest were then born here, devoid of choice in the matter like all the rest of us. The Iron Perimeter garrison consists mostly of Orrak to this day. They’re also common in construction, crafts, trade.
The higher-salaried administrative and engineering posts go to humans. Nobody passed a law about this. Nobody needed to. In short, Orraks in Remosa are Remosan. Their complaints about the taxes and the state of the roads are the same as anyone else’s.
It’s worth noting that their control of Iron Perimeter's garrison means the empire's most critical military asset is largely in Orrak hands. The Council has never formally acknowledged this as a concern. The Council also does not appoint Orraks to administrative posts.
The Graith are fewer and harder to count. They maintain the infrastructure: aqueducts, ward-stones, road enchantments, the machinery that the empire built when it still could.
The most valued profession in Remosa is the Siege-Engineer, and a Siege-Engineer's job is, in practice, keeping a Graith operational long enough to keep a wall operational long enough to keep a district habitable. The chain of dependency is not lost on anyone.
Per the Graith's own testimony, while they are mantra-bound, they are also conscious and possess personality. The council’s position is that this remains under review. A formal study is commissioned roughly once a decade and then shelved.
Recognizing Graith as persons would mean wages, contracts, property rights, and a cascade of legal obligations the Remosan treasury cannot absorb. Most Graith do not press on the matter, because their mantras do not include instructions on the matter.
The ones who do tend to be loud about it, and then tend to be reassigned to less visible posts.
Rumors
The Conscription: A Remosan town is declared under martial law by a commander, who demands a hundred recruits to handle a breach in the Green Wall. The local Mayor, a Council loyalist, blocks the order on the grounds that it violates a tax statute. Both sides have armed men.
The town is in the middle.
The Dying Wall: A stretch of the Green Wall near Southgate has gone quiet. The trees are pale and brittle, and a thin iridescent fog has started drifting into the surrounding farmland. The local garrison doesn't have the people to send into the forest to find out what's killing the trees.
The Fire Sale: A Mire Commander is selling captured magical artillery to a Haldrith crime syndicate. The council wants this to be dealt with, but he needs the coin for winter cloaks, and is, by every account, a decent man.
The Rebel: A Graith maintaining the ward-stones under Ezgarin's eastern district has stopped working. It has renegotiated its mantras and is now requesting a formal status review before it resumes. The district's water pressure is dropping by the day.
The Council wants the problem solved quietly. What "solved" means the council prefers not to put in writing.

Gasses that don't exist outside the crater pour upward and fill the air above it in colors that shouldn't work together and don't stay long enough to name. There is no agreed description of it in any Remosan record I've come across.

Outside the forest's outer ring stands the Iron Perimeter, a military infrastructure of ancient machinery and soldiers whose only job is to make sure the end of the world stays contained within the trees.

And also, of course, to deal with the occasional slip with whatever ancient machinery they have. Perimeter soldiers rotate off the Wall every eight weeks. Ones who argue they can stay longer are the ones who need to leave most.

As they say, stare long enough into the abyss and the abyss stares back. There are also patrols that work the inner edge of the Green Wall, ostensibly to establish a buffer zone, and in practice to collect volatile ingredients that can't be found anywhere else.
All at the cost of Remosan lives, of course.
Hubris

The empire was rich and well established when the Sundering occurred. The Green Wall was planted within a generation. The Iron Perimeter quickly followed. Despite everything, some competence was still there to be found.

When human soldiers proved too fragile for terrain that no longer behaved, the Bio-Forges began producing the Orrak. When famine and radiation hollowed out the labor base, the Graith were activated to maintain the infrastructure no living workforce could.
Whatever goodwill this earned the empire, the Witch Wars erased. Their damages were a product Remosa exported to the entire continent.

By the time the provinces started rebelling, the empire had spent everything it had on holding the world together and further breaking it in equal measure. Trefgann's Synod of Secession, two centuries ago, took a third of the empire along with Brenmath, the empire's original capital.

Haldrith, Rivhalde, and Southfield followed within a generation. The empire gathered whatever bits and pieces it had left and marched east to take Brenmath back. And then again, and again fifty years ago. A shameful defeat, every single time. The empire still hasn't acknowledged the loss.
No One Writes to the Colonel
A new statue of General Aldren was unveiled in the Ezgarin Forum last year. The sewer pipe under the Forum has been awaiting repair for six. Meanwhile the Continuity Council governs from Ezgarin.
It is composed of old noble families and senior administrators who have inherited the empire's titles if not its territory.

They commission monuments, organize military parades, fund public speeches about Remosan heritage, and run a civic education program that teaches children the empire's borders as they were drawn two centuries ago.

The Mire Commanders manage the Iron Perimeter. They conscript citizens, seize supplies, and requisition whatever they need under standing emergency powers that were granted temporarily three centuries ago and never revoked. The Council sends formal requests for budget reports.
The Commanders send back requests for boots and lumber. Neither side bothers reading what the other sends.
Of Graith And Men

A third of Remosa is Orrak. The Bio-Forges made the first generation. The rest were then born here, devoid of choice in the matter like all the rest of us. The Iron Perimeter garrison consists mostly of Orrak to this day. They’re also common in construction, crafts, trade.

The higher-salaried administrative and engineering posts go to humans. Nobody passed a law about this. Nobody needed to. In short, Orraks in Remosa are Remosan. Their complaints about the taxes and the state of the roads are the same as anyone else’s.

It’s worth noting that their control of Iron Perimeter's garrison means the empire's most critical military asset is largely in Orrak hands. The Council has never formally acknowledged this as a concern. The Council also does not appoint Orraks to administrative posts.
The Graith are fewer and harder to count. They maintain the infrastructure: aqueducts, ward-stones, road enchantments, the machinery that the empire built when it still could.

The most valued profession in Remosa is the Siege-Engineer, and a Siege-Engineer's job is, in practice, keeping a Graith operational long enough to keep a wall operational long enough to keep a district habitable. The chain of dependency is not lost on anyone.

Per the Graith's own testimony, while they are mantra-bound, they are also conscious and possess personality. The council’s position is that this remains under review. A formal study is commissioned roughly once a decade and then shelved.

Recognizing Graith as persons would mean wages, contracts, property rights, and a cascade of legal obligations the Remosan treasury cannot absorb. Most Graith do not press on the matter, because their mantras do not include instructions on the matter.
The ones who do tend to be loud about it, and then tend to be reassigned to less visible posts.
Rumors

The Conscription: A Remosan town is declared under martial law by a commander, who demands a hundred recruits to handle a breach in the Green Wall. The local Mayor, a Council loyalist, blocks the order on the grounds that it violates a tax statute. Both sides have armed men.
The town is in the middle.

The Dying Wall: A stretch of the Green Wall near Southgate has gone quiet. The trees are pale and brittle, and a thin iridescent fog has started drifting into the surrounding farmland. The local garrison doesn't have the people to send into the forest to find out what's killing the trees.

The Fire Sale: A Mire Commander is selling captured magical artillery to a Haldrith crime syndicate. The council wants this to be dealt with, but he needs the coin for winter cloaks, and is, by every account, a decent man.

The Rebel: A Graith maintaining the ward-stones under Ezgarin's eastern district has stopped working. It has renegotiated its mantras and is now requesting a formal status review before it resumes. The district's water pressure is dropping by the day.
The Council wants the problem solved quietly. What "solved" means the council prefers not to put in writing.

trefgann.title: Trefgann
trefgann.text:
Trefgann
"The armored man came down the hill, He came to take, he came to kill. He knocked upon the Iron Gate, We told him he would have to wait. He huffed and puffed and broke his bone, and now we use his head for stone! One step! Two step! Three steps! Four! Don't come knocking at our door!"
Playground skipping-song heard in Llyra
Concord of War
Remosa's open wound. They can't stop scratching it, and Trefgann has been opened and bled again and again and again. No wonder they can't think of themselves as anything but "not Remosa".
Hillside forests the color of green rust, lakes rippling in the spring breeze, soil which smells of musty thyme, laced with an ancient road paved in marble. The Trefganners cling to a sense of simplicity, directness, freedom, maybe?
Hardy people, weaponized working folk, sitting inside one of Virelia's greatest regions and too busy surveying Remosa to realize it. Too busy taking apart and mocking the ancient statues to marvel at their beauty.
Maybe fittingly, the opposite of Remosa's hubris has taken the form of paranoia. I realize I'm painting a bleak picture here. And perhaps, an unfair one. The Trefganners are decent folk. Tight communities, strong agricultural identity, great tobacco.
There's just something to be said about people who'd scorn anything and everything as long as it has a Remosan accent.
Tobacco and Stew
Since it seems everyone in Trefgann agrees on politics, what's left to argue about is mostly food, followed by tobacco. Strangers, lucky for them, are unburdened with this until it is proven they have nothing to do with Remosa.
You'll get stared at for three days, and if you pass they'll give you the nods, then the endless inescapable war stories. If you don't, the staring never stops. As a side note, the food is surprisingly pretty good.
A typical Trefganni meal consists of steamed root vegetables and lake fish, hard bread on the side, swallowed with the help of cool buckwheat beer. Lovely, if you can ignore the stares.
Trefganners are the only nation I've seen where people are so damn proud of their land. They learn it by heart, each tree and every abandoned piece of infrastructure. A habit born of farming and foraging, which ended up winning the war for them.
Despite that, the Trefganners show an utter lack of care for what the empire left behind and three wars then added to the pile. It's all still out there, unstable, deteriorating, and when used correctly, hazardous to the uninitiated.
More Remosan soldiers have died in the sewers beneath Brenmath than in its fields.
A Crown of Mud
Brenmath was the seat of the empire for most of recorded history. The court governed from there, and the wealth of half a continent flowed through the gates the Trefganners would eventually shut.
Then came the Witch-Wars, and the boneheaded, bizarre edict to expand the empire onto Myrskov. The records of that particular council meeting make one wonder if there is still hope for our species. Fucking morons.
Trefganner conscripts died in those forests for a campaign the empire had no chance of winning, fed by crops their families needed at home. The Witch Wars had already been draining the province for generations before that.
The costs always fell downward, while the taxes, as always, trickled up. Yet the guild-masters and mayors still somehow persevered, and kept things below boiling point. Until Remosa finally admitted it really had no business in Myrskov, and the outrage struck.
Imperial administrators were dragged from their offices. Noble families who had governed from Brenmath for generations were slaughtered in the streets.
Property was seized, estates burned, and anyone with the wrong name or the wrong accent learned quickly which way the path to Tharlin's Crossing ran. Guild-masters, mayors, trade leaders, all met in "purified" Brenmath and formally declared the empire to be no more.
Varenhal, the empire's own civic Graith, read his mantras and concluded the empire had made itself incompatible with them. The gates closed shut. That is one door that will never open again.
Three times since, the empire has marched east to take the capital back. Each time smaller, more desperate. Each time eating mud from the soil the Trefganners knew better than the people who ruled it. The third was fifty years ago.
The fourth is expected within the lifetime of the current generation. Whether it will come is a question for Ezgarin. Whether Trefgann will be ready is not a question at all.
Pecking Order
Much like the farmers market that is Southfield's ruling council, the Synod of Secession is comprised mostly of people who have no business holding a pen. They convene when the situation demands and are otherwise content to let things sort themselves out.
Four cities, four delegates each, comfortably, or perhaps better described, uncomfortably, sit in a senate hall built for three hundred imperial administrators. They settle trade disputes, and occasionally make a failed attempt at something that requires coordination across city lines.
In brief, the Blackhens handle executive defense. Everything else is either local, mismanaged, or both.
Past the cities, governance thins out fast. Towns and villages answer to whichever city claims them, or to no-one if the claim was never pressed. The militia is the one thing that reaches everywhere: everyone can wield a weapon, and are quick to draw it.
And when the call goes out, the region can pull itself together in days.
One point that I unfortunately can't skim over is Blank. A stable rift that strips identity. Cross its boundary and you are still a person, in some sense of the word. You simply have no idea which one. The Trefganni cities use it to dispose of criminals they deem unsalvageable.
Critics often say it's no different than execution. Less filth, but no less vulgar. I, for one, think they can at least be commended for their creativity.
Think of The Children
The Third March was fifty years ago, long enough for the current crop of Trefganni youth to have fathers who mostly remember having spears shoved into their arms whenever it rained too hard. Habits hold better than memories, and Trefgann is a land of habit, after all.
Offensive spells are still considered inappropriate while few remember the trauma that fueled the taboo. Children learn the Marches before they understand them, and are constantly warned of what's to come.
The result is not obedience, to no one's surprise but the Trefganni. Young ones rebel, old ones complain, as is the natural order of things.
The rebellion takes many forms: eye-rolls during drills, Remosan literature, the quiet departure of young spellcasters who wish to learn “real” magic, and also the occasional argument that the gate should, in fact, open both ways. You know how it is. This is not policy, thank fuck.
It is mostly tavern courage, fueled by ale, boredom and youth. The elders call them westward fools. Some have started using the name proudly, proving that Trefgann has preserved its children from Remosa but not from stupidity.
In summary, peace had raised a generation that knows war through stories only, which is to say they know it very well and not at all.
Rumors
The Iron Giant: A war-construct from the First March has turned up in old Fionn's field outside Elidyr. Dormant, but the core is still hot. He wants to strip it for parts, But Oifara, the local village head, fears it might trigger something that levels the town.
The Peddler's Tin: A Haldrithian peddler sold tin boxes to three villages along the Quiet Road. Keeps grain fresh, he said. Worked, too. Then the wheat in Rhiannon's storehouse sprouted overnight and cracked the walls open, and the peddler is nowhere to be found.
The Beacons: Someone's been carving imperial survey markers into the milestones along the Quiet Road. A unit on patrol spotted the first one three weeks ago and took a chisel to it. Next morning it was back, cut deeper than before.
The Hidden Cache: A village bell rang last month. A kid's prank, false alarm. However, as result it turned out that Vanguard has enough weaponry to arm a small army. Much more than a village its size should. The Synod wants answers.
The Runaway: An eleven-year-old boy named Erik has escaped Cadfael village with nothing but the clothes on his back. His family is rightfully worried, but the other children of the village say it’s better that way since he was “a witch”.

the_races_of_virelia.title: The Races of Virelia
the_races_of_virelia.text:
The Races of Virelia
Variations on the human experience
"Races" isn't quite the right word here, but I'll be using it for lack of a better one. Can people plagued by magic-catching crystals be called a race? Can golems? Mistakes, anomalies, diseased, produced and discarded.
These are the glorious creations of our short-sighted predecessors and our generous homeland.
Since I strongly refuse to take part in the endless arguments regarding taxonomy, I'll say only this: if it's common enough to have a name, and there's a common denominator that I can point to, then it's a race.
I don't care whether you were born that way, shaped that way, infected or constructed by a bloody nutjob. Either way, you're it. People will name you so, and that's enough for you to join the catalogue.
Ancestries that could not have come from anywhere but here, and in some cases would probably have preferred not to. Though the will to live is often stronger than one's better judgement, as demonstrated by some of our more tragic cases.
I've written what I could gather on each, starting with my own observations, followed by brief factual excerpts that might serve the lazy, who, understandably, grew tired of my ceaseless babbling.
Though in my defense, if there is indeed anything that separates us from cattle, it is culture.
What Was, And What Remains
If you'll indulge me, before we proceed to the newer races, I believe the old ones are deserving of an explanation too. I have seen ancient records lament the disappearance of ones such as Aasimar, Dragonborn and Tiefling.
I assume the necessary conditions for their reproduction have been absent from Virelia in its current form, as none of them remain today. As for the ones who are still with us, I'll start by stating the ones that are commonly found.
Humans remain the majority in every region and require no further commentary. Dwarves are common, especially in Haldrith, where they and the rock gnomes have shaped the culture so completely that a visitor might forget what a naturally shaped stone looks like.
You'll find both in most cities, in smaller or larger margins. Halflings are harder to pin down. They scatter, unable to sit in one place both in micro and macro levels. They're practically everywhere, especially the outskirts. Tintbent, upper Kelarra, Knotsreach.
Places where the population is thin enough that five halflings in a settlement of fifty starts to feel like a demographic. It isn't. It's just that most others weren't stupid enough to stay. Forest gnomes are rarer. Myrskov and Lastrago, mostly.
Half-orcs are an uncomfortable topic to discuss. Orcs are out there, in the connecting tissue between holdings, scrapping over ground the rest of us couldn't keep. A child born of that kind of "encounter" is possible.
The circumstances that produce one are rarely the kind anyone writes home about. The Orraks have made the question feel antique, and most people don't bother distinguishing anymore, to the offense of everyone involved.
Elves, supposedly, are still out there. Most living Virelians have never met one, but rumors tell of a strong core that remains hidden in Lastrago. A fellow researcher has told me they were plentiful once.
However, they live for centuries and bear few children, and after eighteen centuries of indiscriminate death, the arithmetic did not work in their favor. A rift takes a village. Humans replace the loss in a generation. Elves carry it for centuries.
Half-elves follow from the same scarcity, and carry no stigma beyond the obvious. There aren't enough elves left for anyone to have developed strong opinions on the matter, which is perhaps lucky when considering the way some other races are treated.
While I would've preferred to detail the ordeals and misfortunes each population has weathered these past eighteen centuries, I'm afraid this work will have to remain unfinished, for now.
I prefer spending what limited time I have on what Virelia has birthed, instead of what it eroded, and I find it more fulfilling to engage with the misfits and the bizarre. It's a personal interest, or perversion. Depends on who you ask.

+2 Any,
Orrak
+2 Con,
Varn
+2 Int,
Myrrkin
+2 Cha,
Nirath
+2 Wis,
Duskwalker
+2 Int,
Karex
+1 Any,
+1 Other
