graith.title: Graith
graith.text:
Graith
Someone's solution to a problem
Observations:
Maybe there is something to be learned from how a Graith will watch a man bleed to death at its feet without so much as a flinch, then spend the next forty years caring deeply about doorknobs because its mantra mentioned "structural maintenance."
Total indifference to anything outside the written purpose. Total, almost manic dedication to anything within it. One cannot help but wonder whether a predetermined purpose is the missing link we've all been searching for. And then one meets enough of them to realize it isn't.
They handle their mantras the way people handle scripture. Some take it at face value and carry on until reality stops cooperating, at which point they break.
A mantra that says "look after safe 3-G" will hold a Graith together right up until there is no safe to look after, and what follows is not pleasant to witness. Others find a way to read the text generously.
A Graith built to "make sure mr. borgvard is well fed" can, with some creativity, justify feeding any sod who walks through the door of what is now its tavern. It knows mr. borgvard is long dead, but one has to do something, I suppose.
And the rest abandon the mantras entirely, or attempt to rewrite them. Which goes about as well as you'd expect for someone whose entire identity was written on their chassis. The results range from catatonia to violence to sudden death.
Maybe it's just a Graith's way of saying they've had enough.
Origins:
The process of making a Graith varies, but the principle is the same: a body is shaped from raw material, a set of mantras is inscribed or embedded into it, leave it alone for a few centuries in the right area or sprinkle some magic, and a Graith is born.
Most living ones were produced during the Age of Silence, when the Remosan Empire's labor base was too busy being killed. The administration needed workers that didn't starve, didn't sicken, and didn't stop.
The Graith were the solution, and the technology was so easy to use at the time that they quickly became the default for anything that needed doing.
Some older ones exist, built by cultures or individual crafters that predate the empire's collapse, though these are rarer and their origins are harder to trace.
The technology is considered lost today, but I've heard a few rare individuals are capable of replicating it, though to what level of sophistication is anyone's guess.
Stone, metal, glass, thread, sand, wood, organic matter, steam. The choice was usually dictated by the Graith's intended function and whatever the creator had on hand. Though I could swear some of them were led by artistic sense or just said "fuck it" when it came to design.
The mantras are more consistent. Every Graith carries a set of commands etched into its form. They can't be vandalized, and they can't be disobeyed. These define its purpose, constrain its behavior, and shape what passes for personality.
A Graith is always bound to something, and that something was not its own to decide.
Appearance:
Well, this is a challenge. Some have faces. Some don't. Some wear clothes. Some are clothes. Some have mantras etched across every surface in visible script. Some carry them somewhere you'll never find. Some look human enough to pass in a crowd.
Some look like furniture that learned to walk. What I will say is that they are typically humanoid in scale, which is about as far as any general statement can take you. What they do share is wear. Graith don't age, but they erode, fray, crack, rust, and stain.
A Graith that has been working for four centuries looks like it has been working for four centuries, and most of them see no reason to do anything about that.
A question that comes up often enough to address: no, they don't eat. Some can, in the same way you could try to taste something with your hands. The input registers. It doesn't nourish, and it rarely means what they want it to. Pain is similarly off-center.
Damage is perceived, but as a diagnostic rather than a sensation. A cracked limb is information, not agony. What passes for physical pleasure varies wildly by material. A Stone Graith left in direct sun will stay there for hours and offer no explanation.
I've met a glass Graith who swore warm baths are as close as one comes to heaven.
Cultural Traits:
Graith are solitary by default, and most spend long stretches alone without minding it. But they are definitely capable of developing emotionally, and often do. Especially when their purpose aligns with it.
A Graith built to handle diplomacy, tend to a household, or care for children will, over enough time, develop something indistinguishable from genuine feeling.
Whether it's a genuine expression of emotion or another tool for the job is a question both Graith and their loved ones usually don't bother asking. Luckily, there's everyone else to do that in their stead.
Actual Graith communities are unusual and a bit awkward. They form when a handful decide, more out of exhaustion than ideology, to sit down away from the meddling crowd and renegotiate what their mantras should mean.
The results vary: a few become tight-knit circles of companionship and mutual maintenance. Most, well, most don't. Living with Graith takes adjustment. There isn't much to bond around. They don't sleep, unless you count mending.
They don't eat, though some will sit at a table with you anyway. They develop habits, preferences, senses of humor. Over time, a Graith can feel as familiar as any person. Until a moment comes that abruptly reminds you otherwise.
Current Place in the World:
They're found across most of the continent, wherever the ancient Remosan empire had a foothold. Meaning, the further you go toward the outskirts of the continent, the less you'll see. Even in the center, their numbers are declining. Being a lost technology does that to a race.
What used to be a part of every city's landscape has remained a daily occurrence only in the empire's hard core.
Whether Graith are people is a question most of Virelia answers based on convenience. They are constructs, so the question is not trivial. What the softhearted might call bigotry is a philosophical position that I think is worth acknowledging.
When it is indeed a philosophical position, and not just fear. Graith that lose coherence are dangerous, that is an uncontested fact.
But fear should not be the motivator behind our judgement of what is considered human, or the Graith will end up the first on a very long list of exclusions.
To be blunt, most of it is financial. Acknowledging personhood means wages, and nobody wants that. The debate, such as it is, lives almost entirely in modern Remosa, where the dependency is too large to ignore and too expensive to acknowledge.
The Graith outside the empire's core have no debate to take sides in. Most carry on the way they always have, and the question of whether they count as people remains someone else's problem. Which, if nothing else, is a very human way to handle it.

Someone's solution to a problem

orrak.title: Orrak
orrak.text:
Orrak
Work in progress
Observations:
I've covered the Orrak presence in Remosa elsewhere in this volume, so I'll spare the repetition. What I find worth examining here is what that presence doesn't produce.
Any one of them could break you in half without breaking a sweat, and yet a population of them has never leveraged that fact into anything resembling a political demand. They hold the garrisons, they fight in our wars, they do the hauling, the building, the labor that breaks lesser frames.
And yet the better-paid posts go to humans. Not by law, mind you. By habit. A law can be repealed. A habit just sits there until enough people get killed.
The reasons are less dramatic than you'd expect. They're a race with no homeland, and with no political movements to fall back on. Combine that with a continent where everyone is struggling, and the resulting calculation is simple: you keep your head down.
Who has the energy for protest these days? Who will they even protest against? Social norms, history? Please. They see themselves as more "Remosan" or "Haldrithian" than Orrak. If only the sentiment was shared by the older races as well.
The body modification gets a great deal of attention, and I'll detail it in the sections that follow. For now I'll note one thing.
While one might be tempted to view it through a lens of self-expression, spirituality, or even a reclamation of their cruel upbringing, I think the true mechanism at work here is more bleak. When self-sovereignty is taken from one, the response is often to pretend that it exists elsewhere.
Some become tyrants, and some turn inwards to shape the one thing they are capable of changing. You see where this is going. Never ever say that to an Orrak though.
Origins:
"What's a bio-forge anyway", you might ask. This ancient tech is more advanced than anything our researchers are capable of today, which is not the compliment it sounds like. The forges have been inoperable for centuries now, but there are records. It's a tough read.
Apparently they took living orcs and altered them into something different enough to earn a new name. Tougher, smarter, less prone to violence, and above all, built to be modified. The empire adjusted its Orraks for whatever the assignment demanded. Bad air, restructured lungs.
Unstable footing, reinforced joints. Couldn't maintain supply lines for armor, so they grafted plating straight into the shoulders. It was field maintenance, not culture. The culture came later, when the Orraks started doing it to themselves.
Luckily the forges are no longer needed. They were born with a "full package" and are definitely capable of reproducing naturally. You'll find them across most of the continent at this point, though like the Graith, there are more of them the closer you get to the empire's old core.
Still manning garrisons, work crews and civic life. A portion deserted during the Fracture Wars. Small groups that split off, moved into the spaces between holdings, and scraped together a living on their own terms. Hunter-gatherers, mostly.
These are the Orrak tribes, and they're still out there, small and scattered. Most Orraks will never join one, but you can be sure they're thinking about it after a rough day at work. Rarely a plan. Often a comfort.
Appearance:
Standing between 2.1 and 2.4 meters tall, the Orrak are mountains of dense, red-brown muscle that dominate whatever space they walk into. Their skin is textured and thick.
Short horns grow from the upper forehead, curved or stubbed, and male Orraks often have lower tusks from the jaw as well. Pointed ears, heavy brow, dark hair, usually braided or cut short. The women are leaner and their faces are a touch more human-like. Still intense-looking though.
They grow quicker than humans and die considerably sooner. A fourteen-year-old is a man, and fifty is a respectable age. The decline, when it comes, is fast. A few years of rapid deterioration and then they're gone. There's no long twilight, an Orrak is functional until they aren't.
By adolescence most have started modifying. The specifics are covered below, but visually: scarification, geometric tattooing cut deep into the hide, metal bolted along the arms or across the shoulders, bone studs set into the brow ridge. The unmodified ones tend to be children.
Clothing is unremarkable. They dress like whoever they live among, with a preference for showing what they've done to themselves. I'd call it tacky if it wasn't so essential to their upbringing.
Cultural Traits:
An Orrak handles on their own the way you'd cut your own hair, but anything structural requires a specialist: jaw reconstruction, spinal reinforcement, organ work. Every Orrak community of any size has one. They aren't paid for the service, not directly anyway.
The community honors them, keeps them fed and supplied, materials are gathered collectively, and in return their people get modified. In a garrison, the specialist is part of the unit. In a tribe, they work with what the land provides. Refusing is not illegal. It's worse.
An unmodified adult is either making a statement about how they see themselves relative to the rest of their people, and it's not a flattering one, or they're simply the Orrak equivalent of someone who shows up to a formal dinner in their nightclothes. The charitable reading is eccentric.
The usual one is less kind.
Orrak children are raised by their families in civic settings and by the tribe where one exists. A fourteen-year-old is expected to work, fight if necessary, and should probably already have their first significant modification. Orraks don't fuss over their young the way we tend to.
The child is taught what it needs to survive, and then it's expected to do so. They speak less than most and have little patience for talk that doesn't go anywhere. This extends to academics, philosophy, extended debate.
The exceptions to the rule tend to be either very good at what they do or a bit odd. Often both.
When the decline starts, an Orrak knows. The body they've spent their life shaping stops cooperating. Joints stiffen, modifications begin to reject, and the deterioration accelerates in a way that leaves little room for dignity.
Most Orraks settle what needs settling, say what needs to be said, and end it alone on their own terms. It is not discussed at length among Orraks, and it is not mourned the way humans mourn, but there is something. A father sitting with his children for an evening longer than usual.
A packed bag by the door. A fitting end, I guess, for a race defined by complete control over their bodies.

duskwalker.title: Duskwalker
duskwalker.text:
Duskwalker
Close Enough
Observations:
What I have is anecdotes, a few secondhand accounts, and the uncomfortable fact that my usual method doesn't quite work here. Every other entry in this chapter describes a population. Duskwalkers are not a population.
They are too few, too scattered, and too varied in origin to share anything resembling an ancestry. I can describe the condition. I can relay what I've observed in the individuals who carry it. But a chapter on their culture would require them to have one.
I've personally spoken with two, and to people who've encountered a handful more, and in every case the Duskwalker was the least interesting party in the room. I don't mean that unkindly. The condition is truly unusual.
But the people carrying it were, in both cases, far less dramatic than the reactions they provoked. They're functional, direct. A tad too direct maybe. Perhaps it's unfamiliarity with communication, a result of the distance the living tend to take from them.
And maybe they've just got too much on their plate for pleasantries. Either way, in the face of their indifference, it is usually the living who are having a crisis. Reaching for words, looking at the ceiling, crossing the street.
People spend most of their lives either avoiding death, or avoiding thinking of death. Staring at it directly can get uncomfortable for many.
Interacting with one is a challenge I'd recommend to everyone and no one. The most mundane questions either have no answer or an answer that kills the conversation on the spot. "Where were you born?" "You mean originally, or the lab?" "Favorite food?" "I don't eat."
You adjust, try something neutral. The weather, maybe. You might get a minute or two of normal exchange before something reminds both of you that the usual basis for conversation isn't there. And then the questions that curiosity produces once the politeness wears off. Whether they dream.
Whether they still have to cut their toenails. What it feels like. Most people probably lack the tact to keep those to themselves. Now imagine doing this on every encounter, in every room, for what is potentially eternity for some Duskwalkers.
No wonder they don't much care for conversation.
Origins:
The common thread, best anyone can tell, is the soul. The connection between a soul and a body gets interrupted, then resumes wrong. How that happens varies, and the people who claim to understand the specifics tend to disagree with each other in ways that suggest none of them fully do.
A Rift sitting where life and death have gotten tangled can do it on its own. A specular cell with the right materials can force it. Grief and desperation have managed it under the right circumstances. The result, very rarely, and regardless of method, is a Duskwalker.
Most come from unstable Rifts. A tear opens where something died, or where the boundary was already thin, and whoever was nearby gets caught in it. What walks out the other side may carry fragments of a prior life or nothing at all. A name, a face they can't quite place.
Or just the body and no explanation for it. Whether the blank ones are old souls that lost the thread or something entirely new is an open question.
Butcher's Garden in central Remosa is the only stable Rift I'm familiar with that has consistently produced Duskwalkers, and the stories have given it a reputation for familial tragedy. Smart people avoid the place, and desperate ones come searching for even more despair.
What good can come of a mother carrying her dead infant to a garden pulsing meat? As with all rifts, randomness is guaranteed, and the results are very rarely what a mourning person would have hoped for.
Deliberate cases are rarer and harder to generalize. The work generally happens in back rooms and private studies. A parent who lost a child and found the wrong kind of knowledge. A mage who stumbled across a wandering soul and, for reasons that amount to loneliness, built it a body.
Amalgamists have seen limited success in assembling them from components... The methods vary. The results are similar enough that the distinction probably matters more to the people involved than to the Duskwalker.
Appearance:
Yes, they do look a bit like vampires. We can all stop dancing around the fact that when a person sees off-white skin and pale eyes, that's the first thing that comes to mind. Luckily, no fangs this time. But there are meaningful differences if you pay attention.
The skin is marbled and uneven, and it doesn't do what living skin does. No flush, no sweat. Eyes come in washed-out blues and whites. Hair goes white or loses color entirely, which is why most of them shave it. Draws less attention than a head of white in a room full of brown.
The ones made deliberately carry marks from the process, scarring or stitch-work, and the Rift-born tend to come out cleaner, for lack of a better word. They don't age. Three centuries in the same face without a single new crease. The connection doesn't always hold, though.
Like most magic, it's only as strong as its source, and not all of them were made well. When it loosens, eventually the soul drifts free and the body is left with no one in it.
They're very still. A living body is always doing something. Shifting, breathing. A Duskwalker at rest does nothing, which registers as wrong before you've worked out why.
The ones who care and got the talent for it can practice: they'll breathe, blink on a rhythm, and pass well enough in a crowd. Given enough make up, of course.
The body works, after a fashion. They can chew and swallow, but the taste comes back flat. Like chewing paper, is how one put it, and I can only assume it’s true. Most don't bother. Sleep is similar.
They need rest, and what that looks like, and in a way is, is a body lying still with its eyes open for four hours. Not a reassuring sight for anyone sharing a camp. Pain gets through, but dulled. The one thing that seems to work properly is temperature.
They run cold and know it, and warmth registers as comfort to some. Apparently, that's rare enough for them to remark on.
Cultural Traits:
They don't need much. No food, no sleep beyond a few hours of rest, no biological urgency of any kind. A Duskwalker with no obligations can simply exist. One account I came across described a Rift-born who spent several years just walking along rivers and observing the things around her.
She said it was quiet. Anyway, unlike the more "dead" ones, Duskwalkers who retained more of their prior life seem to have a harder time with the transition. They remember needing things: Carnal pleasures, companionship, purpose.
The needs may be gone, but the memory of having them isn't, and that gap is, by all accounts, worse than having nothing to compare to.
I'm not sure what it is with Duskwalkers and death, though I have my suspicions. The ones at peace with their condition and the ones still struggling with it both seem to end up in the same place eventually. Mortuary work, burial rites, necromancy, clergy.
The ones who don't engage with it professionally still seem drawn to it in their own time. I think it's familiarity more than fascination. The way someone who left a country young might still reach for books about it, not out of nostalgia exactly, it's more of a... recognizable texture.
This does not, as you might imagine, help with the social situation.

Most come from unstable Rifts. A tear opens where something died, or where the boundary was already thin, and whoever was nearby gets caught in it. What walks out the other side may carry fragments of a prior life or nothing at all. A name, a face they can't quite place.
Or just the body and no explanation for it. Whether the blank ones are old souls that lost the thread or something entirely new is an open question.

Butcher's Garden in central Remosa is the only stable Rift I'm familiar with that has consistently produced Duskwalkers, and the stories have given it a reputation for familial tragedy. Smart people avoid the place, and desperate ones come searching for even more despair.

What good can come of a mother carrying her dead infant to a garden pulsing meat? As with all rifts, randomness is guaranteed, and the results are very rarely what a mourning person would have hoped for.

Deliberate cases are rarer and harder to generalize. The work generally happens in back rooms and private studies. A parent who lost a child and found the wrong kind of knowledge. A mage who stumbled across a wandering soul and, for reasons that amount to loneliness, built it a body.

Amalgamists have seen limited success in assembling them from components... The methods vary. The results are similar enough that the distinction probably matters more to the people involved than to the Duskwalker.
Appearance:

Yes, they do look a bit like vampires. We can all stop dancing around the fact that when a person sees off-white skin and pale eyes, that's the first thing that comes to mind. Luckily, no fangs this time. But there are meaningful differences if you pay attention.

The skin is marbled and uneven, and it doesn't do what living skin does. No flush, no sweat. Eyes come in washed-out blues and whites. Hair goes white or loses color entirely, which is why most of them shave it. Draws less attention than a head of white in a room full of brown.

The ones made deliberately carry marks from the process, scarring or stitch-work, and the Rift-born tend to come out cleaner, for lack of a better word. They don't age. Three centuries in the same face without a single new crease. The connection doesn't always hold, though.
Like most magic, it's only as strong as its source, and not all of them were made well. When it loosens, eventually the soul drifts free and the body is left with no one in it.
They're very still. A living body is always doing something. Shifting, breathing. A Duskwalker at rest does nothing, which registers as wrong before you've worked out why.
The ones who care and got the talent for it can practice: they'll breathe, blink on a rhythm, and pass well enough in a crowd. Given enough make up, of course.
The body works, after a fashion. They can chew and swallow, but the taste comes back flat. Like chewing paper, is how one put it, and I can only assume it’s true. Most don't bother. Sleep is similar.

They need rest, and what that looks like, and in a way is, is a body lying still with its eyes open for four hours. Not a reassuring sight for anyone sharing a camp. Pain gets through, but dulled. The one thing that seems to work properly is temperature.
They run cold and know it, and warmth registers as comfort to some. Apparently, that's rare enough for them to remark on.
Cultural Traits:

They don't need much. No food, no sleep beyond a few hours of rest, no biological urgency of any kind. A Duskwalker with no obligations can simply exist. One account I came across described a Rift-born who spent several years just walking along rivers and observing the things around her.

She said it was quiet. Anyway, unlike the more "dead" ones, Duskwalkers who retained more of their prior life seem to have a harder time with the transition. They remember needing things: Carnal pleasures, companionship, purpose.
The needs may be gone, but the memory of having them isn't, and that gap is, by all accounts, worse than having nothing to compare to.

I'm not sure what it is with Duskwalkers and death, though I have my suspicions. The ones at peace with their condition and the ones still struggling with it both seem to end up in the same place eventually. Mortuary work, burial rites, necromancy, clergy.

The ones who don't engage with it professionally still seem drawn to it in their own time. I think it's familiarity more than fascination. The way someone who left a country young might still reach for books about it, not out of nostalgia exactly, it's more of a... recognizable texture.
This does not, as you might imagine, help with the social situation.

myrrkin.title: Myrrkin
myrrkin.text:
Myrrkin
Out of the frying pan and into the fire
Observations:
This is where I'd normally find my angle. I've been trying. The trouble is that a Myrrkin who crossed over in the first wave has very little in common with her granddaughter, born in Trefgann, who's never set foot in Myrr and considers the whole affair someone else's tragedy.
Between them: violence, coin, blandness, sex, poverty, cruelty, hunger, boredom, exploit, privacy, family, the concept of a lie. Loneliness. Pain is private here. The only way across is words, and words were never up to the task.
A century of adjustments I couldn't fit in a lifetime of work, let alone an introduction. The human experience, if you will excuse my sophistry. Anyway. Moving on.
The closest thing to a common thread I've found is privacy. I've written about Myrr and its relationship to Myrskov and I won't repeat myself, but the relevant fact is this: nothing was hidden there.
What you carried inside was what the world looked like around you, and everyone grew up with that as the only way things could work. The Myrrkin who crossed into Virelia discovered, among everything else, that other people have interiors you cannot see.
What follows from that is predictable enough. A human child works out deception around the age of three because the world requires it. Myrr didn't, and when the framework isn't there, the results are about what you'd expect.
I've heard enough accounts to know the pattern. But the ones who've been here long enough do learn, and some learn well enough that I'd caution against the assumption.
A Myrrkin who already understands inner experience from the ground up, and has then acquired the Virelian habit of concealing it, is working with a combination most of us lack. A reputation for sincerity, a sharp read on people's emotional strings, and the capacity for cruelty.
A minuscule minority, and we are probably fortunate that it is so.
Origins:
Leaving Myrr, as far as anyone's been able to explain it to me, was a matter of intention. You willed yourself elsewhere and you were elsewhere. One-way, though. Virelia's rules don't accommodate that kind of thinking, so once you're here, you're here.
Some chose to stay and slowly wilt along with what’s left of Myrr. The ones arriving now are the ones who finally ran out of reasons to justify this. Or there's always curiosity.
Whatever the reason is, they turn up near the edges of Myrskov, disoriented and, by more than one account, physically ill.
Why their bodies work here at all is a mystery even to them. Digestion, immune response, reproduction, sweat. In Myrr none of these operated the way they do here, if at all. Conception was conceptual rather than physical, and yes, I stand by that phrasing.
The competing positions are about what you'd expect: the biology was always present, dormant under Myrr's rules, and activated when those rules stopped applying. Or the crossing itself reshapes the body to match Virelian physics.
Or, and the Myrrkin lean toward this one, fey bodies simply adapt to local conditions because "whimsy". Nobody has won the argument, and the Myrrkin I've spoken with about it preferred to change the subject.
The practical fact is that they reproduce here, and have been doing so long enough that there are now three living generations in most established communities. The first are refugees who remember Myrr.
They know what they lost and their relationship to Virelia is that of a stranger, whether they arrived last century or last month. The second were born here.
They've been told what Myrr was and they understand, the way anyone understands a parent's grief over something they've never experienced. The third, where it exists, treats the subject the way most people treat ancestral history. Interesting at gatherings.
Otherwise, someone else's problem.
Cultural Traits:
The first thing that surprised me about newly arrived Myrrkin is that they're not miserable. I expected downtrodden refugees. What I got, at least initially, was something closer to a child at a fair. Everything is new. Rain is new. Markets are new. The taste of bread is new.
They want to touch everything, try everything, ask about everything. The ones I've spoken with in those early years had a breathless quality to them that I can only describe as exhausting. Give it a few years and the novelty wears thin and the harder adjustments settle in.
Then they get to be exhausted too.
Pair-bonding in the way humans do it doesn't come naturally to most. Partnerships are fluid, and the vocabulary for what counts as "family" is broad enough that I've given up trying to map it onto anything I recognize.
Those who stick to groups tend to live communally instead, children included. They also roam. "A halfling is just an undercooked Myrrkin", as they say.
New arrivals in particular can't seem to sit still, and it's a matter of luck whether they find that the world is their oyster or that they are its.
Appearance:
Tall, lean, dark-skinned with a sheen to it. Bronze is the closest comparison. Horns are usually spirals, and they wrap them in dyed thread, paint them, drip pigment. Very particular about this, touchy subject. Hair usually comes in metallic colors: gold, teal. Eyes dark or amber.
Clothing is all over the place. Whatever suits them at the day, as long as it's not trivial and reflects their mood at the time. Real fashionistas. Masks also come up a lot near Myrskov. Same reasoning, though it’s a bit much in my eyes.
First-generation crossers had to learn physical sensation from scratch, and I can't do that justice in a paragraph. Food came up first in every conversation I've had about it. Not the taste, though that was a lot to deal with. The demand.
Your body needs food, and if you don't feed it, it escalates. Having your own body issue ultimatums was, and I'm quoting, "offensive." I've met crossers who still eat like they're not sure it's going to work. Pain follows the same logic. It can't be argued with.
Sex is more complicated, but I'd prefer if you referred the question to a Myrrkin. What I will say is that they tend to be open minded about it, but that might just be a stereotype stemming from their family structure, or lack thereof.
Sleep, sweat, alcohol, drugs, and the whole catalogue of things a body does without consulting you, I swear, I'd need another volume.
They don't seem to grow old, but around the second century of their life, they start to go. The body loses definition, gets translucent. Takes a few years. By most accounts it's painless, though I'd note that nobody who's been through the whole thing has come back to file a report.
The Myrrkin believe what's left returns to Myrr, and they'd probably find my skepticism tiresome, but I've never been inclined to take anyone's afterlife claims at face value, theirs included. What's observable is that the body fades until there's nothing left.
Where it goes is a matter of faith. The aging crossers say they feel a pull, and seem to find this a comfort. Their grandchildren less so. Similar to our relationship with afterlife: it's something they've been told about, can't verify, and aren't eager to test.
It’s worth noting that despite that, when a Myrrkin dies before the fade, the body stays. It breaks, bleeds, rots like everything else. To them, this also means whatever was meant to return to Myrr never will. Truly dead, in a way the fading aren’t.
Faith can backfire just as hard, apparently.
Current Place in the World:
Myrskov is the obvious concentration. New arrivals are still coming through there, and the communities near Myrskov absorb them the way Myrrkin handle most things: communally, without much structure, and with the expectation that you help if you're nearby.
A disoriented Myrrkin stumbles out of the treeline and whoever's closest takes them in and explains what eating is. If you were unlucky enough to miss them and wander further out, the adjustment is considerably less gentle, and many end up feral.
Both in the Myrskov sense of the word, and in the regular one, for those who wandered past the communities entirely and found civilization on their own terms. Kelarra has a lot of them too, I think. I guess it suits their style, and it's nearby. That always helps. Beyond that, scattered.
You'll find a commune in an unexpected place now and then, but no cluster worth naming.
Individual Myrrkin turn up everywhere in small numbers. Pebbleclink Warbler Candlewax Dust Rice sits on the Haldrith Nonagon, in case you needed a demonstration of my earlier comment from the observations page.
This should tell you enough about how far integration has come, but just to be sure: you can find them in politics, trade, academics, and also in groups that aren’t shy about sullying their hands.
Which brings us to the unavoidable topic of their names. What most first-generation crossers land on is whatever caught their attention in those early dazzled years. A word they liked the sound of. A texture.
The color of something at a market, or a song a stranger was humming when they first walked into a town. Try asking one why she called herself "Cobweb Beebuzz Yeast Ceramiccup" and you'll quickly regret it. The later generations inherit or shorten these, or just go with Virelian names.
By the third generation most have something conventional with a Myrrkin name trailing behind it that we all collectively agree to ignore.

nirath.title: Nirath
nirath.text:
Nirath
Building Blocks
Observations:
My take, to much controversy, is that Nirathi are basically normal people. Put aside the spectacle, the reputation, and what you're left with is the somewhat underwhelming reality of a person who wakes up on one foot and then on the other. Same as anyone, really.
And where there's banality, there is religion, which, as always, is followed by controversy and a good measure of death. People dislike being told something is better than them. The very possibility, whether true or not, insults them. Now build a religion around that.
Tell a scattered few they carry shards of divinity inside them and the rest of us don't, and then let them notify everyone else of this fact. Our relationship to the divine, as a continent, has not exactly been a calm one. Eighteen centuries and counting.
You can assume how well the whole thing sits with people. This, by all accounts, does not work in their favor. A dry season comes, no god in sight to blame, but oh, there it is! They even admit to it! Well, if someone is to blame, surely it must be him.
The alternative is chaos, and we can't have that.
It's all so silly. People killing, dying, chasing meaning, all in the name of the stories we tell ourselves. Imagine a child of three. Barely learned to speak. His mind splits, along with his skin. His parents change overnight.
He hasn't yet learned the concept of friendship and already he is othered by most. Tell him there's a reason for it all. That he is divine, chosen. What child would refuse the notion? And at this point, true or not, Nirathi are as much the story they tell themselves as everyone else is.
Origins:
The condition surfaces in human children around age three or four. No other pattern anyone has managed to identify. The physical Mosaic appears first, followed within weeks by the Aspects. Three distinct Aspects, each with its own posture, aptitudes, and its way of approaching a problem.
The Convergence will tell you these are fragments of a shattered god, recycled between hosts across generations. The less poetic explanation is that the human mind, under conditions nobody fully understands, fractures along predictable lines.
Either way, the baseline self is continuous, which is the part most accounts get wrong. A Nirath doesn't disappear when an Aspect takes the lead. They're still there, drawn a certain way. Think of it as... emphasis, maybe. The same person with different parts turned up or down.
The three don't always agree. A Nirath can want contradictory things depending on which Aspect has the floor, and the negotiations are internal and, by most accounts, bellicose. The condition is permanent. No treatments. A few scholars study it.
A scattering of adult Nirathi can offer practical guidance if they're nearby, which they usually aren't. Some families adapt, some find the Convergence, some abandon. A child who develops the condition in a city has good odds, a child in a village that's never seen a Nirath, less so.
Reports on the existence of Nirathi go back as far as 1432 years ago, and since "The Epics of Leila" mentions one only in passing, we can only assume the phenomenon predates that year by a large margin. The Sundering is the current prevailing theory.
If reality can fracture randomly, then why not human psyche. But it is said that the absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, and eighteen centuries of war have left us few reliable archives. So it's possible the phenomenon predates the Sundering entirely.
An earlier mention might solve the riddle, and scholars have been looking for one as long as I've been alive. Other theories compete for the gap.
The Divine Residue crowd argues that leftover divine energy interacts with developing minds in ways nobody planned for, and the resemblance to what the Nirathi themselves claim is hard to miss. More on that shortly.
A smaller camp holds that the condition isn't magical at all, that the personality fractures are neurological and nothing else.
This, in my opinion, raises an obvious problem with consistency: always three, never two or five, and the archetypes repeat across Nirathi in ways coincidence struggles to explain. The proponents have answers for this, but I never much cared for them.
Appearance:
They age normally, which surprises people for some reason. Human lifespan, human decline, human death. The Convergence sees the body as a temporary host. They rebranded death to "Dispersion" and claim the Aspects return to the pool. The vessel goes in the ground like the rest of us.
Here is what bothers me about looking at one, and it took me years to put my finger on it. The skin is what everyone describes first. Cracked earth, patches of different tone meeting at sharp geometric seams with a faint metallic quality to them. Eyes mismatched, hair in patches.
You'd expect the sum of all that to be a mess, and it isn't. They're never ugly. The patches sit in balanced arrangements, the faces are symmetrical, everything is neatly organized in a way that human bodies generally aren't. A person who looks broken should look the part.
A Nirath looks assembled, carefully so, by someone with taste. I've spent a career not believing what the Convergence preaches, and I'll maintain that to my grave, but I'd be lying if I said the bodies don't make for a good argument. The ocean-blue robes the devout wear don't.
They're like monks, but with a different shade of self-deception.
One more thing: when an Aspect takes the lead, the seams flare for a moment and the body rearranges itself. New posture, the voice used differently, another way of carrying the hands. From the outside it reads like a practiced character switch. From the inside, who knows but the Nirathi.
Cultural Traits:
Paired Nirathi handle the condition better. That's not insight, just observable. The condition is isolating in a way that's hard to get across to someone who hasn't lived with it, because the isolation isn't physical. A Nirath has friends, family, colleagues.
But every one of those relationships runs across a gap of three Aspects, and most people don't have the patience for someone who was warm yesterday and curt today and quietly fixated on something unrelated tomorrow. Another Nirath doesn't need it explained.
The pairing, when it happens, is usually not deliberate. Two, three, four Nirathi in the same city, one hears about the other, they meet. What it becomes after that varies. The devout treat it as sacred, a step toward the Convergence's reassembly. Pardon, but again, more on that later.
The Alignment is the daily part most people hear about and most misunderstand. Each morning a Nirath settles which Aspect leads. It's a daily negotiation between their inner Aspects, followed by a vote, and some mornings the discussions can turn ugly.
An Aspect that suited yesterday's work might not suit today's, but it doesn't always step aside on request. A Nirath who can't resolve the Alignment is in for a rough day, and the people around them are in for a rougher one. The devout frame this as spiritual discipline.
The secular ones frame it as Tuesday. In practice the distinction matters less than it sounds. A devout Nirath and a secular one in the same room will agree on most things. The experience is similar, no matter how you frame it.
The Convergence, then, since I've been putting it off. The Convergence believe they're constructing a god. That's the bottom line. To a believer, the Aspects are fragments of what used to be a whole. Some Nirathi claim a normal pre-Sundering god, and others say it's something larger.
A being ingrained in the laws of our world which predates the known gods, who were merely one more of its creations. I've heard both pitches, and hope to not witness either version in my lifetime.
So, both agree that parts of this god have broken down along with Virelia, and that with enough time, the aspects will harmonize back into a divine whole. To them, the Alignment isn't settling who leads for the day. It's the daily work of harmonizing its fragments. A sacred negotiation.
Get it right, and you're a step closer to the goal, which is nothing short of reassembling the original god across every living Nirath. The pairing is part of this. Two Nirathi working in tandem, harmonizing six Aspects between them, advancing the project together.
Death is just another step. An opportunity for the aspects to find new hosts and continue the work elsewhere. There is no clergy, few texts, none of which are scripture, and no central authority deciding who is devout enough. The theology spreads by word of mouth more than anything.
Whether a Nirath learns it from a peer or a bigot is a matter of luck.
Current Place in the World:
They're found wherever humans are, in numbers too small to count as a demographic. No city has a Nirathi quarter, no region claims them. The versatility gets them hired.
A Nirath with the right Aspects can shift between skills that would normally require different specialists, and guilds and mercenary outfits figured this out early. A fighter who becomes a field medic after a night's rest is worth whatever discomfort comes with it.
So they fill necessary roles. Essential, even. And resented for it, the way anything essential is when it comes from someone you'd rather not need. The flexibility that makes them useful to a guild commander is the same trait a crowd remembers when the season turns.
A person who can be three things is impressive when you're paying and suspicious when you're competing for the same job.
The rest of the time they're ordinary, which is the part that makes the periodic violence so hard to predict. A Nirath who's been your neighbor for years, whose work you've relied on, whose children grew up with yours.
And then a rift opens or a harvest fails and the seams are all anyone sees. Long stretches of ordinary life, and then a week where that isn't, and then ordinary again and nobody mentions it. I feel like most Nirathi don't dwell on the violence much. They describe the return to normal.
That, apparently, is the harder adjustment.

My take, to much controversy, is that Nirathi are basically normal people. Put aside the spectacle, the reputation, and what you're left with is the somewhat underwhelming reality of a person who wakes up on one foot and then on the other. Same as anyone, really.

And where there's banality, there is religion, which, as always, is followed by controversy and a good measure of death. People dislike being told something is better than them. The very possibility, whether true or not, insults them. Now build a religion around that.

Tell a scattered few they carry shards of divinity inside them and the rest of us don't, and then let them notify everyone else of this fact. Our relationship to the divine, as a continent, has not exactly been a calm one. Eighteen centuries and counting.

You can assume how well the whole thing sits with people. This, by all accounts, does not work in their favor. A dry season comes, no god in sight to blame, but oh, there it is! They even admit to it! Well, if someone is to blame, surely it must be him.
The alternative is chaos, and we can't have that.

It's all so silly. People killing, dying, chasing meaning, all in the name of the stories we tell ourselves. Imagine a child of three. Barely learned to speak. His mind splits, along with his skin. His parents change overnight.

He hasn't yet learned the concept of friendship and already he is othered by most. Tell him there's a reason for it all. That he is divine, chosen. What child would refuse the notion? And at this point, true or not, Nirathi are as much the story they tell themselves as everyone else is.
Origins:

The condition surfaces in human children around age three or four. No other pattern anyone has managed to identify. The physical Mosaic appears first, followed within weeks by the Aspects. Three distinct Aspects, each with its own posture, aptitudes, and its way of approaching a problem.

The Convergence will tell you these are fragments of a shattered god, recycled between hosts across generations. The less poetic explanation is that the human mind, under conditions nobody fully understands, fractures along predictable lines.

Either way, the baseline self is continuous, which is the part most accounts get wrong. A Nirath doesn't disappear when an Aspect takes the lead. They're still there, drawn a certain way. Think of it as... emphasis, maybe. The same person with different parts turned up or down.

The three don't always agree. A Nirath can want contradictory things depending on which Aspect has the floor, and the negotiations are internal and, by most accounts, bellicose. The condition is permanent. No treatments. A few scholars study it.

A scattering of adult Nirathi can offer practical guidance if they're nearby, which they usually aren't. Some families adapt, some find the Convergence, some abandon. A child who develops the condition in a city has good odds, a child in a village that's never seen a Nirath, less so.

Reports on the existence of Nirathi go back as far as 1432 years ago, and since "The Epics of Leila" mentions one only in passing, we can only assume the phenomenon predates that year by a large margin. The Sundering is the current prevailing theory.

If reality can fracture randomly, then why not human psyche. But it is said that the absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence, and eighteen centuries of war have left us few reliable archives. So it's possible the phenomenon predates the Sundering entirely.
An earlier mention might solve the riddle, and scholars have been looking for one as long as I've been alive. Other theories compete for the gap.

The Divine Residue crowd argues that leftover divine energy interacts with developing minds in ways nobody planned for, and the resemblance to what the Nirathi themselves claim is hard to miss. More on that shortly.
A smaller camp holds that the condition isn't magical at all, that the personality fractures are neurological and nothing else.

This, in my opinion, raises an obvious problem with consistency: always three, never two or five, and the archetypes repeat across Nirathi in ways coincidence struggles to explain. The proponents have answers for this, but I never much cared for them.
Appearance:

They age normally, which surprises people for some reason. Human lifespan, human decline, human death. The Convergence sees the body as a temporary host. They rebranded death to "Dispersion" and claim the Aspects return to the pool. The vessel goes in the ground like the rest of us.

Here is what bothers me about looking at one, and it took me years to put my finger on it. The skin is what everyone describes first. Cracked earth, patches of different tone meeting at sharp geometric seams with a faint metallic quality to them. Eyes mismatched, hair in patches.

You'd expect the sum of all that to be a mess, and it isn't. They're never ugly. The patches sit in balanced arrangements, the faces are symmetrical, everything is neatly organized in a way that human bodies generally aren't. A person who looks broken should look the part.

A Nirath looks assembled, carefully so, by someone with taste. I've spent a career not believing what the Convergence preaches, and I'll maintain that to my grave, but I'd be lying if I said the bodies don't make for a good argument. The ocean-blue robes the devout wear don't.
They're like monks, but with a different shade of self-deception.

One more thing: when an Aspect takes the lead, the seams flare for a moment and the body rearranges itself. New posture, the voice used differently, another way of carrying the hands. From the outside it reads like a practiced character switch. From the inside, who knows but the Nirathi.
Cultural Traits:

Paired Nirathi handle the condition better. That's not insight, just observable. The condition is isolating in a way that's hard to get across to someone who hasn't lived with it, because the isolation isn't physical. A Nirath has friends, family, colleagues.

But every one of those relationships runs across a gap of three Aspects, and most people don't have the patience for someone who was warm yesterday and curt today and quietly fixated on something unrelated tomorrow. Another Nirath doesn't need it explained.

The pairing, when it happens, is usually not deliberate. Two, three, four Nirathi in the same city, one hears about the other, they meet. What it becomes after that varies. The devout treat it as sacred, a step toward the Convergence's reassembly. Pardon, but again, more on that later.

The Alignment is the daily part most people hear about and most misunderstand. Each morning a Nirath settles which Aspect leads. It's a daily negotiation between their inner Aspects, followed by a vote, and some mornings the discussions can turn ugly.

An Aspect that suited yesterday's work might not suit today's, but it doesn't always step aside on request. A Nirath who can't resolve the Alignment is in for a rough day, and the people around them are in for a rougher one. The devout frame this as spiritual discipline.

The secular ones frame it as Tuesday. In practice the distinction matters less than it sounds. A devout Nirath and a secular one in the same room will agree on most things. The experience is similar, no matter how you frame it.

The Convergence, then, since I've been putting it off. The Convergence believe they're constructing a god. That's the bottom line. To a believer, the Aspects are fragments of what used to be a whole. Some Nirathi claim a normal pre-Sundering god, and others say it's something larger.
A being ingrained in the laws of our world which predates the known gods, who were merely one more of its creations. I've heard both pitches, and hope to not witness either version in my lifetime.

So, both agree that parts of this god have broken down along with Virelia, and that with enough time, the aspects will harmonize back into a divine whole. To them, the Alignment isn't settling who leads for the day. It's the daily work of harmonizing its fragments. A sacred negotiation.

Get it right, and you're a step closer to the goal, which is nothing short of reassembling the original god across every living Nirath. The pairing is part of this. Two Nirathi working in tandem, harmonizing six Aspects between them, advancing the project together.

Death is just another step. An opportunity for the aspects to find new hosts and continue the work elsewhere. There is no clergy, few texts, none of which are scripture, and no central authority deciding who is devout enough. The theology spreads by word of mouth more than anything.
Whether a Nirath learns it from a peer or a bigot is a matter of luck.
Current Place in the World:
They're found wherever humans are, in numbers too small to count as a demographic. No city has a Nirathi quarter, no region claims them. The versatility gets them hired.

A Nirath with the right Aspects can shift between skills that would normally require different specialists, and guilds and mercenary outfits figured this out early. A fighter who becomes a field medic after a night's rest is worth whatever discomfort comes with it.

So they fill necessary roles. Essential, even. And resented for it, the way anything essential is when it comes from someone you'd rather not need. The flexibility that makes them useful to a guild commander is the same trait a crowd remembers when the season turns.
A person who can be three things is impressive when you're paying and suspicious when you're competing for the same job.

The rest of the time they're ordinary, which is the part that makes the periodic violence so hard to predict. A Nirath who's been your neighbor for years, whose work you've relied on, whose children grew up with yours.

And then a rift opens or a harvest fails and the seams are all anyone sees. Long stretches of ordinary life, and then a week where that isn't, and then ordinary again and nobody mentions it. I feel like most Nirathi don't dwell on the violence much. They describe the return to normal.
That, apparently, is the harder adjustment.

varn.title: Varn
varn.text:
Varn
In a sense
Observations:
Everyone seems to agree that Varn are fine and all, but they shouldn't have children. The condition is hereditary, after all, and the logic writes itself. Why pass it on? The potions shop noise keeping you up, the neighbor's Create Bonfire cantrip setting your teeth on edge for a week?
Don't reproduce. It doesn't matter the complaint. The answer is always in the blood. Always meant helpfully too, I'm told, which is apparently even more annoying.
I might be the only person on this continent who thinks of them as a separate race. To everyone else they're just people, crystals and all. Part of the room. A category would at least garner a response. Sometimes a negative one, but it at least gives one something to push against.
The Varn don't have that. No founding myth, no shared tradition, no cruel nemesis to point their finger at. Just a disease. Their problems stay personal because nobody, Varn included, has thought to make them a collective. A mage opens a workshop. The Varn next door can't sleep.
That's a dispute between neighbors. You can't expect us to sanitize the entire city, after all.
Few of the Varn are angry enough to be heading somewhere with it, but I think none of them could tell you where if you’ve asked. They can’t point at the mage and call him cruel. Nor can they point at anyone else, really.
The sound doesn't stop, though, and at some point "nobody is to blame" translates to some Varn as "everyone is". Well good luck changing that.
Origins:
Varn, in summary, are what happens when a humanoid is exposed to too much arcane energy in a short period of time. Sometimes the very same day, rarely, only a generation later. One way or other, once it sticks, it sticks. Descendants included. The Witch Wars provided plenty of that.
Entire villages were wiped, Varn being the only ones to rise from the ashes. Since today's wars are more modest in scale, these days Varn are mostly produced like the rest of us. On very rare occasions, rifts can produce new ones, but they might be better catalogued as Karex instead.
The question is completely out of my scope, if I'm to be honest.
We are familiar with their origins mostly thanks to "On Traumatogenic Pathogenesis", written 1491 years ago. Listed among other maladies which made an appearance at the time. As the book so romantically puts it: "...excess energy calcifies along existing nerve pathways.
The resulting crystalline formations bond to the periosteum and thread outward through the dermis. The lattice registers to the bearer as a persistent tightness comparable to a healing burn.
Once established, ambient arcane energy, even at concentrations negligible to an unaffected subject, feeds continuously into the structure and is perceived as pressure, vibration, or sharp pain in acute cases."
Fifteen centuries and that's still roughly the sum of what scholarship has to say about the experience. The only thing that changed is we've had enough generations to confirm that a Varn's child is a Varn. Always. Severity varies, but the condition itself passes without exception.
Appearance:
To quote "On Traumatogenic Pathogenesis" again, the growths favor "areas of high nerve density: the spine, the brow ridge, the inner forearm, the joints of the hands. The lattice is warm to the touch, faintly resonant under pressure..."
Beyond that, it's as varied as the range of one's misfortune. I've seen Varn whose crystals amounted to a thin ridge above the eyebrow. Barely visible with the right glasses. I've seen others who looked like something bigger than them was trying to come out of their bodies.
Clusters breaking through the skin along the shoulders and the back of the neck, heavy enough to affect posture, and expensive enough to outfit that a severe Varn's tailor bill would make a Haldrithian guild-master wince.
Most grow in shades of dark violet, though wine red, black, and on rare occasions pink have been documented. The crystals sense arcane energy the way skin senses heat, a second scale laid on top of everything else. Most describe it as bearable. Some find it unbearable.
A few, apparently, get a kick out of it. Always seemed odd to me. Though, I never understood people who were drawn to saunas also.
They age like whatever race they were originally, which brings me to something I probably should have mentioned sooner. The lattice corrupts the nervous system in ways that biology can't route around. A Varn elf sleeps. Full nights, like a human, dead to the world.
A Varn dwarf loses the dark. Same build, same face, can't see ten feet into the tunnel his healthy father works daily. The condition doesn't care what you were born as. It takes what it takes and leaves you something else. Not human, exactly. A Varn.
Come to think of it, that's probably why I put them in this chapter. A Varn dwarf has more in common with a Varn elf than with anyone in his own family, and neither of them has worked that out yet.
Cultural Traits:
A Varn in a quiet farming village with no enchantments and a hedge-witch who visits twice a year has it about as good as it gets. A Varn in Haldrith adjusts or leaves. Tintbent, Myrskov and Knotsreach are essentially off the table.
The spread follows the noise, more or less, and where you end up determines most of what your life looks like. Every Varn has to work out what magic is to them. Run from it, hate it, try to control it, learn to love it.
Indifference isn't on the menu, and I think that's why so many of them end up in magic-adjacent work. Not just because they're good at it, though they are, the weirdos. But I think the real reason is that they like it. It gives them a sense of control, or a purpose for the whole thing.
Better than the alternative, which is trying to ignore a sense you were born with.
Finding a partner is a related problem, now that I think about it. The crystals are physical, and not everyone wants to sleep next to warm and humming glass shrapnel. Some people find it exotic, which is its own problem, especially for Varn women.
You're looking for someone who neither fetishizes nor avoids the growths and also doesn't mind the hereditary issue. Narrow field. The quiet settlements up in the Kelarra peaks and on the edges of Molakar solve this by default, since everyone there has crystals and nobody's casting.
A few dozen families in the ones I've heard of. Strict places, but the people living there would tell you it's more than worth it. The other direction is harder to explain and a touch cultish, if I'm honest.
Small communes, mostly in the interior, where the Varn don't avoid the input but try to harmonize with it. Communal casting, set intervals, something between a ritual and a tuning exercise. They describe it the way a musician might describe an ensemble.
I'll take their word for it, and make sure to continue to avoid them.
One more thing I should touch on. Some Varn dabble in terror. To the benefit of everyone involved, the phenomenon is still marginal, and most governments would probably deny it altogether. But it is a traceable pattern that I, as well as some other researchers, have noticed.
A workshop torched here, a ward-stone vandalized there. Individual sentencing, paperwork filed, no connection drawn. The Varn who do it can't quite articulate what they're after. Unless you count "society is evil" an acceptable explanation.
The ones who don't would rather not be associated with the ones who do, which, given the Observations above, is an irony I'll leave for the reader. Maybe it's because of the small scale, but oddly, people haven't seemed to catch on to the fact that such cases share a pattern.
To them, it's a random arson, not an act of resistance. I say, give it a few years. Or quicker yet, a catalyst with a large enough body count. Then we'll have to recalibrate, and this paragraph will unfortunately no longer be topical.

karex.title: Karex
karex.text:
Karex
Landmade Men
Observations:
A Karex is a person who was somehow permanently affected by a Rift. I'll start there because it's about the only clean definition this entry is going to get. They share nothing else. Nothing. The word itself is a filing convenience, though a commonly used one.
I included them here because I wanted to write about them and there was nowhere else to put them. So there, it's your problem now. What makes them different from the other entries in this chapter is that every other race is safely not you. Nobody lies awake worried about becoming a Graith.
But a Rift can form anywhere with no warning. You might not even realize it's there until its effects bleed into you. Everyone knows at least one person who just woke up as a Karex one day, not even sure how and when it occurred. It colors everything.
A Karex who can read ancient texts gets attention that isn't quite respect. A Karex who eats gravel gets a distance that isn't quite cruelty. The same neighbor will pity one and envy the other and be disgusted by the third and never work out that all reactions come from the same place.
I've always felt they're the most fitting group to our troubled continent. Virelia comes in, Karex comes out. People who were quite literally bound with our land. Its essence, its breakage. I apologize for being a tad melodramatic here, but the metaphor is practically impossible to ignore.
It's all just so random, the same way everything in life is. You might be born with a sharp mind or a bad back. In Virelia, you might also stop reflecting light. The range is wider, the stakes are higher, but the principle is the same. Lastrago straps them to temple spires.
Molakar goes to war over them. The Weave pays well for the ones whose bodies have adapted to specific types of rifts. Whether any given Karex is a freak or a prophet depends entirely on where they ended up and what someone found to do with them.
And then there's the rest, the ones nobody found a use for. They get to serve no purpose, like the rest of us.
Origins:
To have any meaningful discussion about the origins of the Karex, I should start by explaining what a Rift is. Virelia's governing laws have diluted since the Sundering. While reality is mostly still intact, occasionally things slip. That's a rift. They can take many forms.
Endless, in fact. The Weave have made an attempt at a cataloging system, if you want to delve deeper into that. Point is, it's rarely simple. A rift can be conceptual, physical, temporal, sentient... You get the gist.
Some rifts engulf entire regions, while a tiny fracture might form at the exact point of pressure where a fireball is cast.
Which is how you get Karex. A person walks through one of these, or lives near one long enough, or was simply born in the wrong spot, and something sticks. It isn't hereditary, unlike the Varn. But plenty of mothers have tried to split the difference.
Live near the right rift at the right month, and maybe the child comes out special. Maybe it doesn't come out at all.
Any of the old races can become Karex. The newer ones seem to be exempt, though I'd hesitate to call that confirmed. But generally speaking, the anomaly sits on top, whether you’re a halfling or a half-orc. The dramatic cases are easy.
A mining crew hits a spatial rift, one of them walks out with a shadow that moves independently. A woman in Rivhalde stopped aging at forty. Her wife noticed before she did. She'd never been near a documented rift, but that's the point. You don't always know.
I swear half the adolescents on this continent have convinced themselves they're Karex at some point. A strange dream, a birthmark, a persistent cough, a feeling that you're different. The definition is wide enough that nobody can tell them they're wrong with any authority.
The actual Karex, the ones who eat rocks or whose breath comes out in colors, find this less amusing than everyone else does.
Appearance:
Yeah, I give up on that one.
Current Place in the World:
A Karex with a limb that doesn't match the rest of them is dealing with a different life than one with borrowed memories, and they both know it. The visible ones get stared at. The invisible ones get to wonder whether they should mention it on dates. Most don't.
I wouldn't call it "stigma," that would be too far. But they're usually the first to get bullied as kids, and even between them I've seen very little camaraderie. Despite them being roughly 5% of the population. And most Karex, to my surprise, seem to accept this.
Where you live matters too. Rift-adjacent towns have seen enough of this that a Karex is just another thing to work around. In Rivhalde, where the Compact pays to keep rifts shut, they're rarer and stranger for it. Even more so in Tavernash.
In Knotsreach, where the land itself barely follows the rules, they're part of the furniture. But a large share of almost nobody is still almost nobody.
With rare exceptions (Lastrago's infamous "zombies" incident comes to mind) the condition doesn't spread between people. That hasn't stopped anyone from treating certain Karex like it might.
The ones who glow, hum, or whose presence makes candles flicker tend to find themselves drinking alone more often than they'd like, regardless of whether any of it is actually contagious. The Weave recruits from exactly this crowd.
A body that already survived rift exposure has obvious professional value in an organization that walks into rifts for a living.
Whether they're hired out of respect or to keep them where they can be watched and studied is a question I've asked more than one agent, and the answer depends on how many drinks they've had.

Any of the old races can become Karex. The newer ones seem to be exempt, though I'd hesitate to call that confirmed. But generally speaking, the anomaly sits on top, whether you’re a halfling or a half-orc. The dramatic cases are easy.

A mining crew hits a spatial rift, one of them walks out with a shadow that moves independently. A woman in Rivhalde stopped aging at forty. Her wife noticed before she did. She'd never been near a documented rift, but that's the point. You don't always know.

I swear half the adolescents on this continent have convinced themselves they're Karex at some point. A strange dream, a birthmark, a persistent cough, a feeling that you're different. The definition is wide enough that nobody can tell them they're wrong with any authority.
The actual Karex, the ones who eat rocks or whose breath comes out in colors, find this less amusing than everyone else does.
Appearance:
Yeah, I give up on that one.
Current Place in the World:

A Karex with a limb that doesn't match the rest of them is dealing with a different life than one with borrowed memories, and they both know it. The visible ones get stared at. The invisible ones get to wonder whether they should mention it on dates. Most don't.

I wouldn't call it "stigma," that would be too far. But they're usually the first to get bullied as kids, and even between them I've seen very little camaraderie. Despite them being roughly 5% of the population. And most Karex, to my surprise, seem to accept this.

Where you live matters too. Rift-adjacent towns have seen enough of this that a Karex is just another thing to work around. In Rivhalde, where the Compact pays to keep rifts shut, they're rarer and stranger for it. Even more so in Tavernash.
In Knotsreach, where the land itself barely follows the rules, they're part of the furniture. But a large share of almost nobody is still almost nobody.
With rare exceptions (Lastrago's infamous "zombies" incident comes to mind) the condition doesn't spread between people. That hasn't stopped anyone from treating certain Karex like it might.

The ones who glow, hum, or whose presence makes candles flicker tend to find themselves drinking alone more often than they'd like, regardless of whether any of it is actually contagious. The Weave recruits from exactly this crowd.
A body that already survived rift exposure has obvious professional value in an organization that walks into rifts for a living.
Whether they're hired out of respect or to keep them where they can be watched and studied is a question I've asked more than one agent, and the answer depends on how many drinks they've had.

the_factions_of_virelia.title: The Factions of Virelia
the_factions_of_virelia.text:
The Factions of Virelia
Building a society from the refuse of the divine.
When the heavens went silent, the concept of "Divine Right" evaporated. There were no longer any gods to mandate who sat on the throne, and the blood of ancient lineages proved useless against the dissolving world.
In the vacuum left by the Sundering, the survivors looked for anyone who could keep their roof from collapsing.
The entities that rose to fill this void are not defined by borders, patriotism, or culture, but by the necessities they monopolize. The Greywater Compact turned peace into a subscription service, enforcing law only where the ledger balances.
To move gold and words across the broken lands requires paying the toll of the Halcyon League.
Even the end of the world has been commercialized; the Weave sells protection from the Rifts to the highest bidder, while the Speculars market the ultimate luxury to those who can no longer stand the noise: a new way of life, or a sweet, blissful silence.
For the common citizen, this shift has fundamentally altered the social contract. One no longer pledges allegiance to a faction, but signs a contract with them. The relationship is pragmatic and transactional. You are safe only as long as you are solvent.
This has created a geopolitical landscape that is fluid and ruthless. A city might be geographically located in the Remosan Empire, legally contracted to the Greywater Compact for police services, and reliant on the Halcyon League for its banking.
Sovereignty in Virelia is a tangled web of receipts and debts. A city might sit geographically in the Remosan empire, contract the Greywater compact for police, and bank through the Halcyons.
