the_weave.title: The Weave
the_weave.text:
The Weave
“Please lower your voice. We are not a charity, sir. If you cannot afford our services, then I'm afraid I'm going to have to ask you to leave. Try the city-watch.”
Hedda, receptionist, Drauheim office
The Business of Apocalypse
I can't fathom why their waiting-room chairs are so uncomfortable. Nobody wants to be in that room to begin with. The chairs feel like a second fee. Though I suppose it's consistent. Deal with rifts, take everything in return, bum comfort included.
Such is the Weave, the one organization on the continent that handles rifts, a fact they know precisely down to the copper. The testimonies I've collected over the years leave little doubt about their competence, and the Weave leaves little chance of hearing about the exceptions.
Whatever the success rate, most Virelians will never be able to afford them. Nearby rift or not.
The Mill
The Weave has holdings in most cities. Receive customers, mobilize teams. That sort of thing.
Their four main hubs are the Skyward Ledger in Eskahol, all polished mahogany and council chambers; the Knotsreach station, which does mostly research these days; Mirestead, where a man who reaches 32 is considered old; and Drauheim,
which handles most of the logistics of the whole thing but isn't flashy enough for the leadership to reside in.
Funny enough, the Weave's council reminds me of the Southfield one more than anything else. A bunch of Gold-ranked agents past their prime, pulled from the field with a pat on the back after proven to have at least some basic form of common sense.
The ones who don't outright refuse, that is. Plenty prefer the field and an early death to a desk. Those are the ones who turn Obsidian, eventually, if they last. The council handles what you'd expect. Hub appointments, resource allocation, the rare promotion past Gold.
They negotiate with governments, which they do from the position of people who know they'll be called back regardless of how the negotiation goes.
It mostly works, mainly because the people sitting on that council have all survived enough fieldwork to know what matters and what doesn't, and what doesn't is mainly politics and ego.
An Obsidian in the field will follow a directive when it suits the situation and ignore it otherwise, and the council quietly lets this happen because the alternative is not having Obsidians. With the Blacks there isn't even pretense.
You can't discipline someone when the act of disciplining them requires another Black or a whole group of Obsidians. These are some of the most dangerous people on the continent and I don't say that lightly. The council posts a directive. The Black reads it or doesn't.
If he does, the council mostly tries its best to stay out of his way.
Which brings me to the other end. A Tin recruit. Signs their contract without even being given entry to the hub building. The contract itself is three sentences.
The recruit accepts assignment to active rift operations at their Iron's discretion, the organization's liability in case of death is limited to a one-time payment to a named beneficiary, and the probationary period ends after three successful assignments. Successful, not survived.
A Tin who gets pulled out of a collapsed zone missing a leg hasn't completed the job, and has therefore failed to meet the terms of their contract.
It is a known fact, not a hidden one. But the Weave provides a scarce resource in return: an opportunity. A steady income, which can get hefty on the higher ranks. This temptation is what allows the intake desk at Drauheim to process signups the way a mill processes grain.
The line moves, the pen gets handed over, the name dries on the page before it's carved onto a grave. This should tell you exactly what the organization thinks a Tin is worth, and the answer is not much. Three jobs. Maybe half make Copper.
Mirestead is worse, but Mirestead is worse at everything.
If You Must
Rimilde Black started as a monster hunter, ordinary work, and somewhere along the line found she had a knack for a problem most hunters walked away from: rifts.
She took the jobs alone, charged what the client could survive paying, and handled things that had standing bounties older than she was. Villages pooled harvests to bring her in. A Trefgann garrison log records the officers covering her fee out of their own wages, twice.
Ottmar Helvik was chairing the Open Eye in those years, long before the guild's current Nonagon seat. His letters to her go back to 1677, 123 years ago. Rifts everywhere, with no real answer but one woman who insisted on working alone.
Helvik saw this as a proof of concept, but she denied his initial proposal. He wore her down for roughly a decade. Endless letters, until she reluctantly agreed to let him form the organization around her.
Then, in 1687, he finally left his seat, went to Eskahol, and built the aforementioned Skyward Ledger, the Weave's main headquarters. Once you know where he learned his trade the Weave stops being so mysterious. The catalogue, the archives, the contract language, the desks.
An intelligence guild's skeleton, put to a different use. He built the only kind of institution he knew how to build, and it turned out to be a natural pairing.
Now, a correction, if you'll allow me, since common belief has it backwards. Black was never a rank Rimilde held. His original system had ranks tin through gold. Rimilde Black refused a rank and Helvik wrote her surname as an exemption from the ladder.
Obsidian only shows up decades later, when a (loud) council meeting attempted to make the ranking system seem continuous despite the odd category. In general, my impression is that Black didn't particularly care for the whole thing.
She allowed Ottmar to use her name, and even survey some of her methods, but she never bothered with what she considered to be a bureaucratic chore. Though a profitable one. His letters show a level of admiration, though whether that's romantic or professional is above my qualification.
What I can confirm is that she did not seem to particularly like Ottmar. To quote one of her earlier letters: "a scrawny balding ape with more brains than smarts".
In 1714 she took a contract into the Wending and didn't come back. No body, even now. By 1719 the Weave hub at Knotsreach was constructed, officially research. Her retrieval contract is still open, since Helvik opened it himself and never signed an expiration date.
At this point, him being dead and all, it's mostly for appearances. Helvik ran the company another decade and died at his desk in 1724. His old guild reached the Nonagon six years later.
He never saw either institution at its full height, which I suspect would have bothered him less than we'd like to think.
The Art
What I've been able to piece together is roughly this. A crew arrives at the site. Before anyone touches anything, they spend what sounds like an unreasonable amount of time just standing around. Measuring. Walking the edges. Arguing.
They're building a classification string, which I'll get to. The point is that the assessment is not preparation for the work. The assessment is the work, because what you do with a rift depends entirely on what it is, and getting that wrong is often worse than doing nothing.
A spatial rift with a clean boundary and no secondary effects might be collapsed with a correctly placed displacement device. Bag of holding, in the cruder versions, though the Weave's equipment has apparently moved past that.
An anchored rift needs its anchor found and destroyed, which sounds simple until the anchor turns out to be an entire temple or somebody's baby. A rift with a cognitive layer requires the crew to work while actively doubting their own perception, which is exactly as reliable as it sounds.
And the ones classified as entities, the rifts that display something like will, sometimes require what one account generously described as "negotiating". Each combination in the notation points to a different method, different equipment, different expertise.
A crew trained to collapse spatial distortions is useless against a temporal loop, and sending them in anyway is how the Weave loses people. And it does. Higher ranks as well, despite what they'd want you to believe.
This is why the research apparatus exists. Not for scholarship. The Weave is not a university. But a century of fieldwork has taught them that the difference between a successful operation and a dead crew is usually a question someone answered in a library six months earlier.
What does this geometry do when you apply pressure to its anchor? Has this combination of properties been documented before? What happened last time? The archive is the product as much as the fieldwork is. Every field report feeds the catalogue.
Every catalogue entry makes the next crew slightly less likely to die. As I said, the man built what he knew. It turned out to be exactly what this work needed.
Expertise
I should add something to what I said about recruitment. The intake desk is the main pipeline, but it isn't the only one. The Weave actively scouts too, especially in dry spells. Prisons, orphanages, thrill seekers, border villages... anything goes.
Occasionally a Silver might spot a promising candidate in the field and send them to a hub, but these are rarer for obvious reasons. The few who are lucky enough to reach Gold and above are heavily invested in. Equipment, teachers, resources.
A Silver who dies is a big loss for the Weave, and they spend a lot to prevent that from happening. They are especially known for wielding equipment made of rift-produced materials. Whatever that means.
I also find that the higher-ranking agents carry themselves with this sort of... settled quality. Like someone who's made a private agreement with the concept of death. It can go many ways. Gallows humor, indifference, rigidness. Plenty of superstition as well, or so I'm told.
Anyway, they stand out. Especially Black agents. There are perhaps five or six alive at any given time, though the Weave keeps the actual number vague. From the records I've accessed I can only name one with confidence.
Isi Carphine is, by every account, one of the more accomplished mages alive. Her most recent book casually suggests she learned to stop time in order to properly document a persistent temporal rift.
She is described consistently as brilliant, obsessive, and entirely indifferent to anything that does not interest her, which includes most human concerns. The Weave points her at things, and she decides whether it's worth her time. That’s just one.
The Price
As you can imagine, having this sort of characters, in addition to a monopoly on rift knowledge and containment, doesn't garner the Weave a lot of love. They can't be replaced, and everyone has tried.
The Compact tried to tax their operations, and when that didn't work attempted to invest in their own Rift department, which famously collapsed three years down the line.
Remosa issued a decree some thirty years ago requiring Weave crews to operate under military oversight, and the Weave pulled out for six weeks before the empire gave in.
Even Haldrith has tried forcing the Weave to follow the guilds' protocols, and had to swallow their pride when the Weave outright refused.
A Weave hub in your city means your rift problem is someone else's and your sovereignty is slightly fictional, and most governments have decided this is an acceptable trade, if occasionally a pricey one. For the commoners it's a different story.
A rift opens near a farmstead, the village scrapes together what it can, the intake desk quotes the rate. If it isn't enough the messenger goes home and the rift does what rifts do.
This means agents sit in this weird spot where people either admire them, despise them, or both at the same time. A bit like how some men chase after a woman's skirt only to swear at her once she denies their advances.
People need them, want to be them, and will still spit at the floor as they pass by.
Rift Taxonomy
[Grade + Primary Type + (Secondary Types) – Size + Dynamics . Properties]
3S(TC)–3VW.SA
Severe. Primarily spatial, with temporal and cognitive elements. Room-sized. Volatile, wandering. Structured, anchored.
1
Intangible: no physical manifestation
2
Latent: dormant but present
3
Structured: follows clear patterns
4
Anchored: bound to object, person, or place
5
Concealed: undetectable until engaged
Entity: displays will, selfhood, or directed intent
Classification unconfirmed

greywater_compact.title: Greywater Compact
greywater_compact.text:
Greywater Compact
“Have you gone mad? A lienhunter? Don't you dare tell that to your da. Shameful, that. Have you already forgotten what they did to aunt Kellis?”
Overheard in Crosten
Make Ends Meet
I've already spoken at length about the Compact when discussing the Rivhalde region: its history, its methods. Here I'd like to do something else. I realize I've never quite shown you what the Compact looks like from the inside.
The view from outside is simple enough: tariffs, Lienhunters, permits, mundane cruelty. But institutions are more than the sum of their policies.
They're the architects of these policies, the bootlickers who surround them, and the ones who show up at your door when you don't follow them successfully. In short, they're people, with all the trouble that entails.
Soldiers of Fortune
Most Rivhaldeans end up meeting far more Lienhunters than Signatories. Bureaucrats always have a clear preference for papers over people, so it only makes sense that this part of the work was delegated. I think Lienhunters can be split into two groups, broadly. Disciplined, and crude.
Violence is expensive. Medicine isn't cheap, training replacements costs money, and a dead debtor's assets are often worth less than a cooperative one's. The smarter crews who understand this show up in numbers, break a few fingers, and leave with the goods before anyone gets brave.
They get to maintain a pretense of morals through the use of intimidation, implied force, and the knowledge that the last crew to visit this village wasn't so polite. It works, but only provided that last crew actually wasn't.
Which is where our second type comes in. The threat of our first type only holds if somebody, somewhere, is making good on it. The Compact, usually, doesn't technically require violence from its contractors, nor does it forbid it. What it requires is results.
Taxes paid, bounties collected. Crews that earn a reputation for brutality find that Sabots leave them alone, that doors open faster, that the technically-optional parts of the job get simpler. Crews that don't find the opposite.
The system doesn't openly reward cruelty, but it does seem to nudge in that way.
It's not a clean line, of course. But you'd be surprised just how careful Lienhunters are when it comes to their reputation. The more successful crews are recognized by name: "The Blueskulls", "The Lilies", "Grizzly Rats". This is where it gets interesting, so bear with me.
As I said previously, the Compact doesn't employ Lienhunters. It contracts them. A defaulted debt gets posted at the hub with the amount owed, the collection fee, and a list of the debtor's assessed assets so the crew knows what's worth taking before they saddle up. Licensed crews bid.
Sometimes more than one crew bids on the same posting, which drives the fee down, which is the Compact's favorite trick applied to its own dogs.
Whoever takes it goes hunting for results. In their own communities, I should mention. The crew that shows up at your neighbor's farm grew up three villages over. Which is the sort of tragedy that only the rich can come up with.
Young men and women from struggling taxed communities, choosing to cross over to the collection side for a chance to get a look at things from the outside for once. Plus, steady meals. At least until the results stop coming.
A crew that misses its quota loses its tier, and a crew that loses its tier takes worse postings at worse rates until the math stops working. After that it's back to the taxed side of the ledger, which everyone in the village already knows, and nobody forgives.
How It Began
You know the story about the two chickens? How two Remosan nobles decided to solve a land dispute by a competition, in which each sent a chicken on a journey to the edge of the forest, and the first chicken to arrive safely would win its master the forest's eastern edge?
The Compact's rise to power, from the inside, was a bit like that. Each merchant hired mercenaries, strategists, all in an attempt to keep their investments in the region safe. Skavorn's people guarded the granaries because Skavorn owned the granaries.
Hartlepp's sellswords cleared the roads because Hartlepp collected the tolls. While the sellswords bled for Rivhalde's future, the merchants who'd hired them were watching each other. A crew that cleared a stretch of road didn't just make it safe.
It made it Hartlepp's, and the families that moved slower found their neighbors had already taken the good parts. Everybody was saving their own piece of Rivhalde, and by the time they were done, they'd saved the whole thing by accident.
The bandit problem thinned out. The region settled into a quiet, undeclared anarchy where each merchant got to make his own rules in his own tiny kingdom. That lasted roughly eight years, until Orvhald Greywater got tired of paying to guard the same road three times.
The Greywaters were the most influential merchant family at the time, followed by Kelharn and Breskir.
Orvhald proposed the Compact, which, in short, stated that each signatory keeps the territory it had already secured, formalized as a revenue suite: the tolls and collection rights inside it, bundled and heritable, with a Board seat attached.
That all signatories adhere to a shared constitution covering maintenance of shared infrastructure: roads, patrols, Weave services, sewage.
And that disputes between suites go to arbitration by the other signatories, which in practice means disputes go to whoever has the most allies on the Board.
The politics of the signing were about as generous as you'd expect. The Greywaters had spent the most and claimed the most, and after Kelharn and Breskir followed suit, nobody was in a position to argue. Their chicken had already reached the forest's edge. The signing just wrote it down.
Families that had moved too slowly or hired too cheaply found themselves with minor suites and minor seats. At least two names from the original signing aren't on the current Board at all, bought out or squeezed into irrelevance within the first generation.
In retrospect, the whole thing looks less like a demonstration of governance and more like a group of bandits splitting the loot.
How It Goes
Four generations on, the Greywaters are still on the Board, though some would say in name only. When Remosa's second march cut the Heartland Sea trade route, half their revenue disappeared overnight.
The family never successfully pivoted, and nowadays have just enough to keep the seat and not enough to matter.
Kelharn and Breskir have been quietly acquiring Greywater contracts for the better part of a decade, and the only thing preventing an outright carve-up is that neither wants the other to get the bigger piece. That, and the Compact.
Hard to overtake the one whose name is stamped on the top of your government system. In general, most families' competence seems to deteriorate with each passing generation. Spoiled, prideful children, standing on the shoulders of their long gone forefathers.
Rivhaldeans often show pride in their heritage. Overthrew the empire, overthrew nobility, braved the bandits. Free folk, with their own land and their own laws. Right before a signatory who never so much as touched a sickle comes to take their due.
For all their contempt, Rivhalde is very much a monarchy. Try telling them that, though.
Bigger Fish
Tessmund is a riddle to me. The man is sharp. Witty, barbed, pragmatic. The letters I've read show someone who sees the Board clearly, comments on its workings with genuine intelligence, and then does nothing. He seconds Halverd's insulting proposals.
He signs what Brenst puts in front of him. He attends every session, which he doesn't have to, and contributes almost nothing, which he also doesn't have to. I've considered that he might simply be lazy, but lazy men rarely leave this much paperwork behind.
My best guess, and it is a guess, is that Tessmund has decided the chair is worth more occupied than fought over, and a head is worth more on a pair of shoulders.
I think he realized that the moment he starts acting like the name on the charter, he becomes a problem two wealthier families will solve together instead of competing over separately.
The Board protocols from last year's winter session paint a familiar enough picture. Forty pages, eleven seats, and only the big six still bother attending in person. The minor families sent proxies, which tells you how seriously they take it.
Though the six are truthfully down to five: Orsk Skavorn has sent his steward for the third session running, and nothing in the protocols suggests anyone found this worth remarking on.
The steward, Feskren, voted with Halverd on everything, because everybody votes with Halverd, especially those in bed with him. The man is charming, well-liked, apparently handsome, and seemingly incapable of staying out of married couples' homes. None of which has cost him a vote yet.
He delegates his suite to people who are less charming and more competent, and it works fine. He drank, and this was noted in the protocol because the Board was billed for it, eleven glasses of wine in the second session.
Brenst Breskir proposed three new acquisitions at the same session, all former Greywater contracts, and nobody objected because nobody bothers arguing when Brenst wants to buy something. The man collects as if he'll get to keep it all after he's dead: books, paintings, rings, contracts.
His accountant is probably the most stressed person in Virelia, which sets quite a high bar. Between the two of them, they account for most of the Board's substance, and the protocols show no disagreement on anything that mattered.
Drelm Hartlepp showed up, spoke once about a road in his suite, and left before the session ended. This is governance in Rivhalde. What baffles me is that it works. Not the Board. The Board is a circus of inheritance and appetite.
But somewhere between Halverd's wine bill and Brenst's latest acquisition, a layer of assessors and clerks translates all of it into a tax system more sophisticated than anything I've seen outside an imperial capital. The roads stay paved. The grain moves. The Weave gets paid.
I keep looking for the part where the rot at the top should have ruined the machinery underneath, and it's there if you look closely, but somehow stays hidden if you only slightly avert your gaze.

“Have you gone mad? A lienhunter? Don't you dare tell that to your da. Shameful, that. Have you already forgotten what they did to aunt Kellis?”
Overheard in Crosten
Make Ends Meet

I've already spoken at length about the Compact when discussing the Rivhalde region: its history, its methods. Here I'd like to do something else. I realize I've never quite shown you what the Compact looks like from the inside.
The view from outside is simple enough: tariffs, Lienhunters, permits, mundane cruelty. But institutions are more than the sum of their policies.

They're the architects of these policies, the bootlickers who surround them, and the ones who show up at your door when you don't follow them successfully. In short, they're people, with all the trouble that entails.
Soldiers of Fortune

Most Rivhaldeans end up meeting far more Lienhunters than Signatories. Bureaucrats always have a clear preference for papers over people, so it only makes sense that this part of the work was delegated. I think Lienhunters can be split into two groups, broadly. Disciplined, and crude.

Violence is expensive. Medicine isn't cheap, training replacements costs money, and a dead debtor's assets are often worth less than a cooperative one's. The smarter crews who understand this show up in numbers, break a few fingers, and leave with the goods before anyone gets brave.

They get to maintain a pretense of morals through the use of intimidation, implied force, and the knowledge that the last crew to visit this village wasn't so polite. It works, but only provided that last crew actually wasn't.

Which is where our second type comes in. The threat of our first type only holds if somebody, somewhere, is making good on it. The Compact, usually, doesn't technically require violence from its contractors, nor does it forbid it. What it requires is results.

Taxes paid, bounties collected. Crews that earn a reputation for brutality find that Sabots leave them alone, that doors open faster, that the technically-optional parts of the job get simpler. Crews that don't find the opposite.
The system doesn't openly reward cruelty, but it does seem to nudge in that way.

the_zwigots.title: The Zwigots
the_zwigots.text:
The Zwigots
“Receive him, for he is neither stranger nor guest. He comes as water rains on a river from which it first came. Let him return. Let nothing of him be called unclean. Consume him slowly, savor every bite. Until one becomes all and all becomes none.”
Zwigoti prayer for the departed
Due Disclosure
I've made arrangements for my burial, and a Zwigot will not be handling it. I want that said before I write anything else about them, because the rest of this chapter is going to sound more generous than I feel, and I'd rather not be mistaken for a sympathiser.
The largest religious movement on the continent, present in most cities, uncontested everywhere except Lastrago, which I'll get to later.
It would seem that, gods or not, people have to believe in something, and on a continent with this much rot, it only makes sense that somebody would build a religion around it.
Prophet Beltzu did, and fourteen centuries later his monks handle the dead in villages that couldn't name a single line from his book. How disappointing. How practical.
More Cults
Beltzu was a Mazuren priest, ordained in the year 342, some 1458 years ago. And like the other priests, he was a Karex, taken from his family in Naktzu to be strapped to a spire in Azwighen. Before that it's the usual ladder: years of tutelage underground tasting water out of stone pools.
And then work. He was rather successful for about a decade or so. Not in an extraordinary kind of way, but well enough to make a name for himself. However, in 351 he read an entire season wrong.
Three readings one after another, resulting in a documented total of 169 people missing or dead. He was offered the spire a second time, and chose exile instead. He then marched west onto Trefgann, and that's where the temple's account of him ends.
What remains from his later endeavors survived through the Tzikhari. A few hundred sayings, most of them shorter than this sentence, collected by people who'd heard them secondhand and written down well after he was dead. No biography in it.
No argument either, which irritates me to no end. You've already bothered to write it all down, might as well take the extra step and leave a paragraph where he explains his own words. Instead we're left with these maxims, followed by fourteen centuries of monks arguing.
Novices memorize the whole collection while they're young, and spend the rest of their life disagreeing about it with whoever sits across the table. An obvious influence from the Mazuren.
Priests were publicly disputing forecasts long before Beltzu was born, and we can safely assume the habit travelled west alongside him.
Words And Their Meanings
Fittingly, as the prophet's original intentions eroded, so did the name. Zwigot, or Tzigot in the oldest of sources. Then Zhigot by the time Remosan clerks had to file it, and lastly: our very own Zwigot, which is a word in no language anyone has been able to point me at.
Experts in ancient Lastragan claim the original meant something close to "not fearful," but I'm afraid I can't confirm that with any confidence.
The Tzikhari has gone through many translations, which eroded the enigmatic original even more. I'll give you an example. "Chabol zeb komak tzi-ot", commonly translated: "eat what is put in front of you". But this is merely one interpretation. Komak also means sits. Stays. Remains.
You see, several ways to translate, and then several more to interpret each translation. "Chabol zeb komak tzi-ot". Four words, and they can't even agree whether it's about food. One reads: the thing is there, you eat it, and the eating is the whole of the acceptance.
Another takes it nearer to remains, as in leftovers, as in what the world has already finished with, and that's the reading that ends with a monk face down in mud and human flesh.
The third holds that the sentence is about food and nothing else, and is popular among parents who wish their kids would eat more turnip. Underneath all three sits the same core claim. There is one substance. Not gods, not laws. One substance, and everything is it.
To the Zwigot mind, the Sundering didn't split the world, and the world is not, in fact, being broken apart. Because one substance can't be broken down into anything but the same substance. A rift is the world doing what the world does: recycling.
So is rot, and so is the child whose shadow walks off on its own. The only thing that has actually happened in eighteen centuries is that people insisted on struggling against the obvious, clinging to a world that only wants to be remade.
Which brings us back to Lastrago, since I said I would. The Mazuren looked at the same sky and built an apparatus for getting out from under it. A priesthood whose entire function is telling you when it's time to leave. Beltzu's answer to the same phenomenon was that running is wrong.
People, like the Mazuren themselves, ought to accept the Mazurat. Death and all. You can see why Azwighen preferred him elsewhere. Two religions out of one storm, and fourteen centuries on they're still the only declared two on this continent.
Monks And Priests
I've mentioned that Beltzu chose exile over a second drowning. An important caveat to that is that this is the Mazuren version of events, and also the widely accepted one. The Zwigots think differently.
In one of their better known legends, Beltzu never made an incorrect reading, and was scorned by the Mazuren for his success, and for gathering a following that contradicted their teachings. So they put him to the drowning meaning to kill him, and he survived it.
They did it again, and again, for a year, before accepting that the man was beyond death and exiling him instead, before he could be taken for a martyr.
It's the same trick every priesthood pulls on its founder's worst day, and I'd have more patience for it if the Mazuren version didn't have 169 names attached. Which leads me to an obvious point. The two religions don't get along. Who would have thought.
Zwigots are banned from entering Lastrago, and I can't tell you when that started. The temple records treat the prohibition as something that was always true, which in my experience means somebody lost an argument nobody wanted written down. Anyway.
A Zwigot found in a Lastragan village is most likely beaten to death, and then hanged regardless. There are more such cases than I care to list. And should one reach Mazuren hands, as a mockery of their legend, they'll be put to the spire repeatedly until they perish.
What's amusing about the whole thing is that the Zwigots believe this to be a great honor. Retelling the story, becoming one with nature, that sort of thing. Every year some make the journey in hiding, only to reveal themselves to the priests in order to go through the ceremony.
Their brethren will then call them saints. I'd use a different word.
Ashes To Ashes
I'd be surprised if one villager in a thousand could tell you a line from the Tzikhari beyond the ones that have turned into proverbs. It boggles my mind how people just accept the monks on face value: weddings, funerals... Especially funerals. The obvious reason, as always, is practical.
Nobody wants to handle a body that sat outside for three days during summer. And here comes one who would not only do that, but would also only charge you just enough to cover the pyre and a meal or two. But still, the commoners seem so eager to declare one a holy man.
Smear your face with the ashes of the dead, maybe eat some if you're a traditionalist, and there you go - thou art sacred. At least the same can't be said about my peers, thank fuck. Most academics see the Zwigots for what they are. A death cult.
A popular and widely accepted one, but a death cult nonetheless. Their ceremonies are proof enough. While they claim all matter is the same, they seem to revere only the type which disgusts everyone else. They'd claim it is a demonstration of faith, but I see it for what it is.
Showmanship. An attempt to convince the gullible that there is more to them than meets the eye.
A combination of all the above is how they spread. What started as a single temple in Imellah, on the outskirts of Trefgann, spread to the whole region within two generations. The centuries between that and now are harder to trace.
Nobody thought to document a religion that was mostly tolerated and occasionally useful, and by the time anyone noticed it warranted a chapter, the temples were already everywhere. Lastrago excluded.
Governments tolerate their oddities for their free services, and for giving the masses' heads something to play around with which isn't their mandate. The temples are mostly self sufficient: gardening, cooking. It's a simple lifestyle.
They spend most of their time copying books, arguing over the Tzikhari, meditating, and occasionally ceremonial work for the locals. They barely mingle. People are impressed with a monk who's willing to wear their aunt's ashes on their face, but they wouldn't exactly invite him to dinner.
They're still expanding despite that, mostly due to their policy of acceptance. Orphans, Karex, the poor, whoever nobody else wanted. People leave them at the temple door knowing they'll be taken care of for life.
The children learn Old Lastragan before common, in some cases, and are given Lastragan names. They are then expected to recite the Tzikhari by heart. Fail to do so, and you'll be thrown out eventually, which is exactly why most succeed.
The banished are left with no trade, no connections, not even a name.
Modern Lastrago considers the old tongue dead, but the Zwigots speak it freely.
I can't read it myself, which is worth admitting, because it means every Tzikhari translation I've complained about in these pages was made by outsiders working from whatever leaked out of the houses over the centuries.
Which reminds me, Beltzu ends in -u, which is a woman's ending in Old Lastragan. Nobody I've asked has had an explanation, but I do think it’s worth pointing out. The monks have argued about this to no end, but in neither of their conclusions is he a woman.
Lost And Found
The Zwigots say Beltzu kept walking west all the way to Knotsreach, and into the Wending, where he is still alive, frozen in meditation, with his tomb built around him. Which, assuming it's real, is what the grand temple of Tzubilek was built around.
Conveniently, nobody outside the order has ever seen the place. It is the seat of the Mukek, "The Caretaker," and reaching it is the doctrine made literal. You walk into the Wending and "Tobol kan, motol ot" - trust the path to deliver you.
When a Mukek dies, the senior houses each send a candidate, and the first to arrive at Tzubilek is declared the next one. A test of faith. To my eyes, the Wending has no opinion on theology, but I don't make the rules, so here we are.
The current Mukek is Chimek, who has been at Tzubilek for some forty years with a handful of monks who made the walk alongside him.
His rulings on the Tzikhari have a reputation I can't personally verify, but the abbots I've pressed on the matter were respectful in a way that suggests he amounts to more than his title.
He settles disputed readings, rules on the correct form for ceremonies, and decides what counts as heresy. He is also dying. I have this from three separate sources in Luznica, though none of them seemed particularly interested in discussing what comes next.
Which brings me to Luznica, where the senior abbot of the local house serves as Ozbekem, "the one who reads on behalf of."
In practice, this means he opens Chimek's correspondence, receives visiting abbots, certifies new houses, and relays the Mukek's rulings whenever they make it out of the Wending. The mundane stuff, in short.
The current Ozbekem is Kanteb, who has held the position for about fifteen years, and who has spent most of those fifteen years answering questions that should be going to Chimek. Not out of ambition. Oh no, he wouldn't dare.
But only because a letter to Tzubilek takes weeks and a ruling takes longer, and the abbot standing in front of Kanteb's desk needs an answer before his village buries someone wrong. So Kanteb answers, carefully, always noting that the Mukek may rule differently.
The Mukek rarely does, partly because Kanteb is cautious enough to stay within safe readings, and partly because for all I know he might as well be dead.
Kanteb doesn't touch political matters, and Chimek can't, and between the two of them the religion has no position on anything outside the Tzikhari. This has suited everyone for fourteen centuries. What concerns me is arithmetic.
The largest religious movement on the continent, present in most villages, handling every birth and death and wedding that matters to ordinary people, and the only thing keeping it out of politics is a dying man in a forest and a cautious abbot who knows better.
Chimek's successor will be chosen by the Wending, and the Wending will produce a scholar.
But the next Ozbekem is just an appointment, and there is nothing in the structure preventing an abbot with ambitions from taking that desk in Luznica and deciding the correspondence is worth answering. Danilo Pescarin was a Remosan nobleman last year. He's an abbot now.
Anyway, when that finally happens, and I'd bet my library that it will in the coming decade, the Zwigots won't be entering politics. They'll be discovering they were already in it.
Rebirth
The Midwives are harder to talk about, mostly because nobody in the houses wants to talk about them. If the world is one substance remaking itself, and the correct response is acceptance, then the question somebody was always going to ask is why stop at acceptance. A rift recycles.
The Green Wall holds back the Mire. One of these, according to the doctrine, is interference. The Midwives want to correct that.
Their literature circulates inside the houses the way these things always do. Copied pages tucked into commentaries, citations disguised as orthodox disputation, arguments that read as hypothetical until you notice they aren't.
I've seen one piece, a six-page tract in translation, and the theology is sound enough that I understood immediately why the Mukek banned it. It doesn't contradict the Tzikhari. It extends it.
The difference between eating a corpse and dismantling the Green Wall, according to the author, is squeamishness, not principle. The mainstream position is that one is acceptance and the other is interference, and the tract asks, politely and at length, where exactly the boundary sits.
The worst incident I'm aware of was in Ezgarin, 1784. Three monks arrested inside the Green Wall buffer zone by an Iron Perimeter patrol. What they were doing there the Remosan report doesn't specify, though the location speaks clearly enough. Two were hanged.
The third, a woman named Idra Chenne, was not recovered. The disavowal from Luznica arrived within the month. One page. Kanteb's predecessor, presumably, though it isn't signed. The Zwigot position, it argues, is that there is no self apart from the substance.
A monk eating a corpse is not doing something to the world. He is the world, consuming itself. The Midwives, the moment they decided the Green Wall should come down, placed themselves outside the process. An agent, acting on the substance, directing it.
Which is the Mazuren error rebuilt from the other end. The priests flee the storm. The Zwigots withstand it. Tobol kan, motol ot. That's what the page says.
What it doesn't say is that the Zwigots survive on tolerance, and that a religion associated with sabotage and dead Weave agents would not survive very long at all.
The Mukek declared the Midwives heretical, and the houses strip the name from any monk found distributing the literature. This has not, as far as I can tell, done much.
The arguments still circulate, probably because a disputation-based religion has a very hard time telling its monks to stop thinking about something.
Ancient Lastragan
Pronunciation
Tz as in "cats" Ch hard, as in "check" X "sh" (Nabixa = nah-BEE-sha) Stress penultimate
Names
Names are modular: root + ending. Two syllables is common, three is formal. It should sound like a rock hitting another rock.
Vocabulary
Word order: verb first, then subject, then object. Subject drops when obvious from context.
From the Tzikhari

Prophet Beltzu did, and fourteen centuries later his monks handle the dead in villages that couldn't name a single line from his book. How disappointing. How practical.
More Cults

Beltzu was a Mazuren priest, ordained in the year 342, some 1458 years ago. And like the other priests, he was a Karex, taken from his family in Naktzu to be strapped to a spire in Azwighen. Before that it's the usual ladder: years of tutelage underground tasting water out of stone pools.
And then work. He was rather successful for about a decade or so. Not in an extraordinary kind of way, but well enough to make a name for himself. However, in 351 he read an entire season wrong.

Three readings one after another, resulting in a documented total of 169 people missing or dead. He was offered the spire a second time, and chose exile instead. He then marched west onto Trefgann, and that's where the temple's account of him ends.

What remains from his later endeavors survived through the Tzikhari. A few hundred sayings, most of them shorter than this sentence, collected by people who'd heard them secondhand and written down well after he was dead. No biography in it.

No argument either, which irritates me to no end. You've already bothered to write it all down, might as well take the extra step and leave a paragraph where he explains his own words. Instead we're left with these maxims, followed by fourteen centuries of monks arguing.
Novices memorize the whole collection while they're young, and spend the rest of their life disagreeing about it with whoever sits across the table. An obvious influence from the Mazuren.
Priests were publicly disputing forecasts long before Beltzu was born, and we can safely assume the habit travelled west alongside him.
Words And Their Meanings

Fittingly, as the prophet's original intentions eroded, so did the name. Zwigot, or Tzigot in the oldest of sources. Then Zhigot by the time Remosan clerks had to file it, and lastly: our very own Zwigot, which is a word in no language anyone has been able to point me at.
Experts in ancient Lastragan claim the original meant something close to "not fearful," but I'm afraid I can't confirm that with any confidence.

The Tzikhari has gone through many translations, which eroded the enigmatic original even more. I'll give you an example. "Chabol zeb komak tzi-ot", commonly translated: "eat what is put in front of you". But this is merely one interpretation. Komak also means sits. Stays. Remains.

You see, several ways to translate, and then several more to interpret each translation. "Chabol zeb komak tzi-ot". Four words, and they can't even agree whether it's about food. One reads: the thing is there, you eat it, and the eating is the whole of the acceptance.
Another takes it nearer to remains, as in leftovers, as in what the world has already finished with, and that's the reading that ends with a monk face down in mud and human flesh.

The third holds that the sentence is about food and nothing else, and is popular among parents who wish their kids would eat more turnip. Underneath all three sits the same core claim. There is one substance. Not gods, not laws. One substance, and everything is it.

To the Zwigot mind, the Sundering didn't split the world, and the world is not, in fact, being broken apart. Because one substance can't be broken down into anything but the same substance. A rift is the world doing what the world does: recycling.

So is rot, and so is the child whose shadow walks off on its own. The only thing that has actually happened in eighteen centuries is that people insisted on struggling against the obvious, clinging to a world that only wants to be remade.

Which brings us back to Lastrago, since I said I would. The Mazuren looked at the same sky and built an apparatus for getting out from under it. A priesthood whose entire function is telling you when it's time to leave. Beltzu's answer to the same phenomenon was that running is wrong.

People, like the Mazuren themselves, ought to accept the Mazurat. Death and all. You can see why Azwighen preferred him elsewhere. Two religions out of one storm, and fourteen centuries on they're still the only declared two on this continent.
Monks And Priests

I've mentioned that Beltzu chose exile over a second drowning. An important caveat to that is that this is the Mazuren version of events, and also the widely accepted one. The Zwigots think differently.

In one of their better known legends, Beltzu never made an incorrect reading, and was scorned by the Mazuren for his success, and for gathering a following that contradicted their teachings. So they put him to the drowning meaning to kill him, and he survived it.
They did it again, and again, for a year, before accepting that the man was beyond death and exiling him instead, before he could be taken for a martyr.

It's the same trick every priesthood pulls on its founder's worst day, and I'd have more patience for it if the Mazuren version didn't have 169 names attached. Which leads me to an obvious point. The two religions don't get along. Who would have thought.

Zwigots are banned from entering Lastrago, and I can't tell you when that started. The temple records treat the prohibition as something that was always true, which in my experience means somebody lost an argument nobody wanted written down. Anyway.

A Zwigot found in a Lastragan village is most likely beaten to death, and then hanged regardless. There are more such cases than I care to list. And should one reach Mazuren hands, as a mockery of their legend, they'll be put to the spire repeatedly until they perish.

What's amusing about the whole thing is that the Zwigots believe this to be a great honor. Retelling the story, becoming one with nature, that sort of thing. Every year some make the journey in hiding, only to reveal themselves to the priests in order to go through the ceremony.
Their brethren will then call them saints. I'd use a different word.
Ashes To Ashes

I'd be surprised if one villager in a thousand could tell you a line from the Tzikhari beyond the ones that have turned into proverbs. It boggles my mind how people just accept the monks on face value: weddings, funerals... Especially funerals. The obvious reason, as always, is practical.

Nobody wants to handle a body that sat outside for three days during summer. And here comes one who would not only do that, but would also only charge you just enough to cover the pyre and a meal or two. But still, the commoners seem so eager to declare one a holy man.

Smear your face with the ashes of the dead, maybe eat some if you're a traditionalist, and there you go - thou art sacred. At least the same can't be said about my peers, thank fuck. Most academics see the Zwigots for what they are. A death cult.

A popular and widely accepted one, but a death cult nonetheless. Their ceremonies are proof enough. While they claim all matter is the same, they seem to revere only the type which disgusts everyone else. They'd claim it is a demonstration of faith, but I see it for what it is.
Showmanship. An attempt to convince the gullible that there is more to them than meets the eye.

A combination of all the above is how they spread. What started as a single temple in Imellah, on the outskirts of Trefgann, spread to the whole region within two generations. The centuries between that and now are harder to trace.
Nobody thought to document a religion that was mostly tolerated and occasionally useful, and by the time anyone noticed it warranted a chapter, the temples were already everywhere. Lastrago excluded.

Governments tolerate their oddities for their free services, and for giving the masses' heads something to play around with which isn't their mandate. The temples are mostly self sufficient: gardening, cooking. It's a simple lifestyle.

They spend most of their time copying books, arguing over the Tzikhari, meditating, and occasionally ceremonial work for the locals. They barely mingle. People are impressed with a monk who's willing to wear their aunt's ashes on their face, but they wouldn't exactly invite him to dinner.

They're still expanding despite that, mostly due to their policy of acceptance. Orphans, Karex, the poor, whoever nobody else wanted. People leave them at the temple door knowing they'll be taken care of for life.

The children learn Old Lastragan before common, in some cases, and are given Lastragan names. They are then expected to recite the Tzikhari by heart. Fail to do so, and you'll be thrown out eventually, which is exactly why most succeed.
The banished are left with no trade, no connections, not even a name.
Modern Lastrago considers the old tongue dead, but the Zwigots speak it freely.

I can't read it myself, which is worth admitting, because it means every Tzikhari translation I've complained about in these pages was made by outsiders working from whatever leaked out of the houses over the centuries.

Which reminds me, Beltzu ends in -u, which is a woman's ending in Old Lastragan. Nobody I've asked has had an explanation, but I do think it’s worth pointing out. The monks have argued about this to no end, but in neither of their conclusions is he a woman.
Lost And Found

The Zwigots say Beltzu kept walking west all the way to Knotsreach, and into the Wending, where he is still alive, frozen in meditation, with his tomb built around him. Which, assuming it's real, is what the grand temple of Tzubilek was built around.

Conveniently, nobody outside the order has ever seen the place. It is the seat of the Mukek, "The Caretaker," and reaching it is the doctrine made literal. You walk into the Wending and "Tobol kan, motol ot" - trust the path to deliver you.

When a Mukek dies, the senior houses each send a candidate, and the first to arrive at Tzubilek is declared the next one. A test of faith. To my eyes, the Wending has no opinion on theology, but I don't make the rules, so here we are.
The current Mukek is Chimek, who has been at Tzubilek for some forty years with a handful of monks who made the walk alongside him.
His rulings on the Tzikhari have a reputation I can't personally verify, but the abbots I've pressed on the matter were respectful in a way that suggests he amounts to more than his title.

He settles disputed readings, rules on the correct form for ceremonies, and decides what counts as heresy. He is also dying. I have this from three separate sources in Luznica, though none of them seemed particularly interested in discussing what comes next.
Which brings me to Luznica, where the senior abbot of the local house serves as Ozbekem, "the one who reads on behalf of."

In practice, this means he opens Chimek's correspondence, receives visiting abbots, certifies new houses, and relays the Mukek's rulings whenever they make it out of the Wending. The mundane stuff, in short.

The current Ozbekem is Kanteb, who has held the position for about fifteen years, and who has spent most of those fifteen years answering questions that should be going to Chimek. Not out of ambition. Oh no, he wouldn't dare.

But only because a letter to Tzubilek takes weeks and a ruling takes longer, and the abbot standing in front of Kanteb's desk needs an answer before his village buries someone wrong. So Kanteb answers, carefully, always noting that the Mukek may rule differently.
The Mukek rarely does, partly because Kanteb is cautious enough to stay within safe readings, and partly because for all I know he might as well be dead.

Kanteb doesn't touch political matters, and Chimek can't, and between the two of them the religion has no position on anything outside the Tzikhari. This has suited everyone for fourteen centuries. What concerns me is arithmetic.

The largest religious movement on the continent, present in most villages, handling every birth and death and wedding that matters to ordinary people, and the only thing keeping it out of politics is a dying man in a forest and a cautious abbot who knows better.
Chimek's successor will be chosen by the Wending, and the Wending will produce a scholar.

But the next Ozbekem is just an appointment, and there is nothing in the structure preventing an abbot with ambitions from taking that desk in Luznica and deciding the correspondence is worth answering. Danilo Pescarin was a Remosan nobleman last year. He's an abbot now.
Anyway, when that finally happens, and I'd bet my library that it will in the coming decade, the Zwigots won't be entering politics. They'll be discovering they were already in it.
Rebirth

The Midwives are harder to talk about, mostly because nobody in the houses wants to talk about them. If the world is one substance remaking itself, and the correct response is acceptance, then the question somebody was always going to ask is why stop at acceptance. A rift recycles.
The Green Wall holds back the Mire. One of these, according to the doctrine, is interference. The Midwives want to correct that.

Their literature circulates inside the houses the way these things always do. Copied pages tucked into commentaries, citations disguised as orthodox disputation, arguments that read as hypothetical until you notice they aren't.
I've seen one piece, a six-page tract in translation, and the theology is sound enough that I understood immediately why the Mukek banned it. It doesn't contradict the Tzikhari. It extends it.

The difference between eating a corpse and dismantling the Green Wall, according to the author, is squeamishness, not principle. The mainstream position is that one is acceptance and the other is interference, and the tract asks, politely and at length, where exactly the boundary sits.

The worst incident I'm aware of was in Ezgarin, 1784. Three monks arrested inside the Green Wall buffer zone by an Iron Perimeter patrol. What they were doing there the Remosan report doesn't specify, though the location speaks clearly enough. Two were hanged.

The third, a woman named Idra Chenne, was not recovered. The disavowal from Luznica arrived within the month. One page. Kanteb's predecessor, presumably, though it isn't signed. The Zwigot position, it argues, is that there is no self apart from the substance.

A monk eating a corpse is not doing something to the world. He is the world, consuming itself. The Midwives, the moment they decided the Green Wall should come down, placed themselves outside the process. An agent, acting on the substance, directing it.
Which is the Mazuren error rebuilt from the other end. The priests flee the storm. The Zwigots withstand it. Tobol kan, motol ot. That's what the page says.
What it doesn't say is that the Zwigots survive on tolerance, and that a religion associated with sabotage and dead Weave agents would not survive very long at all.
The Mukek declared the Midwives heretical, and the houses strip the name from any monk found distributing the literature. This has not, as far as I can tell, done much.
The arguments still circulate, probably because a disputation-based religion has a very hard time telling its monks to stop thinking about something.
Ancient Lastragan
Pronunciation
Tz as in "cats" Ch hard, as in "check" X "sh" (Nabixa = nah-BEE-sha) Stress penultimate
Names
Names are modular: root + ending. Two syllables is common, three is formal. It should sound like a rock hitting another rock.
Vocabulary
Word order: verb first, then subject, then object. Subject drops when obvious from context.
From the Tzikhari

the_speculars.title: The Speculars
the_speculars.text:
The Speculars
That which observes is, by the act of observation, excluded from the thing observed. A mind within a room perceives not the room but its contents; the room is not among the things it contains, being rather the condition of their containment. So with the eye, which is no part of anything it sees. Nothing is perceived except through some instrument, and no instrument delivers the thing as it is, but only as the surface receives it. To look outward is to be stopped by one's own surface.
Veritas Audax, page 384
Philosophizing:
I've always found it odd that, for all their notoriety, the Speculars' doctrine is so exposed, so public. Most shadow groups, cults and the like, work the other way around: a warm welcome at the door, and the dogma kept for those in too deep to walk out. Here the doctrine is the door.
The core texts are easy enough to find, for something so widely banned. The services are known to all, and so are the risks. And yet the fascination persists, which makes sense, I guess, once you realize that it survives on people not reading the literature.
Nothing undermines the mystique of tampering with minds quite like six hundred pages of perception theory.
It is difficult to discuss philosophy plainly, and the Specular point of view, by their own account, is a philosophy. By others', a dangerous occult fascination. Either way, I intend to give it a fair presentation, if only because my safety might otherwise be put into question.
Which, I might add, does not help their case. And should a Specular come across this and find my conclusions unkind, well. Luckily, this book is written anonymously.
The Doctrine:
The Speculars believe that Virelia doesn't really exist, or that, at the very least, there's a more complete world beyond it, hidden from our eyes. If you're unenthusiastic about theory, feel free to move on now. You got the gist. But for those looking to truly dig in, let's.
The Veritas Audax is the closest thing the movement has to a foundational text. Six hundred pages. Either uninviting or uncompromising, depends on who you ask. The main argument is about perception. We observe through instruments. Eyes, ears...
Each one delivers a processed version of whatever it encountered, and what the mind receives is the processed version, not the thing. Standard philosophy so far. But Veritas Audax refuses to stop there.
If every instrument distorts, and instruments are all we have, the claim that Virelia is as it appears rests on nothing we can verify. You'd need an unmediated observation to check, which is a contradiction. They call this the Closed Room.
The Audax spends its second half arguing that something exists outside it, and they claim evidence for it can be found all over the place in Virelia: Rifts. Things which exist beyond our world, and are only hinted at through fractures in ours. They call it the Mirror Realm.
The name predates the book. I've seen it in confiscated letters at least a century older. It is a bit misleading, as they don't mean an actual place. They mean everything. The full version of whatever Virelia is a partial impression of.
The term is unhelpful and the Speculars know it, but nine centuries of convention are apparently harder to overturn than reality itself.
Contact with the Mirror Realm, assuming it exists, creates an obvious problem. The "instrument" wasn't built for it. What happens when unprocessed information reaches a mind that has no way to contain it isn't theoretical, nor is it pretty.
The Weave's case files are full of people who survived rift exposure and came out perceiving things no one should be able to. Time as a visible surface. Spatial relationships that disagree with themselves... the usual oddities.
What the Weave treats as cognitive damage, the Speculars treat as proof. A problem to be solved. A brief, involuntary glimpse of what's outside the room, received by an eye that was never meant to look at it. This, partly, is what inspired the current iteration of Specular philosophy.
As if it wasn't enough for the Speculars to argue with everyone else, three schools of thought have emerged from the question. Which now allow the Speculars to argue with each other as well. To bloody results, occasionally.
I'll go over all three: Fragmentists, Amalgamists and lastly, Inverters.
The Three Schools
The Fragmentists are the most widespread, which probably stems from it being the easiest school to grasp. The mind, in their view, is the distortion. All of it amounts to scratches on the lens. Their solution is removal.
Subtract the person, and what remains is a surface capable of receiving the Real without imposing itself on the signal. In practice this means the underground Glaskatch shard trade, and a lot of it. A childhood memory goes first, maybe. Then a fear. Then something larger.
The end-goal is a mind smooth enough that there's nothing left to interfere with reception. I've read accounts of senior Fragmentists who can't hold a conversation. There isn't enough of themselves to participate, and they end up reflecting whoever's in front of them instead.
Mannerisms, speech. A Fragmentist would tell you this isn't emptiness, but a pure self. I am not sure I agree, and in any case, they'll have to stand in line with the Tavernashi to have that argument. They made it long before the Speculars took it out of their book, after all.
The Amalgamists start from the opposite end. The mind is fine. The body is the problem. A human brain was built to process a limited reality, and no amount of philosophical trimming will change the physical constraints of the organ. You don't fix the lens. You build a new one.
Their laboratories are the reason most people think of the Speculars as monsters rather than philosophers, and I can't say the reputation is unearned. Consciousness transfer. Hybrid bodies. States that sit in the gaps between alive and dead.
Duskwalkers interest them particularly, since the condition already demonstrates that a soul can operate inside a vessel without the limitations that come with a living body.
I've mentioned elsewhere in this book that a Specular cell with the right materials can force the Duskwalker condition. Well, these are the ones.
The Inverters are more rare, and are harder to explain, which I suspect they would take as a compliment. Their claim is that the problem is already solved. Your reflection already sees the Real. It was made on the other side of the boundary and has always been there.
The work, then, is not construction or subtraction but contact. And eventually, perhaps, exchange. Their reflection, to them, is a person. Someone they've studied all their lives and never met. The resulting relationship is, predictably, complicated.
Add to that their obsession with symmetry, and you get what I consider to be the strangest of the bunch. Some of their members even pursue bodily symmetry through surgery, since a perfectly symmetric body is identical to its own reflection.
I'd call it excessive but at this point it seems almost mild.
Inverter cells spend a great deal of time with mirrors. Attempting to justify the name, perhaps. Trance states, prolonged gazing, years of practice aimed at communication with whatever looks back.
They also closely study the ethereal, and the more powerful ones are rumored to even dabble with inter-dimensional travel. Though how much of that is public relations is anyone's guess.
What Follows An Idiot
The Veritas Audax was written around 300. The author is unknown to us. It was found in 712 in a pre-Mazur temple on the outskirts of Lastrago by a Remosan academic expedition that was cataloguing religious sites.
For the first 143 years it mostly gathered dust in Urik-Van's historical collection, and in the very few times it was read, it was seen as what it is: epistemology. Very, very long epistemology.
Then, in the year 855, it was stolen, and the three guards who were on watch duty at the time disappeared with no trace. Then, and only then, people noticed. While the book was, and still is, missing, a local scribe had been copying it, and got as far as page 600.
The sort of drama that gets attention outside of scholarly circles alone, and that granted the surviving pages their allure. The Speculars, of all people, ought to appreciate the irony: their foundational text is itself a fragment, and nobody knows what comes after.
What began as a modest crowd of occultists and enthusiasts expanded rapidly with the appearance of Godrick Ferass. A Haldrithian guild-trained arcanist who was expelled from the Black Hands around 930 for pursuing research the guild didn't approve of.
I've pieced together what I can of the man from secondhand sources, and the picture I get is less of a genius and more of a particular kind of failure. Smart enough to follow the Audax's argument, vain enough to test it, and stupid enough to do so badly.
However, people do like their self-proclaimed geniuses. And so he gathered followers, gave the movement its name and its vocabulary, and established the Speculars as they are today. No headquarters, no hierarchy, nothing but the name, really.
Ferass didn't trust institutions, having been spat out by one, and the movement he built reflects that bitterness down to its bones. How he died is the kind of question that reveals more about the person answering it than the subject. The Speculars will tell you he completed the work.
He stepped through. The one account I find more convincing, though it's unverified, describes a man who had lost his mind entirely by the end, and was strangled with a pillow by one of his own followers.
We do have verified accounts of the abuse his followers went through, so I find myself hoping it's the latter. The cult moved often enough that even his burial site is uncertain. Or hidden, whichever narrative you prefer.
For the next four centuries the movement spread. Cells appeared in most cities at one point or another, small enough to avoid attention, persistent enough to survive the occasional raid.
The three schools formed during this period, though the exact dates are unclear and the Speculars themselves can't agree on who formalized what. The Fragmentists are the oldest branch, or claim to be.
The Amalgamists likely emerged later, once the Glaskatch shard trade gave them the tools they needed. The Inverters were always small, always strange, and always insistent that they were the original interpretation and everyone else had strayed. I'll leave them to their argument.
Notoriety
The event that turned the Speculars from a nuisance into a genuine threat was the Tintbent plot of 1397.
An Inverter cell led by one Thorro Rent, operating from somewhere in the Tintbent interior, attempted to collapse a section of the mountain range separating the Tintbent peninsula from the continent. The intention, as best anyone has reconstructed it, was to let the anomaly spread.
Trefganni border patrols intercepted the cell before the attempt could be carried out. The trial was brief. The executions were public. Within a decade, most jurisdictions had issued standing orders against Specular cells.
And the bans did what they always do: spread the word. Turn the odd niche into an exciting trend. As was later proved by the Cantemir affair of 1723.
Ciprian Cantemir, youngest son of one of Remosa's established noble houses, was replaced at age fifteen by a common-born Specular named Drazho Morarin. A craft-class kid from Netford who wanted a warm bed and a life where people used his name with respect.
The real Ciprian's identity was stripped and bound into an object using what we'd now call Doppler technique. His body was found in a storage cellar, weeks later, breathing and responding to nothing. Drazho lived as Ciprian for three years. Attended court. Signed papers. Married a girl.
The wife noticed first, told her sister, the sister told a priest. Eventually the rumor got to the boy's family. Drazho, when confronted, couldn't say where the object containing Ciprian had gone. He'd had the memory of the procedure blanked afterward. A safety measure.
The real Ciprian was never recovered. Drazho was executed in 1727. The Cantemir family pushed Remosa to issue a kill-order specifically targeting Speculars, which was granted, and which has accomplished exactly the results you'd expect.
Mirror Arcana
The Speculars coined the term "Mirror Arcana" for their practice, and have declared it a newfound school of magic. Whether it is one is among the longest standing arguments in arcane research, and I will certainly not be the one to solve it here.
I've spoken to colleagues on opposing sides of the debate in an attempt to explain it properly, and each agreed that my account is skewed toward the other's position. I take this as the closest thing my field has to peer review.
The traditionalists claim that every spell the Speculars associate with Mirror Arcana can be explained through an existing school. Be it conjuration, alteration, or otherwise.
The Speculars, on the other hand, think spellcasters have been utilizing the Mirror Realm all along without realizing it, and have since expanded on what they perceive to be an archaic use of misunderstood principles.
Misty Step, for example, or any displacement magic, is widely considered a Conjuration spell. To their eyes, however, since nothing was in fact conjured, none of the accepted schools account for what really occurred. The caster, in their view, passed through the Mirror Realm.
Which connects all points in Virelia the way a surface connects the things reflected on it. The caster moved. But the space he moved through was not our own.
From there the argument extends. If things are already connected through a shared reflective space, then new connections can be established between them, and old ones can be severed. What constitutes a thing's reflection is, in the Specular view, not fixed. Move one, the other follows.
Damage one, the other carries the wound. The connection holds until severed or until it breaks down on its own, which it does, and which the Speculars are less eager to discuss.
Most of what people actually encounter the Speculars doing follows from these two ideas. Broadly: displacement, mainly through reflective surfaces, transfer of properties between linked objects, or the severing of such connections.
Between a person and their own memories, being the most famous example. The Speculars consider all of these the same discipline. Whether or not they're right, the results are real enough, and that's what tends to draw attention.
The discipline is considered volatile and highly experimental, though dangers to casters are nothing new. A failed mirror spell can drive a man mad, but so can a failed illusion. It can leave him cut in half between two places, and evocation has produced messier halves.
On that count alone, no one would have bothered banning it. What distinguishes Mirror Arcana is that, if the Specular hypothesis is true, the practice doesn't merely endanger its practitioner.
It strains the same boundaries the Rifts have already fractured, and could deepen them, or open new ones. Hence the ban, in every jurisdiction I'm aware of. What I find amusing is that the consensus holds Mirror Arcana to be wrong about everything, and yet it is banned as if it is not.
This is not how a convinced academic community operates.
To Them The Streets
Officials tend to describe the Speculars the same way: inhumane, reckless. No place in civilized society. They do so right up until they have to pay a cell to erase a gambling debt from their wife's memory. And continue to do so afterwards. This is how the Speculars survive.
Not through cunning or secrecy, though some cells have plenty of both, but because the people responsible for destroying them keep finding reasons not to do it completely.
Practitioners organize into what official jargon calls cells. Three people in an abandoned house with a crate of shards, a funded operation behind a legitimate front, or a herbalist in a village nobody cares about.
Ferass' distrust of structured systems, or lack of foresight, turned out to be their greatest asset. You can't dismantle a structure that was never built, and certainly not when everyone meant to be fighting it seems to be paying it out of pocket. Wealthy families, guild officers...
Even when they don't seek the Speculars out, many pay a retainer for the guarantee that the service exists when a rival's judgment needs quiet altering, or a problem needs to go away without leaving a document trail. It's pragmatic, cynical, short-sighted and selfish. Politics, in short.
In fairness, most of what they sell is small. A memory shed here, a fear excised there, the client usually being the merchandise's original owner. Work on the scale of the Cantemir affair is rare, and treated as a line even inside the movement.
What a line is worth to people who erase things for a living, I leave to the reader.
Recruitment, supposedly, is handled through the Rite of the Glass. A ceremony repeated in occult circles enough times that it bled into general knowledge.
Supposedly, to emphasize again: stare into a mirror for twenty-four hours without food, speech, or looking away, and "they" will find you. I half believe it. It has the theatrical self-seriousness of Inverter practice, and the few accounts I've found do involve mirror-focused cells.
But given how decentralized the whole affair is, I don't see how the logistics work out. A specific cell's gimmick, perhaps. Who knows. Most recruits arrive by duller roads. Sanatoriums, universities, occult circles, mean-looking alehouses.
And the margins of Glaskatch, of course, where someone buying Static shards, the clouded dregs of the memory trade, has probably already accepted half of what they teach in the introductory courses.
Speculars don't advertise, unless you count the atrocities, which, to be fair, seem to draw attention very effectively. The ban, the mystique, and general desperation with the state of things do the rest.
VIP
In this day and age I don't believe the Speculars have a defined leadership. But I'll name some of the more influential living practitioners, both to paint a picture and because these are genuinely interesting specimens.
One name I keep encountering, and probably the closest thing the movement has to a leader, is Einar. No family name. He is said to have lived for several centuries by moving between bodies, and the documentation is more plausible than I'd like.
Someone operating under that name has been connected to shard and erasure operations in at least four regions across 167 years. Either the man has been swapping vessels for longer than most institutions have existed, or the name is passed along with the operation.
An Inverter by inclination and a merchant by practice. His network, if it is one man's network, is the largest Specular operation I'm aware of, and it sells forgetting. Espionage and assassination appear in the margins of his file as well. That's all I have on him, unfortunately.
Then there's Noella Dyann, "Nenne". An Amalgamist, and a beloved figure in Specular circles. She is, by every account, motherly, pleasant, patient and deeply knowledgeable. The type who makes a lot of tea and remembers her assistants' birthdays.
She is also, to my knowledge, the only active researcher systematically studying souls. Her position is that the Fragmentists are chasing the wrong target. Subtract personality all you like, the soul persists, still imposing its limits on perception.
The soul is the barrier, and she means to prove it. I've read some of her published work. Fascinating stuff. What the research looks like in practice is, unfortunately, gruesome.
Her hypothesis also creates a genuine problem for the movement, because if she's right, everything the Fragmentists have done to themselves amounts to pointless mutilation. The Fragmentists, for their part, have not slowed down.
If anything, the prospect of proving her wrong has given them a second wind.
Mirror School Spells
Cantrips
Minor Binding
Cantrip, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action Range: 30 feet
Components: S, M (two objects of similar nature)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You create a link between two Tiny objects you can see within range.
For the duration, when you use your action to move one object up to 15 feet, the other moves the same distance in the same direction, provided it is not held or worn by a creature and its path is not blocked by a solid surface.
If the second object's path is blocked, it stops and the binding ends.
The objects must share some degree of similarity (two stones, two coins, two pieces of wood). The GM determines whether the objects are sufficiently similar.
Reflection
Cantrip, divination
Casting Time: 1 action Range: Touch Components: S Duration: Instantaneous
You touch a reflective surface (a mirror, still water, polished metal) and receive a single still image of something the surface reflected within the last 5 hours, at a moment of the GM's choosing.
Repeated castings on the same surface return the same image until the surface reflects something new. The image is visual, with no detail finer than what a person standing before the surface would have seen. Magical disguises and illusions appear as they did to the surface at the time.
Tether
Cantrip, divination
Casting Time: 1 action Range: Touch
Components: S, M (a piece of the target, such as a hair, splinter, or fragment, which the spell consumes)
Duration: Concentration, up to 10 minutes
You touch a creature or object and establish a faint link. For the duration, you know the direction to the target, provided it is on the same plane of existence and within 120 feet of you.
If the target moves beyond 120 feet, you know the direction it was last in before leaving range, but receive no further updates until it returns.
1st Level
Exchange
1st-level, conjuration
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 30 feet
Components: V, S
Duration: Instantaneous
You and one willing creature you can see within range instantly swap positions. Each of you appears in the space the other occupied. Neither movement provokes opportunity attacks.
If either destination space cannot hold its new occupant, the spell fails and the slot is not expended.
2nd Level
Yank
2nd-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (a small hook or bent nail)
Duration: Instantaneous
You establish a momentary binding between yourself and a creature you can see within range, then wrench the connection. The target must make a Strength saving throw. On a failure, the target is pulled up to 30 feet in a straight line toward you.
