If the target strikes a solid surface or creature during this movement, the movement stops and both the target and whatever it struck take 3d6 bludgeoning damage. On a success, the target is pulled up to 10 feet and takes no damage.
This movement does not provoke opportunity attacks.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the pull distance increases by 10 feet and the collision damage increases by 1d6 for each slot level above 2nd.
Flesh Link
2nd-level, necromancy
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (a strand of sinew or gut, tied in a knot)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You forge a link between two creatures you can see within range. Each unwilling creature can make a Constitution saving throw to resist the binding. If either target succeeds, the spell fails.
For the duration, whenever one linked creature takes damage from a single source (an attack, a spell, a fall), you can use your reaction to force the other linked creature to take necrotic damage equal to half the damage the first creature took, after any resistances or reductions are applied.
Damage transferred by this spell does not trigger further transfers. If an effect damages both linked creatures simultaneously (such as an area spell covering both), no transfer occurs.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 4th level or higher, you no longer need to use your reaction to trigger the transfer. It occurs automatically once per turn (the first time either linked creature takes damage on each turn).
Mirror Ward
2nd-level, abjuration
Casting Time: 1 reaction, which you take when you are hit by an attack
Range: Self Components: S, M (a reflective surface held in one hand, such as a hand mirror or polished blade)
Duration: Instantaneous
You angle the reflective surface against the incoming strike. You gain +3 to your AC against the triggering attack, potentially causing it to miss.
If the attack misses, whether or not the bonus was the cause, the attack is reflected. Choose a creature within 15 feet of you; the attack is rerolled against that creature, using the original attacker's attack bonus, and deals its normal damage on a hit.
A reflected attack cannot trigger reactions, and cannot be reflected again.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the AC bonus increases by 1 for each slot level above 2nd.
3rd Level
Binding
3rd-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action Range: 60 feet Components: V, S, M (a piece of chain or rope) Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You create a sustained binding between yourself and a creature you can see within range. The target must make a Strength saving throw. On a failure, the target is bound to your movement for the duration.
Whenever you move on your turn, the bound creature is dragged the same distance in the same direction. If the creature has its reaction available, the strain of resisting consumes it. This movement provokes opportunity attacks.
If the creature would be dragged into a solid surface, it takes 2d6 bludgeoning damage and its movement stops at the surface; your own movement is unaffected.
The bound creature can repeat the Strength saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on a success.
Limitations. The binding breaks if you and the target are ever more than 120 feet apart, or on different planes of existence.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 5th level or higher, the collision damage increases to 3d6 and the creature has disadvantage on its saves to end the effect.
Prism Shell
3rd-level, abjuration
Casting Time: 1 action Range: Self Components: V, S, M (a glass prism)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You surround yourself with a shell of refracted light. For the duration:
You have half cover (+2 to AC and Dexterity saving throws) against attacks originating from more than 10 feet away.
When a ranged attack (weapon or spell) misses you while this spell is active, you can use your reaction to redirect the attack toward a creature within 15 feet of you.
The attack is rerolled against the new target, using the original attacker's attack bonus, and deals its normal damage on a hit.
The shell sheds dim light in a 5-foot radius and is faintly visible as a distortion in the air.
Sever
3rd-level, abjuration
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: Touch
Components: V, S, M (a small mirror, which is cracked as part of the casting)
Duration: Instantaneous
You sever a specific connection affecting the target creature. Choose one of the following:
Magical Bond. You end one spell currently affecting the target, provided it is of 3rd level or lower and is a charm, fear, compulsion, or curse effect. For qualifying spells of 4th level or higher, make an ability check using your spellcasting ability (DC = 10 + the spell's level).
This spell cannot end curses that are not spells (a cursed item's attunement, lycanthropy, a divine punishment); those require Remove Curse or stronger magic.
Temporary Suppression. You suppress a specific memory in a willing creature. The target loses access to one memory of your choice (specified during casting) for 24 hours. The memory returns fully after this period. The target is aware something has been suppressed but cannot recall what.
A Remove Curse or Greater Restoration spell ends this effect early.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 5th level or higher, the Temporary Suppression duration extends to 7 days, and Magical Bond automatically ends qualifying spells of a level equal to or lower than the slot used.
When you use a slot of 7th level or higher, the suppression duration extends to 30 days.
4th Level
Mirror Scry
4th-level, divination
Casting Time: 10 minutes Range: Touch (Prepare) or Unlimited, same plane (Observe) Components: V, S, M (a silver mirror worth at least 50 gp)
Duration: Instantaneous (Prepare) or Concentration, up to 10 minutes (Observe)
When you cast this spell, choose one of its two functions. Each function requires its own casting.
Prepare. You touch a reflective surface (a mirror, polished metal, a still pool of water) and mark it with an invisible arcane sigil. The sigil lasts until dispelled or until the surface is destroyed. You can have up to 5 surfaces prepared at a time.
Preparing a new surface beyond this limit causes the oldest sigil to fade.
Observe. Using a silver mirror as a focus, you can see and hear through any surface you have previously prepared, as if you were standing directly before it. You can switch between prepared surfaces as an action. The observed surface shows whatever is within 30 feet of it.
Creatures can detect the scrying sensor with a successful Wisdom (Perception) check against your spell save DC, noticing a faint shimmer in the reflective surface.
5th Level
Glasswalk
5th-level, conjuration
Casting Time: 1 action Range: 10 feet Components: V, S Duration: 1 round
You step into a mirror or reflective surface large enough for you to pass through (at least 5 feet tall for a Medium creature) and instantly teleport to another such surface that you have physically touched at some point in the past, on the same plane of existence.
You emerge from the destination surface.
The entry surface remains an open portal until the end of your next turn. During this time, any creature that can fit through the surface can step through and arrive at the same destination.
Once used as a portal, both surfaces become nonmagical and cannot be used for this spell again for 24 hours.
The destination surface must still exist and be intact at the time of casting. If the destination surface has been destroyed, the spell fails and the spell slot is not expended.
Unsynchronize
5th-level, enchantment
Casting Time: 1 minute
Range: Touch
Components: V, S, M (a Glaskatch personality shard worth at least 500 gp, which the spell consumes)
Duration: Instantaneous
You permanently sever the connection between a creature and a specific aspect of its identity. The target must be willing or incapacitated. An unwilling target, even an incapacitated one, makes a Wisdom saving throw as the casting completes.
On a success, the spell fails and the shard is consumed anyway. Choose one of the following:
Memory. A specific memory, up to one hour of continuous experience, is permanently erased. The target retains skills and proficiencies learned during that time but loses all episodic recollection of the events.
Trait. A personality trait, bond, ideal, or flaw is permanently removed. The target's behavior shifts accordingly over the following days. This cannot remove racial traits, class features, or proficiencies.
Emotion. The target's capacity for a specific emotion (grief, fear, jealousy, love for a specific person) is permanently deadened. The target can still recognize situations where the emotion would apply but does not experience it.
A Greater Restoration spell cast within 24 hours of the severance restores what was removed. After that window closes, the severance cannot be reversed by anything besides a Wish spell. If the target was willing, they must confirm consent aloud as part of the casting.
The target is aware of what will be removed but cannot, by the spell's nature, fully anticipate the consequences.
Repeated castings on the same creature are cumulative. A creature that has undergone more than three severances must make a Wisdom saving throw (DC 15) after each subsequent casting. On a failure, the creature suffers indefinite madness as determined by the GM.
Major Binding
5th-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (two lengths of chain, linked)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You create a powerful binding between yourself and a creature you can see within range. The target must make a Strength saving throw. On a failure, the creature is bound to you for the duration, with the following effects:
Mirrored Movement. As with Binding, the target is dragged to match your movement, and the strain consumes its reaction if one is available. This movement provokes opportunity attacks. If the creature would be dragged into a solid surface, it takes 4d6 bludgeoning damage.
Shared Fate. When you are forced to make a saving throw against a spell or effect, you can use your reaction to force the bound creature to make the same saving throw against the same effect, as though it were also a target. The creature uses its own saving throw modifiers.
The bound creature can repeat the Strength saving throw at the end of each of its turns, at disadvantage, ending the effect on a success. The binding breaks if you and the target are ever more than 120 feet apart or on different planes.
6th Level
Mirror Prison
6th-level, conjuration
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (a silver-framed mirror worth at least 1,000 gp)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 hour
You attempt to trap a creature you can see within range inside a reflective surface. The component mirror must be large enough to display the target's full reflection; if it is not, the spell fails and the slot is not expended. The target must make a Charisma saving throw.
On a failure, the creature is pulled into the mirror used as the material component for this spell. On a success, the creature is unaffected.
While imprisoned, the creature is aware of its surroundings as seen from within the mirror. It can see out and speak, though its voice sounds distant and distorted.
The creature cannot interact with the physical world, cast spells that target anything outside the mirror, or take physical actions.
If the imprisoned creature is within line of sight of another reflective surface (a second mirror, a pool of water, polished armor), it can use its movement to transfer to that surface on its turn, provided the surface is large enough to display its full reflection.
It cannot leave the reflective surface by any means while the spell persists.
The imprisoned creature can repeat the Charisma saving throw each time it transfers to a new surface, and once every 10 minutes otherwise, ending the effect on a success.
The prison also ends when the spell's duration expires, when your concentration is broken, when the surface currently holding the creature is destroyed (the creature appears in the nearest unoccupied space, taking 4d6 force damage), or when the spell is dispelled.
7th Level
Doppler
7th-level, enchantment
Casting Time: 1 hour Range: Touch Components: V, S, M (a Glaskatch personality shard worth at least 5,000 gp, a mirror large enough to reflect both targets, and a drop of blood from the source creature — all consumed) Duration: Until dispelled
You overwrite one creature's identity onto another. This spell requires two creatures: the source (whose identity is copied) and the vessel (who receives it). Both must be present for the full casting time. The vessel must be incapacitated or willing.
The source can be willing, incapacitated, or dead (dead no longer than 10 days).
Upon completion, the vessel's personality, memories, mannerisms, and emotional patterns are replaced with those of the source.
The vessel retains its own physical body, hit points, and physical ability scores (Strength, Dexterity, Constitution), but its mental ability scores (Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma) are replaced with those of the source.
The vessel gains the source's proficiencies and class features, up to a total class level no greater than the vessel's own level or Hit Dice; capabilities beyond that limit are present as knowledge and memory but do not function, surfacing over time or never, at the GM's discretion.
The source creature is unaffected if alive and willing. Its identity is copied, not moved. If the source is dead, the copy is drawn from the body's residual imprint.
The vessel's original identity is suppressed, not destroyed. It persists beneath the surface. Under extreme duress, magical compulsion, or exposure to deeply personal stimuli from the vessel's original life, the GM may call for a Wisdom saving throw (DC equals your spell save DC).
On a success, the vessel's original identity reasserts itself for 1d4 hours before being suppressed again. Each reassertion lowers the DC by 1.
The spell can be ended by Dispel Magic cast at 7th level or higher, by a Wish spell, or by performing this spell again on the vessel with intent to strip the overwritten identity without replacing it (consuming materials as normal, leaving the vessel in a confused,
identity-less state for 2d6 days before their original self gradually returns).
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a 9th-level spell slot, you can designate an object as the vessel. The source creature's identity is stripped from its body and bound to the object.
The body is left alive but empty — breathing, responsive to stimulus, but with no personality, memory, or will.
The identity within the object has no senses and no means of communication unless the object is reflective (a mirror, polished metal), in which case the trapped identity can perceive what the surface reflects and can speak, faintly, to those nearby.
8th Level
Refraction
8th-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 120 feet
Components: V, S, M (a shattered mirror, the pieces of which are thrown into the air during casting)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You fracture the spatial geometry of a 60-foot cube originating from a point you can see within range. For the duration, the affected area is warped by broken reflective symmetry:
Distorted Space. The area is difficult terrain for all creatures except you. Creatures other than you have disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws while within the area.
Bent Trajectories. Ranged weapon attacks and ranged spell attacks that pass through any part of the area have disadvantage.
Spatial Displacement. The first time a creature enters the area or starts its turn there, it must make an Intelligence saving throw.
On a failure, the creature is teleported to a random unoccupied space within the area (roll a d8 for direction, d6 × 10 for distance in feet; if the result would place it outside the area, it appears at the nearest space within it).
A creature that has made this save, whatever the outcome, is not subject to Spatial Displacement again unless it leaves the area and re-enters.
Mirror Passages. You can use a bonus action on your turn to swap the positions of two creatures within the area. Each creature must make a Charisma saving throw. The swap occurs only if both creatures fail; otherwise, neither moves.
Creatures with truesight are immune to the Spatial Displacement effect but are still affected by the other properties.
9th Level
Inversion
9th-level (classification never settled)
Casting Time: 1 minute
Range: Self
Components: V, S, M (a flawless mirror worth at least 25,000 gp, which shatters when the spell is cast)
Duration: Instantaneous
The ultimate expression of Specular philosophy. You step through the boundary between Virelia and the Mirror Realm.
Upon casting, your body on this side of the boundary becomes a reflection: visible in mirrors and reflective surfaces but physically absent. Your consciousness crosses into the Mirror Realm, whatever that may be. This is a one-way effect.
There is no known counterspell, no reversal, no return. Wish can restore the caster's body to its last physical state, but it is unclear whether the consciousness that returns is the original or the reflection.
The flawless mirror shatters upon completion and cannot be repaired or reconstructed by any means short of divine intervention.
The caster's reflection persists in mirrors and reflective surfaces near the casting location for 1d10 days, occasionally moving or speaking, before fading permanently.
GM Note. This spell is included for narrative completeness. It is not intended as a standard player option. A character who casts Inversion has, in mechanical terms, left the campaign.
Whether the Mirror Realm exists, whether the caster survives the crossing, and what (if anything) looks back from the other side is entirely at the GM's discretion. The Speculars consider this spell a success. Everyone else considers it suicide. Neither side has conclusive evidence.

segments.text: The Speculars

That which observes is, by the act of observation, excluded from the thing observed. A mind within a room perceives not the room but its contents; the room is not among the things it contains, being rather the condition of their containment. So with the eye, which is no part of anything it sees. Nothing is perceived except through some instrument, and no instrument delivers the thing as it is, but only as the surface receives it. To look outward is to be stopped by one's own surface.
Veritas Audax, page 384
Philosophizing:

I've always found it odd that, for all their notoriety, the Speculars' doctrine is so exposed, so public. Most shadow groups, cults and the like, work the other way around: a warm welcome at the door, and the dogma kept for those in too deep to walk out. Here the doctrine is the door.

The core texts are easy enough to find, for something so widely banned. The services are known to all, and so are the risks. And yet the fascination persists, which makes sense, I guess, once you realize that it survives on people not reading the literature.
Nothing undermines the mystique of tampering with minds quite like six hundred pages of perception theory.

It is difficult to discuss philosophy plainly, and the Specular point of view, by their own account, is a philosophy. By others', a dangerous occult fascination. Either way, I intend to give it a fair presentation, if only because my safety might otherwise be put into question.
Which, I might add, does not help their case. And should a Specular come across this and find my conclusions unkind, well. Luckily, this book is written anonymously.
The Doctrine:

The Speculars believe that Virelia doesn't really exist, or that, at the very least, there's a more complete world beyond it, hidden from our eyes. If you're unenthusiastic about theory, feel free to move on now. You got the gist. But for those looking to truly dig in, let's.

The Veritas Audax is the closest thing the movement has to a foundational text. Six hundred pages. Either uninviting or uncompromising, depends on who you ask. The main argument is about perception. We observe through instruments. Eyes, ears...

Each one delivers a processed version of whatever it encountered, and what the mind receives is the processed version, not the thing. Standard philosophy so far. But Veritas Audax refuses to stop there.

If every instrument distorts, and instruments are all we have, the claim that Virelia is as it appears rests on nothing we can verify. You'd need an unmediated observation to check, which is a contradiction. They call this the Closed Room.

The Audax spends its second half arguing that something exists outside it, and they claim evidence for it can be found all over the place in Virelia: Rifts. Things which exist beyond our world, and are only hinted at through fractures in ours. They call it the Mirror Realm.

The name predates the book. I've seen it in confiscated letters at least a century older. It is a bit misleading, as they don't mean an actual place. They mean everything. The full version of whatever Virelia is a partial impression of.
The term is unhelpful and the Speculars know it, but nine centuries of convention are apparently harder to overturn than reality itself.

Contact with the Mirror Realm, assuming it exists, creates an obvious problem. The "instrument" wasn't built for it. What happens when unprocessed information reaches a mind that has no way to contain it isn't theoretical, nor is it pretty.

The Weave's case files are full of people who survived rift exposure and came out perceiving things no one should be able to. Time as a visible surface. Spatial relationships that disagree with themselves... the usual oddities.

What the Weave treats as cognitive damage, the Speculars treat as proof. A problem to be solved. A brief, involuntary glimpse of what's outside the room, received by an eye that was never meant to look at it. This, partly, is what inspired the current iteration of Specular philosophy.

As if it wasn't enough for the Speculars to argue with everyone else, three schools of thought have emerged from the question. Which now allow the Speculars to argue with each other as well. To bloody results, occasionally.
I'll go over all three: Fragmentists, Amalgamists and lastly, Inverters.
The Three Schools

The Fragmentists are the most widespread, which probably stems from it being the easiest school to grasp. The mind, in their view, is the distortion. All of it amounts to scratches on the lens. Their solution is removal.

Subtract the person, and what remains is a surface capable of receiving the Real without imposing itself on the signal. In practice this means the underground Glaskatch shard trade, and a lot of it. A childhood memory goes first, maybe. Then a fear. Then something larger.

The end-goal is a mind smooth enough that there's nothing left to interfere with reception. I've read accounts of senior Fragmentists who can't hold a conversation. There isn't enough of themselves to participate, and they end up reflecting whoever's in front of them instead.

Mannerisms, speech. A Fragmentist would tell you this isn't emptiness, but a pure self. I am not sure I agree, and in any case, they'll have to stand in line with the Tavernashi to have that argument. They made it long before the Speculars took it out of their book, after all.

The Amalgamists start from the opposite end. The mind is fine. The body is the problem. A human brain was built to process a limited reality, and no amount of philosophical trimming will change the physical constraints of the organ. You don't fix the lens. You build a new one.

Their laboratories are the reason most people think of the Speculars as monsters rather than philosophers, and I can't say the reputation is unearned. Consciousness transfer. Hybrid bodies. States that sit in the gaps between alive and dead.
Duskwalkers interest them particularly, since the condition already demonstrates that a soul can operate inside a vessel without the limitations that come with a living body.
I've mentioned elsewhere in this book that a Specular cell with the right materials can force the Duskwalker condition. Well, these are the ones.

The Inverters are more rare, and are harder to explain, which I suspect they would take as a compliment. Their claim is that the problem is already solved. Your reflection already sees the Real. It was made on the other side of the boundary and has always been there.

The work, then, is not construction or subtraction but contact. And eventually, perhaps, exchange. Their reflection, to them, is a person. Someone they've studied all their lives and never met. The resulting relationship is, predictably, complicated.

Add to that their obsession with symmetry, and you get what I consider to be the strangest of the bunch. Some of their members even pursue bodily symmetry through surgery, since a perfectly symmetric body is identical to its own reflection.
I'd call it excessive but at this point it seems almost mild.
Inverter cells spend a great deal of time with mirrors. Attempting to justify the name, perhaps. Trance states, prolonged gazing, years of practice aimed at communication with whatever looks back.
They also closely study the ethereal, and the more powerful ones are rumored to even dabble with inter-dimensional travel. Though how much of that is public relations is anyone's guess.
What Follows An Idiot

The Veritas Audax was written around 300. The author is unknown to us. It was found in 712 in a pre-Mazur temple on the outskirts of Lastrago by a Remosan academic expedition that was cataloguing religious sites.
For the first 143 years it mostly gathered dust in Urik-Van's historical collection, and in the very few times it was read, it was seen as what it is: epistemology. Very, very long epistemology.

Then, in the year 855, it was stolen, and the three guards who were on watch duty at the time disappeared with no trace. Then, and only then, people noticed. While the book was, and still is, missing, a local scribe had been copying it, and got as far as page 600.

The sort of drama that gets attention outside of scholarly circles alone, and that granted the surviving pages their allure. The Speculars, of all people, ought to appreciate the irony: their foundational text is itself a fragment, and nobody knows what comes after.

What began as a modest crowd of occultists and enthusiasts expanded rapidly with the appearance of Godrick Ferass. A Haldrithian guild-trained arcanist who was expelled from the Black Hands around 930 for pursuing research the guild didn't approve of.

I've pieced together what I can of the man from secondhand sources, and the picture I get is less of a genius and more of a particular kind of failure. Smart enough to follow the Audax's argument, vain enough to test it, and stupid enough to do so badly.

However, people do like their self-proclaimed geniuses. And so he gathered followers, gave the movement its name and its vocabulary, and established the Speculars as they are today. No headquarters, no hierarchy, nothing but the name, really.

Ferass didn't trust institutions, having been spat out by one, and the movement he built reflects that bitterness down to its bones. How he died is the kind of question that reveals more about the person answering it than the subject. The Speculars will tell you he completed the work.

He stepped through. The one account I find more convincing, though it's unverified, describes a man who had lost his mind entirely by the end, and was strangled with a pillow by one of his own followers.

We do have verified accounts of the abuse his followers went through, so I find myself hoping it's the latter. The cult moved often enough that even his burial site is uncertain. Or hidden, whichever narrative you prefer.
For the next four centuries the movement spread. Cells appeared in most cities at one point or another, small enough to avoid attention, persistent enough to survive the occasional raid.

The three schools formed during this period, though the exact dates are unclear and the Speculars themselves can't agree on who formalized what. The Fragmentists are the oldest branch, or claim to be.

The Amalgamists likely emerged later, once the Glaskatch shard trade gave them the tools they needed. The Inverters were always small, always strange, and always insistent that they were the original interpretation and everyone else had strayed. I'll leave them to their argument.
Notoriety
The event that turned the Speculars from a nuisance into a genuine threat was the Tintbent plot of 1397.

An Inverter cell led by one Thorro Rent, operating from somewhere in the Tintbent interior, attempted to collapse a section of the mountain range separating the Tintbent peninsula from the continent. The intention, as best anyone has reconstructed it, was to let the anomaly spread.

Trefganni border patrols intercepted the cell before the attempt could be carried out. The trial was brief. The executions were public. Within a decade, most jurisdictions had issued standing orders against Specular cells.
And the bans did what they always do: spread the word. Turn the odd niche into an exciting trend. As was later proved by the Cantemir affair of 1723.

Ciprian Cantemir, youngest son of one of Remosa's established noble houses, was replaced at age fifteen by a common-born Specular named Drazho Morarin. A craft-class kid from Netford who wanted a warm bed and a life where people used his name with respect.

The real Ciprian's identity was stripped and bound into an object using what we'd now call Doppler technique. His body was found in a storage cellar, weeks later, breathing and responding to nothing. Drazho lived as Ciprian for three years. Attended court. Signed papers. Married a girl.

The wife noticed first, told her sister, the sister told a priest. Eventually the rumor got to the boy's family. Drazho, when confronted, couldn't say where the object containing Ciprian had gone. He'd had the memory of the procedure blanked afterward. A safety measure.

The real Ciprian was never recovered. Drazho was executed in 1727. The Cantemir family pushed Remosa to issue a kill-order specifically targeting Speculars, which was granted, and which has accomplished exactly the results you'd expect.
Mirror Arcana

The Speculars coined the term "Mirror Arcana" for their practice, and have declared it a newfound school of magic. Whether it is one is among the longest standing arguments in arcane research, and I will certainly not be the one to solve it here.

I've spoken to colleagues on opposing sides of the debate in an attempt to explain it properly, and each agreed that my account is skewed toward the other's position. I take this as the closest thing my field has to peer review.
The traditionalists claim that every spell the Speculars associate with Mirror Arcana can be explained through an existing school. Be it conjuration, alteration, or otherwise.

The Speculars, on the other hand, think spellcasters have been utilizing the Mirror Realm all along without realizing it, and have since expanded on what they perceive to be an archaic use of misunderstood principles.

Misty Step, for example, or any displacement magic, is widely considered a Conjuration spell. To their eyes, however, since nothing was in fact conjured, none of the accepted schools account for what really occurred. The caster, in their view, passed through the Mirror Realm.
Which connects all points in Virelia the way a surface connects the things reflected on it. The caster moved. But the space he moved through was not our own.

From there the argument extends. If things are already connected through a shared reflective space, then new connections can be established between them, and old ones can be severed. What constitutes a thing's reflection is, in the Specular view, not fixed. Move one, the other follows.
Damage one, the other carries the wound. The connection holds until severed or until it breaks down on its own, which it does, and which the Speculars are less eager to discuss.

Most of what people actually encounter the Speculars doing follows from these two ideas. Broadly: displacement, mainly through reflective surfaces, transfer of properties between linked objects, or the severing of such connections.

Between a person and their own memories, being the most famous example. The Speculars consider all of these the same discipline. Whether or not they're right, the results are real enough, and that's what tends to draw attention.

The discipline is considered volatile and highly experimental, though dangers to casters are nothing new. A failed mirror spell can drive a man mad, but so can a failed illusion. It can leave him cut in half between two places, and evocation has produced messier halves.
On that count alone, no one would have bothered banning it. What distinguishes Mirror Arcana is that, if the Specular hypothesis is true, the practice doesn't merely endanger its practitioner.

It strains the same boundaries the Rifts have already fractured, and could deepen them, or open new ones. Hence the ban, in every jurisdiction I'm aware of. What I find amusing is that the consensus holds Mirror Arcana to be wrong about everything, and yet it is banned as if it is not.
This is not how a convinced academic community operates.
To Them The Streets

Officials tend to describe the Speculars the same way: inhumane, reckless. No place in civilized society. They do so right up until they have to pay a cell to erase a gambling debt from their wife's memory. And continue to do so afterwards. This is how the Speculars survive.
Not through cunning or secrecy, though some cells have plenty of both, but because the people responsible for destroying them keep finding reasons not to do it completely.

Practitioners organize into what official jargon calls cells. Three people in an abandoned house with a crate of shards, a funded operation behind a legitimate front, or a herbalist in a village nobody cares about.

Ferass' distrust of structured systems, or lack of foresight, turned out to be their greatest asset. You can't dismantle a structure that was never built, and certainly not when everyone meant to be fighting it seems to be paying it out of pocket. Wealthy families, guild officers...

Even when they don't seek the Speculars out, many pay a retainer for the guarantee that the service exists when a rival's judgment needs quiet altering, or a problem needs to go away without leaving a document trail. It's pragmatic, cynical, short-sighted and selfish. Politics, in short.

In fairness, most of what they sell is small. A memory shed here, a fear excised there, the client usually being the merchandise's original owner. Work on the scale of the Cantemir affair is rare, and treated as a line even inside the movement.
What a line is worth to people who erase things for a living, I leave to the reader.
Recruitment, supposedly, is handled through the Rite of the Glass. A ceremony repeated in occult circles enough times that it bled into general knowledge.

Supposedly, to emphasize again: stare into a mirror for twenty-four hours without food, speech, or looking away, and "they" will find you. I half believe it. It has the theatrical self-seriousness of Inverter practice, and the few accounts I've found do involve mirror-focused cells.

But given how decentralized the whole affair is, I don't see how the logistics work out. A specific cell's gimmick, perhaps. Who knows. Most recruits arrive by duller roads. Sanatoriums, universities, occult circles, mean-looking alehouses.
And the margins of Glaskatch, of course, where someone buying Static shards, the clouded dregs of the memory trade, has probably already accepted half of what they teach in the introductory courses.

Speculars don't advertise, unless you count the atrocities, which, to be fair, seem to draw attention very effectively. The ban, the mystique, and general desperation with the state of things do the rest.
VIP

In this day and age I don't believe the Speculars have a defined leadership. But I'll name some of the more influential living practitioners, both to paint a picture and because these are genuinely interesting specimens.

One name I keep encountering, and probably the closest thing the movement has to a leader, is Einar. No family name. He is said to have lived for several centuries by moving between bodies, and the documentation is more plausible than I'd like.

Someone operating under that name has been connected to shard and erasure operations in at least four regions across 167 years. Either the man has been swapping vessels for longer than most institutions have existed, or the name is passed along with the operation.

An Inverter by inclination and a merchant by practice. His network, if it is one man's network, is the largest Specular operation I'm aware of, and it sells forgetting. Espionage and assassination appear in the margins of his file as well. That's all I have on him, unfortunately.

Then there's Noella Dyann, "Nenne". An Amalgamist, and a beloved figure in Specular circles. She is, by every account, motherly, pleasant, patient and deeply knowledgeable. The type who makes a lot of tea and remembers her assistants' birthdays.

She is also, to my knowledge, the only active researcher systematically studying souls. Her position is that the Fragmentists are chasing the wrong target. Subtract personality all you like, the soul persists, still imposing its limits on perception.
The soul is the barrier, and she means to prove it. I've read some of her published work. Fascinating stuff. What the research looks like in practice is, unfortunately, gruesome.

Her hypothesis also creates a genuine problem for the movement, because if she's right, everything the Fragmentists have done to themselves amounts to pointless mutilation. The Fragmentists, for their part, have not slowed down.
If anything, the prospect of proving her wrong has given them a second wind.
Mirror School Spells
Cantrips
Minor Binding
Cantrip, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action Range: 30 feet
Components: S, M (two objects of similar nature)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You create a link between two Tiny objects you can see within range.

For the duration, when you use your action to move one object up to 15 feet, the other moves the same distance in the same direction, provided it is not held or worn by a creature and its path is not blocked by a solid surface.
If the second object's path is blocked, it stops and the binding ends.
The objects must share some degree of similarity (two stones, two coins, two pieces of wood). The GM determines whether the objects are sufficiently similar.
Reflection
Cantrip, divination
Casting Time: 1 action Range: Touch Components: S Duration: Instantaneous
You touch a reflective surface (a mirror, still water, polished metal) and receive a single still image of something the surface reflected within the last 5 hours, at a moment of the GM's choosing.

Repeated castings on the same surface return the same image until the surface reflects something new. The image is visual, with no detail finer than what a person standing before the surface would have seen. Magical disguises and illusions appear as they did to the surface at the time.
Tether
Cantrip, divination
Casting Time: 1 action Range: Touch
Components: S, M (a piece of the target, such as a hair, splinter, or fragment, which the spell consumes)
Duration: Concentration, up to 10 minutes
You touch a creature or object and establish a faint link. For the duration, you know the direction to the target, provided it is on the same plane of existence and within 120 feet of you.
If the target moves beyond 120 feet, you know the direction it was last in before leaving range, but receive no further updates until it returns.
1st Level
Exchange
1st-level, conjuration
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 30 feet
Components: V, S
Duration: Instantaneous
You and one willing creature you can see within range instantly swap positions. Each of you appears in the space the other occupied. Neither movement provokes opportunity attacks.
If either destination space cannot hold its new occupant, the spell fails and the slot is not expended.
2nd Level
Yank
2nd-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (a small hook or bent nail)
Duration: Instantaneous

You establish a momentary binding between yourself and a creature you can see within range, then wrench the connection. The target must make a Strength saving throw. On a failure, the target is pulled up to 30 feet in a straight line toward you.

If the target strikes a solid surface or creature during this movement, the movement stops and both the target and whatever it struck take 3d6 bludgeoning damage. On a success, the target is pulled up to 10 feet and takes no damage.
This movement does not provoke opportunity attacks.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the pull distance increases by 10 feet and the collision damage increases by 1d6 for each slot level above 2nd.
Flesh Link
2nd-level, necromancy
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (a strand of sinew or gut, tied in a knot)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You forge a link between two creatures you can see within range. Each unwilling creature can make a Constitution saving throw to resist the binding. If either target succeeds, the spell fails.

For the duration, whenever one linked creature takes damage from a single source (an attack, a spell, a fall), you can use your reaction to force the other linked creature to take necrotic damage equal to half the damage the first creature took, after any resistances or reductions are applied.
Damage transferred by this spell does not trigger further transfers. If an effect damages both linked creatures simultaneously (such as an area spell covering both), no transfer occurs.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 4th level or higher, you no longer need to use your reaction to trigger the transfer. It occurs automatically once per turn (the first time either linked creature takes damage on each turn).
Mirror Ward
2nd-level, abjuration
Casting Time: 1 reaction, which you take when you are hit by an attack
Range: Self Components: S, M (a reflective surface held in one hand, such as a hand mirror or polished blade)
Duration: Instantaneous
You angle the reflective surface against the incoming strike. You gain +3 to your AC against the triggering attack, potentially causing it to miss.

If the attack misses, whether or not the bonus was the cause, the attack is reflected. Choose a creature within 15 feet of you; the attack is rerolled against that creature, using the original attacker's attack bonus, and deals its normal damage on a hit.
A reflected attack cannot trigger reactions, and cannot be reflected again.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the AC bonus increases by 1 for each slot level above 2nd.
3rd Level
Binding
3rd-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action Range: 60 feet Components: V, S, M (a piece of chain or rope) Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute

You create a sustained binding between yourself and a creature you can see within range. The target must make a Strength saving throw. On a failure, the target is bound to your movement for the duration.

Whenever you move on your turn, the bound creature is dragged the same distance in the same direction. If the creature has its reaction available, the strain of resisting consumes it. This movement provokes opportunity attacks.
If the creature would be dragged into a solid surface, it takes 2d6 bludgeoning damage and its movement stops at the surface; your own movement is unaffected.
The bound creature can repeat the Strength saving throw at the end of each of its turns, ending the effect on a success.
Limitations. The binding breaks if you and the target are ever more than 120 feet apart, or on different planes of existence.
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 5th level or higher, the collision damage increases to 3d6 and the creature has disadvantage on its saves to end the effect.
Prism Shell
3rd-level, abjuration
Casting Time: 1 action Range: Self Components: V, S, M (a glass prism)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You surround yourself with a shell of refracted light. For the duration:
You have half cover (+2 to AC and Dexterity saving throws) against attacks originating from more than 10 feet away.
When a ranged attack (weapon or spell) misses you while this spell is active, you can use your reaction to redirect the attack toward a creature within 15 feet of you.
The attack is rerolled against the new target, using the original attacker's attack bonus, and deals its normal damage on a hit.
The shell sheds dim light in a 5-foot radius and is faintly visible as a distortion in the air.
Sever
3rd-level, abjuration
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: Touch
Components: V, S, M (a small mirror, which is cracked as part of the casting)
Duration: Instantaneous
You sever a specific connection affecting the target creature. Choose one of the following:

Magical Bond. You end one spell currently affecting the target, provided it is of 3rd level or lower and is a charm, fear, compulsion, or curse effect. For qualifying spells of 4th level or higher, make an ability check using your spellcasting ability (DC = 10 + the spell's level).
This spell cannot end curses that are not spells (a cursed item's attunement, lycanthropy, a divine punishment); those require Remove Curse or stronger magic.

Temporary Suppression. You suppress a specific memory in a willing creature. The target loses access to one memory of your choice (specified during casting) for 24 hours. The memory returns fully after this period. The target is aware something has been suppressed but cannot recall what.
A Remove Curse or Greater Restoration spell ends this effect early.

At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a spell slot of 5th level or higher, the Temporary Suppression duration extends to 7 days, and Magical Bond automatically ends qualifying spells of a level equal to or lower than the slot used.
When you use a slot of 7th level or higher, the suppression duration extends to 30 days.
4th Level
Mirror Scry
4th-level, divination
Casting Time: 10 minutes Range: Touch (Prepare) or Unlimited, same plane (Observe) Components: V, S, M (a silver mirror worth at least 50 gp)
Duration: Instantaneous (Prepare) or Concentration, up to 10 minutes (Observe)
When you cast this spell, choose one of its two functions. Each function requires its own casting.

Prepare. You touch a reflective surface (a mirror, polished metal, a still pool of water) and mark it with an invisible arcane sigil. The sigil lasts until dispelled or until the surface is destroyed. You can have up to 5 surfaces prepared at a time.
Preparing a new surface beyond this limit causes the oldest sigil to fade.

Observe. Using a silver mirror as a focus, you can see and hear through any surface you have previously prepared, as if you were standing directly before it. You can switch between prepared surfaces as an action. The observed surface shows whatever is within 30 feet of it.
Creatures can detect the scrying sensor with a successful Wisdom (Perception) check against your spell save DC, noticing a faint shimmer in the reflective surface.
5th Level
Glasswalk
5th-level, conjuration
Casting Time: 1 action Range: 10 feet Components: V, S Duration: 1 round

You step into a mirror or reflective surface large enough for you to pass through (at least 5 feet tall for a Medium creature) and instantly teleport to another such surface that you have physically touched at some point in the past, on the same plane of existence.
You emerge from the destination surface.
The entry surface remains an open portal until the end of your next turn. During this time, any creature that can fit through the surface can step through and arrive at the same destination.
Once used as a portal, both surfaces become nonmagical and cannot be used for this spell again for 24 hours.
The destination surface must still exist and be intact at the time of casting. If the destination surface has been destroyed, the spell fails and the spell slot is not expended.
Unsynchronize
5th-level, enchantment
Casting Time: 1 minute
Range: Touch
Components: V, S, M (a Glaskatch personality shard worth at least 500 gp, which the spell consumes)
Duration: Instantaneous

You permanently sever the connection between a creature and a specific aspect of its identity. The target must be willing or incapacitated. An unwilling target, even an incapacitated one, makes a Wisdom saving throw as the casting completes.
On a success, the spell fails and the shard is consumed anyway. Choose one of the following:

Memory. A specific memory, up to one hour of continuous experience, is permanently erased. The target retains skills and proficiencies learned during that time but loses all episodic recollection of the events.

Trait. A personality trait, bond, ideal, or flaw is permanently removed. The target's behavior shifts accordingly over the following days. This cannot remove racial traits, class features, or proficiencies.

Emotion. The target's capacity for a specific emotion (grief, fear, jealousy, love for a specific person) is permanently deadened. The target can still recognize situations where the emotion would apply but does not experience it.

A Greater Restoration spell cast within 24 hours of the severance restores what was removed. After that window closes, the severance cannot be reversed by anything besides a Wish spell. If the target was willing, they must confirm consent aloud as part of the casting.
The target is aware of what will be removed but cannot, by the spell's nature, fully anticipate the consequences.

Repeated castings on the same creature are cumulative. A creature that has undergone more than three severances must make a Wisdom saving throw (DC 15) after each subsequent casting. On a failure, the creature suffers indefinite madness as determined by the GM.
Major Binding
5th-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (two lengths of chain, linked)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute

You create a powerful binding between yourself and a creature you can see within range. The target must make a Strength saving throw. On a failure, the creature is bound to you for the duration, with the following effects:

Mirrored Movement. As with Binding, the target is dragged to match your movement, and the strain consumes its reaction if one is available. This movement provokes opportunity attacks. If the creature would be dragged into a solid surface, it takes 4d6 bludgeoning damage.

Shared Fate. When you are forced to make a saving throw against a spell or effect, you can use your reaction to force the bound creature to make the same saving throw against the same effect, as though it were also a target. The creature uses its own saving throw modifiers.

The bound creature can repeat the Strength saving throw at the end of each of its turns, at disadvantage, ending the effect on a success. The binding breaks if you and the target are ever more than 120 feet apart or on different planes.
6th Level
Mirror Prison
6th-level, conjuration
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 60 feet
Components: V, S, M (a silver-framed mirror worth at least 1,000 gp)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 hour

You attempt to trap a creature you can see within range inside a reflective surface. The component mirror must be large enough to display the target's full reflection; if it is not, the spell fails and the slot is not expended. The target must make a Charisma saving throw.
On a failure, the creature is pulled into the mirror used as the material component for this spell. On a success, the creature is unaffected.
While imprisoned, the creature is aware of its surroundings as seen from within the mirror. It can see out and speak, though its voice sounds distant and distorted.
The creature cannot interact with the physical world, cast spells that target anything outside the mirror, or take physical actions.

If the imprisoned creature is within line of sight of another reflective surface (a second mirror, a pool of water, polished armor), it can use its movement to transfer to that surface on its turn, provided the surface is large enough to display its full reflection.
It cannot leave the reflective surface by any means while the spell persists.
The imprisoned creature can repeat the Charisma saving throw each time it transfers to a new surface, and once every 10 minutes otherwise, ending the effect on a success.

The prison also ends when the spell's duration expires, when your concentration is broken, when the surface currently holding the creature is destroyed (the creature appears in the nearest unoccupied space, taking 4d6 force damage), or when the spell is dispelled.
7th Level
Doppler
7th-level, enchantment

Casting Time: 1 hour Range: Touch Components: V, S, M (a Glaskatch personality shard worth at least 5,000 gp, a mirror large enough to reflect both targets, and a drop of blood from the source creature — all consumed) Duration: Until dispelled

You overwrite one creature's identity onto another. This spell requires two creatures: the source (whose identity is copied) and the vessel (who receives it). Both must be present for the full casting time. The vessel must be incapacitated or willing.
The source can be willing, incapacitated, or dead (dead no longer than 10 days).
Upon completion, the vessel's personality, memories, mannerisms, and emotional patterns are replaced with those of the source.

The vessel retains its own physical body, hit points, and physical ability scores (Strength, Dexterity, Constitution), but its mental ability scores (Intelligence, Wisdom, Charisma) are replaced with those of the source.

The vessel gains the source's proficiencies and class features, up to a total class level no greater than the vessel's own level or Hit Dice; capabilities beyond that limit are present as knowledge and memory but do not function, surfacing over time or never, at the GM's discretion.
The source creature is unaffected if alive and willing. Its identity is copied, not moved. If the source is dead, the copy is drawn from the body's residual imprint.

The vessel's original identity is suppressed, not destroyed. It persists beneath the surface. Under extreme duress, magical compulsion, or exposure to deeply personal stimuli from the vessel's original life, the GM may call for a Wisdom saving throw (DC equals your spell save DC).
On a success, the vessel's original identity reasserts itself for 1d4 hours before being suppressed again. Each reassertion lowers the DC by 1.

The spell can be ended by Dispel Magic cast at 7th level or higher, by a Wish spell, or by performing this spell again on the vessel with intent to strip the overwritten identity without replacing it (consuming materials as normal, leaving the vessel in a confused,
identity-less state for 2d6 days before their original self gradually returns).
At Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using a 9th-level spell slot, you can designate an object as the vessel. The source creature's identity is stripped from its body and bound to the object.
The body is left alive but empty — breathing, responsive to stimulus, but with no personality, memory, or will.

The identity within the object has no senses and no means of communication unless the object is reflective (a mirror, polished metal), in which case the trapped identity can perceive what the surface reflects and can speak, faintly, to those nearby.
8th Level
Refraction
8th-level, transmutation
Casting Time: 1 action
Range: 120 feet
Components: V, S, M (a shattered mirror, the pieces of which are thrown into the air during casting)
Duration: Concentration, up to 1 minute
You fracture the spatial geometry of a 60-foot cube originating from a point you can see within range. For the duration, the affected area is warped by broken reflective symmetry:
Distorted Space. The area is difficult terrain for all creatures except you. Creatures other than you have disadvantage on Dexterity saving throws while within the area.
Bent Trajectories. Ranged weapon attacks and ranged spell attacks that pass through any part of the area have disadvantage.
Spatial Displacement. The first time a creature enters the area or starts its turn there, it must make an Intelligence saving throw.

On a failure, the creature is teleported to a random unoccupied space within the area (roll a d8 for direction, d6 × 10 for distance in feet; if the result would place it outside the area, it appears at the nearest space within it).
A creature that has made this save, whatever the outcome, is not subject to Spatial Displacement again unless it leaves the area and re-enters.

Mirror Passages. You can use a bonus action on your turn to swap the positions of two creatures within the area. Each creature must make a Charisma saving throw. The swap occurs only if both creatures fail; otherwise, neither moves.
Creatures with truesight are immune to the Spatial Displacement effect but are still affected by the other properties.
9th Level
Inversion
9th-level (classification never settled)
Casting Time: 1 minute
Range: Self
Components: V, S, M (a flawless mirror worth at least 25,000 gp, which shatters when the spell is cast)
Duration: Instantaneous
The ultimate expression of Specular philosophy. You step through the boundary between Virelia and the Mirror Realm.

Upon casting, your body on this side of the boundary becomes a reflection: visible in mirrors and reflective surfaces but physically absent. Your consciousness crosses into the Mirror Realm, whatever that may be. This is a one-way effect.

There is no known counterspell, no reversal, no return. Wish can restore the caster's body to its last physical state, but it is unclear whether the consciousness that returns is the original or the reflection.
The flawless mirror shatters upon completion and cannot be repaired or reconstructed by any means short of divine intervention.
The caster's reflection persists in mirrors and reflective surfaces near the casting location for 1d10 days, occasionally moving or speaking, before fading permanently.
GM Note. This spell is included for narrative completeness. It is not intended as a standard player option. A character who casts Inversion has, in mechanical terms, left the campaign.

Whether the Mirror Realm exists, whether the caster survives the crossing, and what (if anything) looks back from the other side is entirely at the GM's discretion. The Speculars consider this spell a success. Everyone else considers it suicide. Neither side has conclusive evidence.

the_halcyon_league.title: The Halcyon League
the_halcyon_league.text:
The Halcyon League
A Matter of Opinion
Unpopular as it is, I retain my position that the Halcyons are a bank dressed up as something more in order to claim neutrality, exploit its workers and retain a virtuous image, with the goodwill that comes alongside it.
An army of skilled runners, inns to house them, and the only established financial network on the continent.
The more generous narrative is that they're an organization which dedicates itself to maintaining communication throughout Virelia, which also maintains a banking front, "on the side," to fund its pursuit of this grand goal.
Most Virelians, and certainly most Halcyons, prefer the latter narrative. That's not to say that it's more true, only that it is more convenient.
Some of my colleagues argue we should judge the Halcyons by their philosophy and intentions, which are, by all accounts, rather noble. Silly old me prefers to judge things by the physical reality, not some naive notion of what might be going through someone's head.
And in the physical reality, the Halcyons possess more money and more leverage than most governments, and a history of using both, with a splash of violence here and there.

glaskatch.title: Glaskatch
glaskatch.text:
Glaskatch
"It was the weirdest date of my life. I think she was wearing a 'Witty' shard that had belonged to an old man? She kept cracking jokes about the price of wool and calling me 'sonny'. I wasn't sure if she was flirting or vetting me for her bridge club."
- Overheard in a tavern
Overview
Glaskatch sits at the southern terminus of the Quiet Road, on the northern shore of Trail's End Lake, technically inside Southfield but operating with enough autonomy that nobody in the region pretends otherwise.
It is not a large city, perhaps eight thousand permanent residents, but it carries an outsized reputation across most of Virelia. Glaskatch is where the dead are made portable.
The city is the only place in the world that practices the personality shard trade at scale. Mediators, Extractors, Resonance Houses, and the Ethics Tribunal that licenses all of them have grown together over two centuries into a single integrated economy that does almost nothing else.
People come here to preserve the dead, to graft skill they couldn't otherwise afford, and occasionally to remove parts of themselves they no longer want. The city accommodates all three with the same quiet professionalism. It does not advertise. It does not need to.
The Trade
When someone dies, their family contracts with a licensed Extractor to harvest specific aspects of the deceased's personality before the imprint fades.
The Extractor takes a psychic impression of chosen traits, a master blacksmith's sense of proportion, a mother's warmth, a diplomat's patience, and binds it into a small crystalline medium.
The shard can then be worn or temporarily integrated by a living person, who carries the fragment as long as they need it.
The most common use is grief. A bereaved spouse buys a sliver of their partner's warmth and carries it in a locket, and the dead are not gone in the way the dead are gone elsewhere. The second most common use is craft.
An apprentice blacksmith saves for years to afford a fragment of a legendary smith's instinct for metal, and the years it would have taken to develop that instinct on his own become months. Beyond these two, the trade extends in every direction the human personality can be cut into pieces.
Negotiators rent slivers of historic mediators for difficult treaties. Officers wear fragments of famous tacticians' battlefield clarity before a campaign. Some buyers come for things they don't admit to wanting.
The practice is invasive. Wearing a shard means hosting a fragment of someone else's mind, and the fragment occasionally leaks.
A merchant carrying a patience-shard might suddenly recall a childhood memory that isn't his, or speak in an unfamiliar dialect for a few seconds, or laugh in a way his wife doesn't recognize. The locals call this
bleeding
, and the etiquette around it is absolute: when someone bleeds, you wait, you say nothing, you do not draw attention. Children are taught the rule before they can read.
If someone bleeds, be still and kind.
The other half of the etiquette is Memory Fasting. A citizen who has been wearing too many shards for too long voluntarily removes them all and spends days or weeks reconnecting with their authentic self.
They wear a grey ribbon on the wrist while doing it, the way someone elsewhere might wear a sling, and the city accommodates them. Conversations stay simple. Decisions are not asked of them.
The Still House and the Fasting Hall both offer rooms for the practice, ranging from comfortable to monastic depending on how serious the fast is.
Not all souls are equal, and the market reflects this with brutal precision. The rare temperament patterns, the perfect calm and inspired genius and masterful intuition that integrate seamlessly with any host, are called Pristine grade and sell for enough to buy a house.
Most working professionals wear Commercial grade, the steady useful traits a craftsman or scholar can save for.
At the bottom of the market are Static shards: clouded, low-quality fragments that offer nothing but vague urges and confusion, sold in plain cloth pouches in the Main Market for copper. The desperate buy them anyway. Some never stop buying them.
The Look
Glaskatch is the quietest city in Virelia. Not silent in the Southfield way, where conversation is a duty kept in check, but quiet by design. The streets are paved with stone laid over packed earth to muffle footfalls.
The buildings are constructed with thick walls and sound-dampening panels in the ceilings. Nobody hangs signs that creak, nobody installs door chimes, and the carts that move through the wider avenues run on padded wheels.
The result is a city where you can hear a kettle boil three rooms away and where a raised voice carries half a district.
The colors match the sound. Muted greys, soft browns, undyed wool, slate, weathered timber. The Resonance Houses are pale stone with shuttered windows and no decoration on the facades.
The wealthier townhouses are larger versions of the same, with carved plaques beside their doors instead of signs. There is no civic statuary anywhere, no triumphal arches, no monuments.
Glaskatch built itself for trade and contemplation, in that order, and it has never seen a reason to ornament either.

segments.text: Glaskatch

"It was the weirdest date of my life. I think she was wearing a 'Witty' shard that had belonged to an old man? She kept cracking jokes about the price of wool and calling me 'sonny'. I wasn't sure if she was flirting or vetting me for her bridge club."
- Overheard in a tavern
Overview

Glaskatch sits at the southern terminus of the Quiet Road, on the northern shore of Trail's End Lake, technically inside Southfield but operating with enough autonomy that nobody in the region pretends otherwise.
It is not a large city, perhaps eight thousand permanent residents, but it carries an outsized reputation across most of Virelia. Glaskatch is where the dead are made portable.

The city is the only place in the world that practices the personality shard trade at scale. Mediators, Extractors, Resonance Houses, and the Ethics Tribunal that licenses all of them have grown together over two centuries into a single integrated economy that does almost nothing else.

People come here to preserve the dead, to graft skill they couldn't otherwise afford, and occasionally to remove parts of themselves they no longer want. The city accommodates all three with the same quiet professionalism. It does not advertise. It does not need to.
The Trade
When someone dies, their family contracts with a licensed Extractor to harvest specific aspects of the deceased's personality before the imprint fades.
The Extractor takes a psychic impression of chosen traits, a master blacksmith's sense of proportion, a mother's warmth, a diplomat's patience, and binds it into a small crystalline medium.
The shard can then be worn or temporarily integrated by a living person, who carries the fragment as long as they need it.

The most common use is grief. A bereaved spouse buys a sliver of their partner's warmth and carries it in a locket, and the dead are not gone in the way the dead are gone elsewhere. The second most common use is craft.

An apprentice blacksmith saves for years to afford a fragment of a legendary smith's instinct for metal, and the years it would have taken to develop that instinct on his own become months. Beyond these two, the trade extends in every direction the human personality can be cut into pieces.

Negotiators rent slivers of historic mediators for difficult treaties. Officers wear fragments of famous tacticians' battlefield clarity before a campaign. Some buyers come for things they don't admit to wanting.
The practice is invasive. Wearing a shard means hosting a fragment of someone else's mind, and the fragment occasionally leaks.

A merchant carrying a patience-shard might suddenly recall a childhood memory that isn't his, or speak in an unfamiliar dialect for a few seconds, or laugh in a way his wife doesn't recognize. The locals call this

If someone bleeds, be still and kind.

The other half of the etiquette is Memory Fasting. A citizen who has been wearing too many shards for too long voluntarily removes them all and spends days or weeks reconnecting with their authentic self.
They wear a grey ribbon on the wrist while doing it, the way someone elsewhere might wear a sling, and the city accommodates them. Conversations stay simple. Decisions are not asked of them.
The Still House and the Fasting Hall both offer rooms for the practice, ranging from comfortable to monastic depending on how serious the fast is.

Not all souls are equal, and the market reflects this with brutal precision. The rare temperament patterns, the perfect calm and inspired genius and masterful intuition that integrate seamlessly with any host, are called Pristine grade and sell for enough to buy a house.
Most working professionals wear Commercial grade, the steady useful traits a craftsman or scholar can save for.

downsview.title: Downsview
downsview.text:
Downsview
"They voted three times on whether the sky was clear enough to hold the Spring View. By the time it passed, it was nearly dusk. So the first clear day of spring, officially, was held in the dark."
- A merchant from Glenroot, telling the story for the fourth time
The Village Above the Quiet
Downsview is what happens when a handful of Southfielders decide they have had enough of potatoes, whispering, and dying politely among their flock.
It sits on a cluster of high hills roughly three days off the Quiet Road, reached by a switchback track that punishes carts and rewards walkers. From almost any window in the village, the land falls away into a long sweep of grazing pasture and scrub.
On clear days you can see Henon Bay in the distance. On the clearest, the fishing boats. The name does what names should.
The village is barely thirty years old and looks it: tall, narrow houses built tight against the slope, whitewashed walls, painted shutters in whatever color the owner felt like that year, slate roofs angled into the wind. There are no sound-baffles, no padded doors, no heavy curtains.
Windows actually open. Older Southfielders visiting for the first time sometimes stand in the main square for a full minute, unsure what to do with the sound of their own footsteps.
The Defectors
Downsview was founded by farmers who walked out on the agricultural interior and by visitors who came for the view and simply never left. The founding families were tired of whispering.
Children are allowed to run in the lanes, musicians play outdoors, and arguments happen in full sentences. Neighboring villages send sternly worded letters about once a season, Widow Parns frames the best of them and hangs them behind the bar at her inn.
The letters are a point of quiet pride.
Most of Southfield considers the place a mild embarrassment. Downsview, for its part, has been called worse and in fuller voices.
The Calendar of Excuses
The village lives on visitors, and visitors come for festivals. Any excuse will do.
There is the Spring View, held on the first clear day of the season by council vote; the Harvest Bleating, which is exactly what it sounds like; the Midsummer Fair, the largest gathering of the year; the Lantern Climb, held in autumn and somehow both dangerous and mandatory; and, most recently,
the Livestock Beauty Contest, heading into its fourth year and already responsible for two feuds, one engagement, and one minor stampede. Most locals will happily explain which festival is the real one and why the others were invented by rival families to spite theirs.
Between festivals, the village runs on wool and lodging. The Fletcher Sisters — three spinster weavers who finish each other's sentences and judge everyone who walks into their shop — produce the finest blankets in Southfield.
Nearly every household keeps a spare bed or two for travelers; Garrick the blacksmith will rent you the loft above his forge, and Mistress Hennie the baker will rent you the chair by her oven if you ask at the right hour.
A single stubborn vegetable farmer supplies the village's greens and insists that the hillside soil is the finest in the region, a claim he will defend with his fists if pressed.
Quiet Business
The mayor is Barnaby Parns, a round, flustered man in a sash half a size too tight, who makes most of the village's official decisions. His mother, Widow Parns, makes most of those.
Between them the village runs on a mix of show-of-hands voting and maternal decree, which outsiders sometimes mistake for corruption. The Compact knows Downsview exists, collects its taxes, and otherwise leaves it alone.

Notable Locations
•
The Lamb & Flag:
Widow Parns' inn and tavern on the main square, and the heart of the village. Low timber beams, a fire that's never allowed to go out, a Shepherd's Pie that's 80% potato, and a strict no-politics rule (sheep genetics excepted).
•
The Chapel:
A drafty old stone chapel at the eastern edge, its bell tower collapsed in a storm years ago and never rebuilt. Father Thomas sells herbal poultices and "blessed rain," and rents out the rectory's spare rooms to the occasional traveler.
•
Hennie's Oven:
Mistress Hennie's bakery, and the village's gossip exchange. Heavy sourdough, honey-cakes, and meat pasties for the field hands. If you want to know who is courting whom, you buy a bun here.
•
The Iron-Shoe:
Garrick's smithy. Smells of hot iron and wet horse. Mostly horseshoes, plowshares, and nails; he can sharpen a sword but will look mildly offended about it. The local farmers loiter here to smoke pipes and complain about the weather.
•
The Spindle & Loom:
The Fletcher Sisters' weaving shop. Three spinning wheels turning in perfect unison, the finest wool blankets in Southfield, and a great deal of silent judgment.
•
The General Ledger:
Mayor Barnaby's office and the village's dry-goods store. Salt, sugar, candles, rope, and a desk piled high with judging forms for the beauty contest. Organized chaos.
•

The largest sheep operation on the lower slopes. Patrolled by a goose. Home to the prize bull. No casual visitors.

•
The Fourth Ribbon:
Old Man Krell, the largest sheep farmer on the lower slopes, has won the Livestock Beauty Contest three years running and is paralyzed by the thought of losing the fourth.
His prize bull is guarded day and night by two terrified shepherd twins and a goose called Honk, whose hatred is the purest thing in the village.
In the tavern, the farmer Jareth — who drinks more than he farms — nurses a plan to humiliate Krell at this year's contest without hurting the bull.

The party arrives the week of the fair.
•
What's in the Basement:
The two scholars currently lodging at the Hollow Chapel — a dreamy elven minstrel named Liriam and her cynical human partner Corin — are not here for the view.
Whatever they are looking for in Father Thomas's forgotten archive, they are not volunteering to explain it, and Thomas has started to notice.
•
Ghost Goblins:
Krell's shepherds keep losing sheep to what they swear are ghosts in the scrub east of the village. The ghosts are goblins. The council would rather not discuss it during festival season.

segments.text: Downsview
"They voted three times on whether the sky was clear enough to hold the Spring View. By the time it passed, it was nearly dusk. So the first clear day of spring, officially, was held in the dark."
- A merchant from Glenroot, telling the story for the fourth time
The Village Above the Quiet

It sits on a cluster of high hills roughly three days off the Quiet Road, reached by a switchback track that punishes carts and rewards walkers. From almost any window in the village, the land falls away into a long sweep of grazing pasture and scrub.
