glenroot.title: Glenroot
glenroot.text:
Glenroot
"The first rule of the Long-Iron is that the handle is fifteen feet long for a reason. The second rule is that fourteen feet is how you lose an apprentice. The third rule is that the head outlasts the handle ten to one. Replace handles every season."
- A Glenroot apprentice's first day of training
The Quiet Fields
Glenroot sits on the bank of the Grenset River, one day upstream from Lake Verdane, deep in the conservative interior of Southfield.
From a distance it looks like any other riverside village — low stone houses, roofs thatched in thick sound-dampening moss, packed-dirt streets kept deliberately soft underfoot. The pontoon docks are the first thing that gives the place away.
They float because the Grenset cannot be trusted to stay at any particular level for long. The second clue is that nobody, not the dockworkers, not the children, not the woman dropping a bucket, makes any sound at all.
This is Southfield at its most observant.
Glenroot keeps the silence the way a temple keeps its rites — not from any belief that the crops still need it, since that magic is three generations gone, but because dropping a tool here is a faux pas and raising one's voice is roughly equivalent to throwing a punch.
Locals communicate in Field-Sign, a pragmatic dialect of farm-hand gestures, or by writing on slates and chalkboards. Visitors are tolerated; loud visitors are escorted to the village boundary by Captain Bord, who finds the whole business of law enforcement a chore but does it anyway.
Anomaly Agriculture
What makes Glenroot more than another quiet riverside village lies just past its eastern fields.
The Patchwork Fields are a grid of farmland crisscrossed by stable temporal anomalies — pockets where the local rate of time has, since some forgotten event, settled into something other than the rest of the world's. The villagers do not pretend to understand them. They farm them.
The Deep-Wait zones are pockets where time crawls at one-tenth the outside rate. Crops inside them take a full decade of external sunlight to grow what a normal field manages in a year, and they soak up the entire ten years of sun, rain, and slow ripening before harvest.
The result is dense, complex, and ruinously expensive: Stone-Root turnips so calorie-rich a fist-sized one will feed a family, and grapes that produce wines of impossible vintage inside a single calendar year.
Farmers work these pockets from outside, using Long-Irons — hoes and rakes with fifteen-foot handles — and apprentices are taught from their first day to never, ever step inside "just for a moment."
An apprentice who slips in to pull a weed for what feels like ten minutes will emerge to find the sun low, his shift over, and his master furious.
The Quick-Step zones run at ten times the outside rate, and the crops there grow furiously without ever absorbing enough nutrients to be worth eating.
The result is "water-balloon" produce — radishes the size of melons that taste like wet cardboard, sold in bulk to the Greywater Compact as cheap army rations. Working these fields ages a farmer brutally fast.
An hour's labor inside burns through nearly half a day of life; hands gray, joints stiffen, skin peels.
The Quick-Steppers wear mechanical clickers called Timer-Canaries to track exposure, and the village's most prominent example of what the work costs is Jory "Spring" Miller, twenty-four years old and prematurely silver, working double shifts to afford something called a Stasis-Bed.
The third zone is the Rot-Bed, a fenced-off patch of accelerated entropy at the village edge. Organic waste dumped there becomes black, fertile soil in hours.
It smells of sulfur and aggressive life, and is overseen by "Rotty" Hobb, an oil-skinned compost master with three missing fingers who is, through the careful application of fertilizer fees, one of the wealthiest men in Glenroot.
The Patchwork Fields are also why most outsiders bother making the long quiet trip upriver in the first place.
A steady trickle of scholars from the Greywater academies and farther afield comes through Glenroot each year to study how a village of dirt-streaked farmers casually manages, every season, what their archmages can barely sustain in a laboratory: the stable,
agricultural exploitation of rift phenomena. The scholars take notes, ask polite questions on slates, and leave more impressed than when they arrived. The villagers tolerate them, charge them inn rates, and have long since stopped finding them interesting.
Quiet Business
Glenroot is governed, technically, by a council of elders, and in practice by Elder Olenna, a stern silver-haired woman in heavy wool shawls who carries a tuning fork on a staff and communicates exclusively through her slate.
She maps the borders of the anomalies herself, walking the fields each morning to check whether the Deep-Wait has crept a foot east overnight. Her authority is unquestioned and her patience for outsiders is finite.
Mother Gimm, the village's tiny, clouded-eyed herbalist, treats the Quick-Step farmers when they come in burned. She brews a tea that slows the aging, or claims to, but its primary ingredients grow only in Knotsreach and her supplier has been three months late.
Torren "Soft-Hammer" is the blacksmith, a massive man who whispers, wraps his hammer in leather, and forges the village's Long-Irons; he has been trying for years to invent a silent bellows and is, by all accounts, losing.
Notable Locations
•
The Triver Inn:
Mara Triver's bunker of comfort, walls hung with heavy wool tapestries to absorb every sound. Patrons drink alone or play cards in hand-signs. A large slate on the back wall serves as the village square — news, poetry, and grievances are written there rather than spoken.
Mara's ward Kip, a scrawny ink-stained sixteen-year-old with a stash of stolen maps and a forbidden interest in the Halcyon League, sweeps the floors and dreams loudly about leaving.
•
The Clay Clock:
A pottery workshop full of dust and silence, run by Elara Clay, a deaf dwarven potter who reads lips perfectly and is, by some margin, the calmest person in town.
Her specialty is Stasis-Jars: vessels fired from clay harvested in the Deep-Wait, which retain a faint fragment of the slowed time and preserve food inside them for months. They are her livelihood and, currently, her smuggling operation.
•
The Grenset Docks:
Floating pontoons rising and falling on the Grenset's unreliable currents. The flat-bottomed river-haulers tie up here to load Stasis-Jars for the trip downstream to Lake Verdane.
The current senior hauler, Lisbet, has refused to sail at night for two months and will not say what she saw the last time she did.
•
The Long-Iron Forge:
Torren's smithy. Larger than it needs to be to accommodate the fifteen-foot tool handles. The hammer falls are wrapped, the anvil sits on a thick wool pad, and the bellows are still loud enough to make Torren wince every time he pumps them.
•
Mother Gimm's Hut:
A low stone shed at the village edge, smelling of dried sage and bitter tea. Patients lie on a cot inside while Gimm explains, in perfect clinical detail and with no bedside manner whatsoever, exactly how their condition will progress.
•
The Rot-Bed:
A fenced compost pit east of the Patchwork Fields, where the Quick-Step's twin runs in reverse. Hobb runs it. Nobody else willingly stands downwind.
Plot Hooks
•
The Audit:
Silas Vane, a gaunt grey-velvet Compact tax auditor in the late stages of what locals call Silence Sickness, has been camped at the Triver Inn for three weeks and knows the harvest numbers don't add up. The village is producing more Deep-Wait luxury crops than it's reporting.
Olenna and Hobb are hiding the surplus in Stasis-Jars buried inside the Rot-Bed, betting Silas is too fastidious to dig through accelerated compost to find them. He has just threatened to summon a Lienhunter squad from Rivhalde if the books aren't balanced by tomorrow.
The village is preparing to riot, quietly.
•
The River Thing:
Lisbet has not sailed at night in two months. She will not explain what she saw on the Grenset between Glenroot and Lake Verdane, and the late-evening haulers have started losing cargo and crews.
Whatever is out there is getting bolder, and the village's livelihood depends on the route staying open.
•
What Old Kaelen Remembers:
Old Kaelen, a one-legged, one-eyed retired adventurer in his nineties, sits on a bench facing the Rot-Bed every day, muttering about something he calls "The Mire." Locals think he's senile.
He has also been trying to remember where, decades ago, he hid an old enchanted sword — and he is getting close. Someone patient enough to listen might learn what The Mire is before whatever's left of it learns about Glenroot.

brenmath.title: Brenmath
brenmath.text:
Brenmath
"They told me at the gate that the Legion Road would take me straight to the Forum, and I started walking. That was four hours ago. The road is still going. The Forum is, I am told, ahead."
- A Compact courier, in a letter
Overview
Brenmath is the largest city in Trefgann and one of the largest in Virelia.
The Remosan Empire built it at the height of the Shining Age as a provincial capital, designed to administer half a continent, and even after two centuries of Trefganner rule the population has only grown into about two-thirds of the original walls.
The other third is empty: weed-grown plazas, half-collapsed barracks, the slow ruin of the old patrician quarter where nobody has lived in a century. Brenmen joke that the city has more buildings than residents and more residents than anyone can keep track of.
Brenmath sits a week east of Tharlin's Crossing, on the eastern shore of Lake Verdane. It is the first major city anyone reaches after crossing into Trefgann from Remosa, and the gates see a constant trickle of refugees, defectors, merchants, smugglers, deserters, and Compact couriers.
It is also the rallying point for three successful wars against the Empire that built it, and the institutional home of Trefgann's largest military tradition.
The First Impression
You come through the West Gate after a week's walk from Tharlin's Crossing, and the first thing that hits you is the scale. The gate itself is a Remosan triumphal arch fifty feet high, with the names of three lost legions still legible on the lintel after two centuries of weather.
The road inside was built for a legion to march six abreast. It is currently full of vegetable carts, a militia patrol in worn leather, two children chasing a chicken, and a fishwife arguing with a moneylender in the flat Brenman accent that swallows half the consonants.
Above the rooftops you can see the great triumphal column with three lines of laundry strung from it, and beyond that the marble dome of the old governor's palace.
Nobody bothered to rename anything. The forum is still the forum. The baths are still the baths. The avenue you walked in on is still called the Legion Road, because that was its name under the Emperors and changing it seemed like effort no one wanted to spend.
The Look
Marble everywhere, in every district, all of it gone slightly grey.
Brenmath was built in the Shining Age, when the Remosan Empire could call buildings into being out of stone the gods had given them, and what they made was uniformly white, uniformly massive, and uniformly meant to last forever.
Two centuries later the marble still stands, but it has lost its shine. Wind and rain have darkened it. Soot from the dye-houses has streaked it. Every wall in the city looks slightly tired, like a banquet hall the morning after.
The shape of the city is still imperial. Wide ceremonial avenues meet at right angles in great open squares. Ranges of identical barracks march up the slopes in formation.
Every public building is colonnaded, every doorway twice as tall as it needs to be, every fountain carved with the curve of some forgotten relief. The Trefganns inherited all of this and have spent two centuries trying to make it livable. Marketplaces fill the old forums.
Bathhouses still operate in the old imperial baths, miraculously well-plumbed. Squatter families have built lower wooden additions inside the cavernous shells of patrician homes, dividing single rooms into three.
The poor districts are not architecturally different from the rich ones. Everyone in Brenmath lives in white stone, because there is no other material the Remosans built with. The difference shows in upkeep.
In the wealthier districts the marble is washed, the additions are tasteful, and the cracks have been pointed. In the poorer districts the cracks are spreading, the wooden additions are sagging, and the grand entrance hall has been turned into three workshops and a chicken coop.
The humiliation of the old architecture is deliberate and ongoing. The lake-facing wall has a long scar where the carved names of Remosan generals were chiseled off, and the city refreshes the cut every decade so it doesn't weather smooth.
The triumphal column had its imperial eagle replaced a century ago with a weathervane shaped like a chicken. None of this is subtle, and no Brenman wants it to be.
The People
A Brenman is a Trefgann through and through. The same blunt practicality, the same generational hatred of the Empire, the same low taxes and local courts and voluntary militia.
The only real difference is that a Brenman lives in a city of forty thousand instead of a village of four hundred, and has therefore developed an urban version of the same instincts: warier of strangers in a denser way, slower to vouch for a neighbor,
more tolerant of small foreign things at the edges of life because the alternative is impossible.
The population is also unusually mixed for a Trefgann city. A continuous lineage of Remosan-descended families goes back to the city's founding, since not every imperial citizen left at secession, and that lineage has been added to by every wave of refugees and defectors since.
After two centuries the mixing has blurred at the edges. There are old Brenman families with imperial surnames who would consider themselves Trefganns to the bone, and there are recently arrived refugees who will never be considered anything else by their neighbors.
Accents shift block by block. A grandmother might still be named for some forgotten imperial general, while her grandson is called something blunt and Trefganner.

- A Compact courier, in a letter

netclam.title: Netclam
netclam.text:
Netclam
"I asked the innkeeper why the fishermen had to yell at each other from opposite ends of the village at four in the morning. She said it was so the old ones could hear. I asked why the old ones didn't walk closer to listen. She said because then the yelling wouldn't carry to the ones still in bed."
- A traveler, in a letter home
The Four Waters
Netclam sits on a narrow patch of firm ground where four bodies of water cluster within a short walk of each other: Lake Vardane to the east, a smaller lake to the north, a freshwater pond to the west, and Henon Bay to the south.
Three hundred people live here, almost all of them fishermen or clammers, and every family in the village works water for a living. The Quiet Road passes through Netclam as a matter of geography rather than importance.
Nothing along the road exists because of the road except the Wet Rock inn, and even it does not have a porch.
The houses are low stone with thatched roofs weathered gray, clustered in the middle of the spit between docks on the lake side and docks on the bay side. The ground between them smells of salt, fish, wet rope, and weed drying in the sun. The dawn is loud.
Fishermen go out before first light and yell across the village to coordinate which boat is taking which water, a conversation conducted at maximum volume across two hundred paces of packed earth, with insults, weather reports, and the occasional reminder about a daughter's birthday.
The village wakes whether it likes it or not, and by the time the sun is up the boats are gone and the women are setting out the morning market on the bay-side beach.
Netclammers are Trefganner stock in the daily-grind version of that rather than the militia one: blunt, practical, uninterested in anything that does not directly involve a fish or a clam. They are not unfriendly to travelers. They are just indifferent to them.
They sell whatever did not move at the morning market to passing carts at full price and ignore the negotiation. Children are taught early that an outsider asking questions on the dock is to be answered politely and without saying anything useful. It is not suspicion.
It is the local idea of manners.
Under the Rock
Above ground, the four waters look like four separate bodies sitting close together. They are not. Lake Vardane drains through a subterranean channel into the Small Lake, from the Small Lake into the Pond, and from the Pond out to Henon Bay.
Under the rock of the village they are one slow current running from the lake to the sea. This is the reason Netclam exists.
You can walk from the lake docks to the bay docks in twenty minutes and work four different waters in a single morning, and nowhere else on the coast can you do that.
The Lake gives perch, pike, and the silvery trout that fetch good prices at the northern markets. The Small Lake is slower and warmer and weedier, and gives a smaller catch of lake-fish plus the eels that a weedy bottom supports.
The Pond is where the salt from the bay starts reaching back up the underground channel, brackish and biologically strange in the way mixing zones always are, and it is the most productive water in the cluster by a wide margin.
The Bay gives open salt: larger fish, slower nets, and whatever the tide brings in. A fish born in the lake can end up in a bay-net by the end of a week, and nobody in Netclam finds this remarkable.
The village is named for the drifters. A drifter is a small clam that breeds in the Pond and rides the underground flow in both directions depending on how the current is running that day. On a strong lake-to-bay day they end up in the Bay nets.
On a bay-push day after a storm they come up against the Small Lake's outflow. Knowing where to be with a net on a given morning is the whole of the skill, and the skill is entirely a matter of reading how the subterranean flow is running. The older runners do this by feel.
The younger ones walk to a marked stone at the edge of the Pond before dawn and read the water level against ten parallel lines carved at different heights. Brask, the senior drifter-runner, has been doing it by feel for forty years.
He has been teaching his nephew against the stone for the last six months, with an urgency he has not explained.
The working population is organized into four extended families, one for each water, and has been for as long as anyone remembers. A lake-family son who marries a bay-family daughter marries into a different working life and has to learn it from the start.
The four families coexist by not arguing about which water is best, because the answer is obvious and depends on who is asking. Fish and clams from all four waters end up in the same caskets in the morning market, and locals can tell them apart by shell and scale without looking twice.
Travelers cannot, and do not care.
Nobody's Business
Netclam is governed by nobody. The Synod of Secession lists it among its associated villages by default, on the logic that anything on this side of Lake Vardane must belong to somebody, but no tax is collected and no Synod functionary visits.
Disputes that cannot be settled at the docks go to Velka, a widow in her sixties who has worked the bay her whole life and would rather they did not. She settles arguments grudgingly, in her own kitchen, while gutting fish, and her rulings stick because the alternative is worse.
The four families coexist by habit. That is the whole apparatus.
Both regions terminate their Quiet Road patrols at Netclam. The Southfield road wardens walk the long stretch up from Glaskatch in the south and overnight at a low building at the south edge of the village before turning back.
The Trefgann patrol walks the shorter stretch down from Brenmath in the north and overnights at a slightly better-kept building at the north edge. Neither crew rotates onto the other's territory. Neither has authority over the village between them.
They are tired men at the end of a walk, eating Darva's stew, sleeping on her floor-straw, and leaving in the morning. The villagers treat them like weather.
On nights when both patrols are in town at once the Wet Rock fills in a way it does not otherwise.
The Southfielders and the Trefganners have been walking the same road from opposite ends for long enough to know each other by name, and the end-of-route inn is the only place they ever overlap.
They push two tables together, trade news from their halves of the road, complain about the same weather from different angles, and compare notes on which carts are making the run this month.
A Southfielder hears the week's gossip from the north here before any merchant does, and the Trefganners hear about the south the same way.
Halen Vesk, a senior Southfield warden who walks this route more than most, has a running dice game with a Trefganner veteran named Oskar that goes back two years. Neither wins consistently enough to stop playing.
Darva charges them all full price and tolerates the noise because they tip like men who have just finished walking for a week.
The villagers consider all of this none of their business. Several of them also consider it free entertainment, and on double-patrol nights they stand outside the Wet Rock in the dark and listen to the news from both ends of the road through the inn's thin walls.
Notable Locations
•
The Wet Rock:
Netclam's only inn, and the only building along the Quiet Road that exists because of the Quiet Road. The sign is a rock hammered into the wood with water painted above it, spilling from nowhere in particular.
Inside: floor-straw beds, walls too thin for the fishermen's dawn shouting to miss, and a giant barrel in the middle of the common room that overflows with whatever the boats brought in. The clam casket is all you can eat for one silver. The fish stew is surprisingly very good.
Darva runs the place, loud and crude and in no mood to explain herself to anybody.
•
The Lake Docks:
The busier of the two dock sets, on the Vardane side of the spit. Long and solidly built, because Lake Vardane is the biggest market and the biggest boats launch from here. Nets hung to dry on every post, and the lake family's compound sits at the landward end.
On a clear morning you can see the white sails of the northern fleet working the lake in the distance, which travelers occasionally mistake for a sign that Netclam is part of something larger.
•
The Morning Market:
A strip of bay-side beach where the women of the four families lay out the dawn catch on flat stones and old planks. It runs from sunrise until the carts from the road arrive, at which point the locals fold up what is left and head home. Prices do not move.
Negotiation is tolerated as a form of entertainment and does not affect the outcome.
•
Velka's Kitchen:
A low stone house near the lake docks with smoke curling from the chimney at all hours. Petitioners wait on a bench by the door while Velka hears them out and keeps gutting fish. Her rulings are final because nobody has the energy for the alternative.
Her stew is good and she does not sell it.
•
The Pond Stone:
A flat gray stone at the edge of the Pond, half a mile west of the village through light wood, carved with ten parallel lines at different heights. The drifter-runners walk out here before dawn to read the water level against the marks and decide which water will give drifters that day.

segments.text: Netclam

"I asked the innkeeper why the fishermen had to yell at each other from opposite ends of the village at four in the morning. She said it was so the old ones could hear. I asked why the old ones didn't walk closer to listen. She said because then the yelling wouldn't carry to the ones still in bed."
- A traveler, in a letter home
The Four Waters

Netclam sits on a narrow patch of firm ground where four bodies of water cluster within a short walk of each other: Lake Vardane to the east, a smaller lake to the north, a freshwater pond to the west, and Henon Bay to the south.

Three hundred people live here, almost all of them fishermen or clammers, and every family in the village works water for a living. The Quiet Road passes through Netclam as a matter of geography rather than importance.
Nothing along the road exists because of the road except the Wet Rock inn, and even it does not have a porch.

The houses are low stone with thatched roofs weathered gray, clustered in the middle of the spit between docks on the lake side and docks on the bay side. The ground between them smells of salt, fish, wet rope, and weed drying in the sun. The dawn is loud.

Fishermen go out before first light and yell across the village to coordinate which boat is taking which water, a conversation conducted at maximum volume across two hundred paces of packed earth, with insults, weather reports, and the occasional reminder about a daughter's birthday.
The village wakes whether it likes it or not, and by the time the sun is up the boats are gone and the women are setting out the morning market on the bay-side beach.

Netclammers are Trefganner stock in the daily-grind version of that rather than the militia one: blunt, practical, uninterested in anything that does not directly involve a fish or a clam. They are not unfriendly to travelers. They are just indifferent to them.

They sell whatever did not move at the morning market to passing carts at full price and ignore the negotiation. Children are taught early that an outsider asking questions on the dock is to be answered politely and without saying anything useful. It is not suspicion.
It is the local idea of manners.
Under the Rock

Above ground, the four waters look like four separate bodies sitting close together. They are not. Lake Vardane drains through a subterranean channel into the Small Lake, from the Small Lake into the Pond, and from the Pond out to Henon Bay.
Under the rock of the village they are one slow current running from the lake to the sea. This is the reason Netclam exists.
You can walk from the lake docks to the bay docks in twenty minutes and work four different waters in a single morning, and nowhere else on the coast can you do that.

The Lake gives perch, pike, and the silvery trout that fetch good prices at the northern markets. The Small Lake is slower and warmer and weedier, and gives a smaller catch of lake-fish plus the eels that a weedy bottom supports.

The Pond is where the salt from the bay starts reaching back up the underground channel, brackish and biologically strange in the way mixing zones always are, and it is the most productive water in the cluster by a wide margin.
The Bay gives open salt: larger fish, slower nets, and whatever the tide brings in. A fish born in the lake can end up in a bay-net by the end of a week, and nobody in Netclam finds this remarkable.

The village is named for the drifters. A drifter is a small clam that breeds in the Pond and rides the underground flow in both directions depending on how the current is running that day. On a strong lake-to-bay day they end up in the Bay nets.

On a bay-push day after a storm they come up against the Small Lake's outflow. Knowing where to be with a net on a given morning is the whole of the skill, and the skill is entirely a matter of reading how the subterranean flow is running. The older runners do this by feel.

The younger ones walk to a marked stone at the edge of the Pond before dawn and read the water level against ten parallel lines carved at different heights. Brask, the senior drifter-runner, has been doing it by feel for forty years.
He has been teaching his nephew against the stone for the last six months, with an urgency he has not explained.

The working population is organized into four extended families, one for each water, and has been for as long as anyone remembers. A lake-family son who marries a bay-family daughter marries into a different working life and has to learn it from the start.

The four families coexist by not arguing about which water is best, because the answer is obvious and depends on who is asking. Fish and clams from all four waters end up in the same caskets in the morning market, and locals can tell them apart by shell and scale without looking twice.
Travelers cannot, and do not care.
Nobody's Business

Netclam is governed by nobody. The Synod of Secession lists it among its associated villages by default, on the logic that anything on this side of Lake Vardane must belong to somebody, but no tax is collected and no Synod functionary visits.

Disputes that cannot be settled at the docks go to Velka, a widow in her sixties who has worked the bay her whole life and would rather they did not. She settles arguments grudgingly, in her own kitchen, while gutting fish, and her rulings stick because the alternative is worse.
The four families coexist by habit. That is the whole apparatus.

Both regions terminate their Quiet Road patrols at Netclam. The Southfield road wardens walk the long stretch up from Glaskatch in the south and overnight at a low building at the south edge of the village before turning back.

The Trefgann patrol walks the shorter stretch down from Brenmath in the north and overnights at a slightly better-kept building at the north edge. Neither crew rotates onto the other's territory. Neither has authority over the village between them.
They are tired men at the end of a walk, eating Darva's stew, sleeping on her floor-straw, and leaving in the morning. The villagers treat them like weather.
On nights when both patrols are in town at once the Wet Rock fills in a way it does not otherwise.
The Southfielders and the Trefganners have been walking the same road from opposite ends for long enough to know each other by name, and the end-of-route inn is the only place they ever overlap.
They push two tables together, trade news from their halves of the road, complain about the same weather from different angles, and compare notes on which carts are making the run this month.
A Southfielder hears the week's gossip from the north here before any merchant does, and the Trefganners hear about the south the same way.

Halen Vesk, a senior Southfield warden who walks this route more than most, has a running dice game with a Trefganner veteran named Oskar that goes back two years. Neither wins consistently enough to stop playing.
Darva charges them all full price and tolerates the noise because they tip like men who have just finished walking for a week.

The villagers consider all of this none of their business. Several of them also consider it free entertainment, and on double-patrol nights they stand outside the Wet Rock in the dark and listen to the news from both ends of the road through the inn's thin walls.
Notable Locations
The Wet Rock:

Netclam's only inn, and the only building along the Quiet Road that exists because of the Quiet Road. The sign is a rock hammered into the wood with water painted above it, spilling from nowhere in particular.

Inside: floor-straw beds, walls too thin for the fishermen's dawn shouting to miss, and a giant barrel in the middle of the common room that overflows with whatever the boats brought in. The clam casket is all you can eat for one silver. The fish stew is surprisingly very good.
Darva runs the place, loud and crude and in no mood to explain herself to anybody.

The busier of the two dock sets, on the Vardane side of the spit. Long and solidly built, because Lake Vardane is the biggest market and the biggest boats launch from here. Nets hung to dry on every post, and the lake family's compound sits at the landward end.

Negotiation is tolerated as a form of entertainment and does not affect the outcome.

A low stone house near the lake docks with smoke curling from the chimney at all hours. Petitioners wait on a bench by the door while Velka hears them out and keeps gutting fish. Her rulings are final because nobody has the energy for the alternative.

vanguard.title: Vanguard
vanguard.text:
Vanguard
"Two apples for a copper or five for two, and don't tell me the ones at the bottom are bruised because I packed them myself. If you want unbruised apples you can come at dawn like everybody else."
- A woman at the Vanguard market
The Watchtower
Vanguard sits two days south of Brenmath on the Quiet Road, on the northern shore of Lake Verdane. Every Remosan March in living memory has come through it.
In the long decades between Marches the village brews beer, grows apples, forges ironwork, and provisions the city it is sworn to warn.
About six hundred people live here in stone houses along narrow lanes. The Quiet Road widens at the center of the village into a small square with a low stone marker at its middle, carved with the first day of each of the three Marches and nothing else.
People walking past will sometimes touch the marker without thinking about it.
West of the village the land opens into grain fields and old apple orchards, the orchards dense and overgrown in places, crossed by paths that are not obvious to outsiders and cache-pits in the older trees that have been there for generations.
South, Lake Verdane, close enough for village fishing docks and a small wharf for the provisioning boats that run up to the city when the road is slow.
The smells are cooked grain from the brewery on one side of the square and hot iron from Ciar's forge on the other, at all hours, mixed with the weedy smell off the lake.
Vanguarders are Trefganner stock in a register that even Brenmath finds slightly intense.
Proud, hardy, suspicious in a way that has been earned three times over, and bound to Brenmath by blood and obligation to a degree that makes the two-day gap in the road feel more like a commute than a distance. A Vanguarder girl who marries into the city is still a Vanguarder.
A Brenmath man who marries in is a Vanguarder within a year or he leaves. The hostility to strangers is the scrutiny a parent gives an unknown adult walking up to their child, and it relaxes the moment a traveler can prove no Remosan connection.
Locals will answer your questions truthfully and watch your hands while they do it. After three days they will start to be friendly. After a week they will tell you war stories. Toward anyone of Remosan descent the watching never relaxes, regardless of how many decades pass.
The wait
The peacetime life of the village is provisioning. Grain and vegetables from the fields, apples from the orchards, ironwork from the forge, beer from the brewery, and the steady minor trade that has accumulated around the village over the centuries.
Carts leave for Brenmath every third morning and come back two days later with whatever the city has sent down in return. On market days the square is crowded, the forge is loud, and children run in the lanes the way children run anywhere.
The chapel bell does not tell time. It rings once a year on the anniversary of the Third March, and otherwise has only one meaning. Every adult in Vanguard has trained for the moment it rings outside of spring, and most of them check the bell rope in passing without thinking about it.
The orchard paths, the connected cellars under the houses, the three ways out of the square in the dark: these are things the village knows and does not discuss.
The Forge
Ciar Ni Hemmarth came to Brenmath on a Haldrith guild commission thirty-odd years ago, finished the work in eight years, stayed in the city for another eight, and then walked two days south on the Quiet Road to find somewhere he could work in peace.
The villagers tolerated him fast because his work is undeniable and because a Haldrith dwarf with no Remosan connection is exactly the kind of outsider Vanguard can stomach. He has been here for most of three decades and considers himself a local.
The villagers consider him a local with caveats.
His apprentice is Cliona, a gnome wizard of some seventy years' service, who decided early that she would never find a more fitting specimen to learn from than Ciar and has been enchanting his work ever since. She is very good.
A blade she has finished can hold an edge no whetstone would produce, shed blood without dulling, and do things in a hand that are not written down anywhere. The prices reflect it.
The wait list is currently about two years for anything more ambitious than a well-made kitchen knife, and the clients who can afford that wait include Brenmath's Warons, a handful of private buyers up and down the Quiet Road,
and the occasional Synod functionary who has learned to pay out of pocket because the city will not approve the expense. Ciar and Cliona insist they are not a couple. She cooks his meals, lives in his house, and finishes his sentences. The village has stopped pretending to believe them.
That the best smithing operation in Trefgann is housed in Vanguard is not an accident.
A village that has served as the staging ground for every invasion in living memory attracts a craftsman whose work is bought up at every muster, and Ciar's forge has outfitted Vanguard's council and much of Brenmath's senior militia for three decades running.
Ciar did not come here for this reason. He came for the quiet. The village recognized what his presence meant inside a season.
The Brewery
Valor Brewery is the village's other pride and its largest building, a squat stone hall at the south end of the square that smells of cooked grain and hops at all hours.
Valor brews corn and buckwheat beer, which is what the local soil gives, and the standard comparison up and down the Quiet Road is that Valor is as good as beer gets on this side of the water.
Most inns between the Southfield border and Brenmath carry at least one Valor cask, and the ones that do not are either trying to pass off a cheaper substitute or have annoyed the brewery enough to lose their allocation.
Old Vassik runs the place, eighty-something and a child of the Third March, small and mean and personally known to every innkeeper on the road.
The brewery is also the closest thing Vanguard has to a civic building. Weddings are held in the yard. Harvest dinners happen in the mash room after the vessels have been cleaned.
The back room is where a council of four militia veterans meets when there is something to decide and ignores each other when there is not. The council has no formal authority and is universally obeyed.
Its current senior member is Karsa Halric, sixty-eight, who fought in the Third March as a teenager and has been on the council for twenty years. She is the woman strangers are warned about by anyone friendly enough to warn them.
The council coordinates the muster, settles property disputes, and decides which travelers are allowed to stay at the Etched Spear.
Vassik is not on the council and has not been invited. He is, however, in the next room during every meeting, and the council does not bother closing the door.
This has made him the quiet fifth member of every decision the village has made in the last forty years without his name appearing on anything. He has not bought a bottle of Eoghan's wine in fifty years and has no plans to start.
Notable Locations
•
The Etched Spear:
The inn for outsiders, run by Eoghan, a half-elf who fought on the Remosan side in the Third March and deserted at the end of it to find a quiet life in Trefgann.
Inside is a composition of low tables, mismatched pillows, and patched chairs arranged in an order that only makes sense once you have sat in it for ten minutes. He serves tea, wine, and vegetable dishes from the walled garden behind the building, without apology for any of them.
A single Remosan grape vine grows against the garden wall and produces enough fruit for two bottles of wine a year. He prunes it obsessively. Nobody in the village has ever asked about it.
•
The Standing Mug:
The locals' drinking house, an unmarked door on a side street off the square, run as a side concern by the brewery. Strangers are not refused entry. They are simply not poured a drink, and most figure out what is happening within fifteen minutes and leave.
•
Ciar's Forge:
A stone-built workshop near the lakeside docks with a chimney that smokes most of the day. Ciar works at the main anvil.
Cliona has a smaller workbench by the window where the light is better for the inscriptions, surrounded by jars of things the villagers do not know the names of and do not want to. Commissions taken in person, on a two-year wait, at prices set the day of.
•
Valor Brewery:
The squat stone hall at the south end of the square, smelling of grain and hops at all hours. Visitors can buy a cask at the front door if they have a cart to haul it and if Vassik is in a mood to sell, which he usually is.
The yard holds weddings, the mash room holds harvest dinners, and the back room holds the council.
•
The Marker Stone:
A low stone in the center of the square, carved with three dates. No inscription explains them. Villagers passing it will sometimes touch the stone on the way somewhere else, and its corners are worn smooth.
•
The Chapel:
A small stone chapel on the east side of the square, plain inside and lightly used. The bell in the low tower rings once a year on the spring anniversary and otherwise only for one reason.
Father Ossir, the aging cleric, keeps the chapel's records in a locked chest and has not opened it in six years.
Plot Hooks
•
The Bell:
Two months ago the chapel bell rang for about fifteen seconds, outside any anniversary, and nobody has admitted to ringing it. Nobody in the village has discussed it openly since. The runners' horses have been kept fresh for eight weeks.
Karsa Halric has been checking the western horizon at dawn for the same eight weeks. The question of who rang it and why is not being asked, because asking it out loud is the same as saying out loud that something is coming, and nobody wants to be the first to do that.
The party arrives in a village that is not quite admitting it is on a war footing.
•
The Commission:
A Synod functionary from a northern city commissioned a pair of ceremonial blades from Ciar two years ago, paid up front in good coin, and is arriving to collect them in twelve days. Ciar finished the blades a month ago.
Cliona has not finished the enchantments, will not say why, and will not let Ciar near them. Ciar has stopped sleeping. The functionary is not a patient man, and the village does not know which side of the argument they want to be on when he arrives.
•
The Traveler at the Spear:
Eoghan is hosting a young woman who says she is on a trading journey from the western country, and whose surname is unmistakably Remosan. She is eighteen years old and was born in Trefgann. Eoghan has seen her papers and believes her.
The council has heard about her and is meeting on Thursday to decide whether to escort her out of the village at sundown or let her leave in her own time.
Eoghan is refusing to evict her on his own, for the first time in fifty years, and Karsa Halric is furious that he is making her make the call.

Karsa Halric has been checking the western horizon at dawn for the same eight weeks. The question of who rang it and why is not being asked, because asking it out loud is the same as saying out loud that something is coming, and nobody wants to be the first to do that.
The party arrives in a village that is not quite admitting it is on a war footing.
The Commission:

A Synod functionary from a northern city commissioned a pair of ceremonial blades from Ciar two years ago, paid up front in good coin, and is arriving to collect them in twelve days. Ciar finished the blades a month ago.

Cliona has not finished the enchantments, will not say why, and will not let Ciar near them. Ciar has stopped sleeping. The functionary is not a patient man, and the village does not know which side of the argument they want to be on when he arrives.
The Traveler at the Spear:

Eoghan is hosting a young woman who says she is on a trading journey from the western country, and whose surname is unmistakably Remosan. She is eighteen years old and was born in Trefgann. Eoghan has seen her papers and believes her.
The council has heard about her and is meeting on Thursday to decide whether to escort her out of the village at sundown or let her leave in her own time.
Eoghan is refusing to evict her on his own, for the first time in fifty years, and Karsa Halric is furious that he is making her make the call.

herdine.title: Herdine
herdine.text:
Herdine
"In the city they ask you how was work. Up here Don asks me what's today's find. Suits me better."
- Overheard in the Travelling Owl
The Forest Provides
Herdine sits three days uphill northwest of Brenmath, in mixed highland forest with no road in or out. About two hundred and fifty people live here in timber and stone houses scattered loosely across a wooded shoulder of the mountain, not clustered the way Trefganner villages usually are.
Footpaths rather than streets, and the footpaths do not run in straight lines because they follow the contour of the land and the old deer trails the first villagers used.
Every house has its own kitchen garden, its own drying rack for mushrooms and herbs, and its own set of baskets hung from the eaves. In spring and summer the air smells of pine, woodsmoke, and whatever is drying on the racks. In autumn it smells of mushrooms and honey.
In winter it smells of woodsmoke and nothing else.
The village lives off the forest. There is no road, no river worth fishing, and no farmable land beyond a few household plots.
What Herdine has instead is a stretch of old highland wood that has never been logged or pushed too hard, and two centuries of inherited knowledge about what it gives and when.
Mushrooms in real variety, wild berries, honey from a dozen managed hives, herbs that fetch good prices in the city, roots, game, and the clean water of small springs scattered through the hills that only a Herdiner knows how to find.
The villagers know their patches the way fishermen know their tides. A child here learns which slope gives morels in April and which one gives them two weeks later, and why.
An outsider walking the same ground would find half of what a child does and damage the other half by taking it at the wrong time.
Four times a year a mule-train walks down to Brenmath carrying dried mushrooms, preserved herbs, honey, smoked game, and the small quantities of rarer things the city's apothecaries and wealthier kitchens pay good money for. It comes back loaded with grain, salt, iron, cloth, and news.
The muleteers are all Herdiners and the route is theirs, and the relationship with Brenmath is otherwise nonexistent. The Synod nominally claims the village. No tax has been collected and no functionary has made the climb in a decade.
The People
Herdiners are quiet, patient, and competent in the wilderness in a way that unsettles visitors who think of themselves as outdoorsmen. The core of the village is Trefganner stock, but a high proportion of the population came up the mountain from somewhere else and stayed.
Three days uphill through pathless forest is a filter. People who make the climb without a clear reason tend to have a reason they are not saying, and the villagers do not ask. What matters is whether a person pulls their weight and learns the patches they are taught.
The village does not advertise its foraging knowledge to outsiders, and does not refuse to share it either. Outsiders are not told where the patches are because outsiders have nothing to reciprocate with, and the balance only works if everybody has skin in it.
A traveler who stays a season and proves they are not going to take more than they should might be shown a patch or two by the family that works it, and then a few more, and at that point they are no longer a traveler.
There is no formal leadership.
When something needs deciding the meeting happens at the Travelling Owl after dinner: Ada puts the word out during the day, the affected parties come, anyone else who cares to listen comes too, and the room talks the matter through until a rough consensus settles in.
No vote, no chair, no formal authority. The convention is that anyone can speak and that the meeting is over when nobody is still arguing. It works because the village is small and because people who could not stand it left long ago.
Notable Locations
•
The Travelling Owl:
Herdine's only inn and the closest thing the village has to a square. A long timber building with a wide kitchen, a common room hung with drying herbs from the rafters, and a long wooden table outside in the clearing where people sit on good evenings.
Ada runs it, a woman in her late fifties who has been taking in strangers for thirty years and asking none of them about their pasts.
She offers a room and work in exchange for a roof until the new arrival finds their feet, and a number of her current regulars came to her the same way and never left. She is a good cook who became a better one after Herdine taught her what the forest gives in every season.
•
Mara Voss's Workshop:
A low building at the upper edge of the village, ringed by drying racks and smelling of bruised leaves and beeswax.
Mara is a working herbalist in her forties, the third generation of her family in the trade, and she knows what every plant within a half-day's walk of Herdine is good for, including the ones that will kill you.
She brews teas, salves, poultices, and the practical remedies that keep a village without a doctor functional. Her preparations go down to Brenmath with the mule-train and fetch good prices in the city because they are made from forest stock the city herbalists cannot get.
Brisk, unsentimental, and good at what she does.
•
The Mast Grove:
A stretch of old oak and beech about half a day's walk southwest of the village, where the pig-herders run their drifts in autumn.
Three families in Herdine keep pigs the old forest way: turn them out into the wood under the mast-fall, follow them on foot for six or eight weeks, and bring them home fat on acorns and beech-nuts.
The pigs are half-wild and recognize their handlers, and the largest drift belongs to Bero Halse, a heavy quiet man in his fifties whose dozen pigs each have names and who can find any of them in the forest within an hour.
Herdine ham and smoked pork go down with the mule-train and fetch the kind of prices that make Brenmath butchers quietly furious. The grove itself is unremarkable when the pigs are not there, just old wood with the forest floor cleared by generations of rooting.
•
The Long Cave:
A narrow opening in the rock about an hour's walk above the village, half-hidden behind a stand of pines. The mouth is a horizontal slit you have to duck to enter, opening into a low passage that runs straight back into the hill. As far as the villagers know, the passage does not end.
Nobody has ever reached a wall, a chamber, or a turning. The air inside stays the same temperature year-round and the floor is dry, and the walls are unmarked stone the whole way in. Children dare each other to go in. Adults do not.
Foragers walk a little way inside for the cave mushrooms and the pale moss that grows along the lower walls, and then quickly come back out. Every Herdiner knows at least some version of a story where someone went into the cave and never came out.
•
Old Algud's House:
A weathered cabin on the south side of the village belonging to the village's oldest resident, a retired muleteer in his seventies who has lived in Herdine longer than anyone.
He keeps to himself, he spends the mornings in his porch rocking chair in his infamous red underwear, and at the evenings he sits at the long table outside the Owl. He knows where every patch in the woods is and who works it.
•
The Mule Yard:
A fenced enclosure on the downhill edge of the village, with a long shed for tack and the seven mules that make the four-times-a-year run to Brenmath. The muleteers keep their own counsel and their own gear.
The yard smells of mules and oiled leather, and the gate is always open because there is nowhere for a mule to wander to that a Herdiner could not find it.
Plot Hooks
•
Bero's Missing Drifter:
One of Bero Halse's pigs has not come back from the mast grove. A sow named Hessa, a veteran of six autumns who has never wandered before and who Bero can usually whistle in from half a mile away. She has been missing for four days.
Bero has been walking the grove and the surrounding wood alone from dawn to dusk and not finding her, which he will tell you is impossible, because he could find Hessa blindfolded. He is not panicked. He is something quieter and worse.
He will pay, modestly, for help searching ground he has already covered twice, because a second set of eyes is the one thing he does not have, and because whatever took a pig that size did not leave the tracks it should have.
•
The Quiet Theft:
Somebody has been working a foraging patch that is not theirs, quietly, over the last season. Old Algud has noticed because Old Algud notices everything in the woods, and he has not raised it at the Owl yet because he is waiting to see if it resolves itself. It is not going to.
The patch in question belongs to a family who are about to notice on their own, and when they do the meeting at the Owl is going to be the kind of meeting Herdine has not had to hold in a generation.
The thief is somebody nobody would suspect, for a reason that is sympathetic enough to make the village's consensus-by-arguing system buckle.
•
The Light Mule-Train:
Last month's mule-train came back from Brenmath with less grain than the village had paid for, and the merchant the Herdiners have dealt with for fifteen years had no explanation that satisfied them.
The muleteers were too tired to push the matter on the spot, and now the village is two months out from running short of salt and four months out from running short of iron. The next run is in three weeks.
Somebody needs to go down to the city ahead of it and find out what changed, and the village would prefer that somebody not be a Herdiner, because Herdiners going to Brenmath to ask questions of merchants is the kind of thing that ends with a Herdiner shouting in a city street,
which is bad for trade.

ashfield_marsh.title: Ashfield Marsh
ashfield_marsh.text:
Ashfield Marsh
"It smells like rotten eggs on a hangover morning."
- Nizch, Remosan guard, during his first patrol
The Marsh
Ashfield Marsh sits on Remosan territory west of the Broadfen River, which marks the practical border with Trefgann. It is roughly four days across for someone who knows the paths and five or six for someone who does not. Most people do not.
The Second March came through here 108 years ago. The Trefganners chose the marsh as their ground because it took away everything the Remosan army was good at: heavy infantry cannot hold formation in waist-deep water, and war-constructs sink. The bloody fighting lasted weeks.
Eventually the Remosans broke through by attrition, crossed the Broadfen, and continued east toward Brenmath, where they lost the war. Nobody came to clean up the marsh afterward.
The Terrain
Flat, wet, grey, overbearing. Black water between ridges of firmer ground, reeds taller than a man in places, and fog throughout most hours of the day. The air smells of rotting plant matter: sulfurous and thick, and the smell sticks to your clothes like bonfire smoke.
What looks solid is often waterlogged peat under a skin of grass. Knowing which vegetation allows for firm footing is necessary if you don't want to sink up to your thigh. Between the ridges the water is shin-deep to waist-deep depending on season. Basically, You are never dry.
The air is damp, your boots are soaked, and the morning fog wets anything and everything.
A kilometer in Ashfield takes thrice as long to walk, sometimes more. You route around standing water, test footing, pull your boots out of sucking mud with every other step. Your legs tire quickly, and the whole experience is a sorry one. Navigation is bad.
Everything looks the same: reeds, water, mud, more reeds. Landmarks are scarce because nothing is tall enough to see over the vegetation, and many have been lost in the marsh to never return.
Mosquitoes and flies breed in the standing water and they are constant from dawn to dusk, worse near the water.
Old Remosan causeways cross parts of the marsh, built during the Second March to move troops and never maintained since. Some stretches still hold weight. Others have sunk far enough that they sit underwater and trip you instead of carrying you.
At this point only the smugglers who work the marsh know which sections are usable.
What the Battle Left
Both armies laid field-works during the engagement: stake-pits, trip-lines, sharpened palisades dug into the ridges. Most of it has rotted or sunk past function in 108 years. The wood is soft, the rope is gone, the iron is corroded.
A Remosan stake-pit covered by a century of leaf-fall and marsh growth looks like solid ground. The stakes inside are often still sharp, preserved by the anaerobic mud.
Corroded trip-lines strung between submerged posts will catch an ankle and put a person face-down in stinking black water. Equipment surfaces after heavy rain: helmets, sword hilts, buckles, bones. Living memories of the swamp's bloody past.
What the Magic Left
Several weeks of sustained battle-magic has left the swamp with much residue.
A stretch of marsh might be quiet for months and then loop the same thirty seconds of noise for a week: shouting, the crash of metal, a horn call that cuts off halfway through.
Some echoes are visual: the outline of a palisade where no palisade stands, a smear of torchlight on the fog, the silhouette of soldiers crossing a ridge that is empty when you reach it. Also smells: smoke, hot metal, something chemical that burns the nose.

castra_vull.title: Castra Vull
castra_vull.text:
Castra Vull
"Village population: 97. Granary capacity: adequate. Road condition between markers 14 and 16: serviceable. Garrison readiness: N/A (no garrison assigned since Year 1822)."
- Quarterly Compliance Report, Castra Vull, filed by Station Clerk Duscha Pell
The Mandate
Imperial Road Maintenance Protocol, Section 4, Subsection 11: "supply points shall be established at intervals not exceeding forty kilometers along any segment of the Imperial Path within three days' march of the Mire perimeter.
Each supply point shall maintain housing for no fewer than 250 support personnel, a granary of standard capacity, stabling for 30 horses, one public house of no fewer than twelve rooms, and road maintenance facilities sufficient to service the adjacent segment."
Castra Vull was built to this specification 400 years ago. It has been maintained to this specification since, and it currently holds 97 people.
The inn has twelve rooms because the protocol says twelve rooms. On a good night three of them are occupied. The innkeeper, Vesna Drol, keeps the place clean because it is her livelihood, not because she has read the protocol. She has not read the protocol.
Nobody in Castra Vull has read the protocol except Duscha Pell, the station clerk, who everyone treats as a nuisance they have to deal with so that the village receives its yearly budget.
Travelers, soldiers mostly, come off the Imperial Path, which is smooth white stone and in good repair, and step into a muddy clearing that passes for the village square. After rain, the yard is a thick brown mess.
A few benches along the edges hold the same old men every morning, with nut casings on the floor next to them, which have had years to accumulate. Three or four market stalls sell vegetables and candles and whatever came in on the last cart.
Outside the inn Vesna has set up tables under a wooden awning where the same five men play dice every afternoon.
The buildings beyond the yard are white stone foundations gone grey, laid out on an imperial grid, streets too wide for the foot traffic they carry and spaced for a population that did not arrive.
Not everyone in Castra Vull thinks about Castra Vull the way Castra Vull thinks about itself. The road crew, five men and two women who maintain the Imperial Path between markers 14 and 18, take genuine pride in their stretch.
The road is in better condition here than in most of the segments closer to Mirestead, and the crew knows it. They do not care about the protocol. They care about the road, which is different.
A few of the younger residents have plans to leave and a few of the older ones had plans that did not work out, and in between is a village of people getting on with things in a place that happens to be where they live.
The relationship with Trazh is worth mentioning, since it might just be the one interesting thing about the place. Trazh is a day's ride south, breeds horses, punches people for recreation, and has never filed a quarterly report in its life.
The two villages have been pulling at each other for as long as anyone can remember. Trazh has stolen Castra Vull's road sign twice and filled the village well with horse dung last spring.
Castra Vull has responded by letting the road surface near Trazh's end of the segment go just slightly to hell, overcharging Trazh riders at the stable, and on one occasion somebody loosened a paddock gate in the night and let three of Trazh's mares wander for a day and a half.
Nobody in Castra Vull has admitted to the gate. Trazh is bigger, louder, and better in a fight, which means Castra Vull's contributions tend toward the quiet and the deniable.
A road worker named Gresch went to Trazh to demand an apology for the well, came back two days later having lost a fistfight and acquired a friend named Kolev, and now rides down to visit every few weeks without discussing it at home.
Plot Hooks
•
The Rejected Report:
For the first time in 400 years, Castra Vull's quarterly compliance report has been returned from Mirestead with a notation: "Discrepancy in road segment 14-16. Clarify and refile." Duscha has never had a report returned. She does not know what the discrepancy is.
The road crew says the segment is fine. Duscha has walked it herself and it looks fine.
She is going to refile the report with the same numbers and a note saying she has inspected the segment personally, and if it comes back again she is going to have to go to Mirestead for the first time to ask in person.
•
Gresch's Favor:
Gresch's friend Kolev in Trazh has asked him for a quiet favor involving Castra Vull's granary. Kolev will not say what it is for, exactly, but it involves borrowing a quantity of grain that Gresch does not have the authority to lend, and returning it before the next quarterly count.
•
The Empty Stable:
One of Castra Vull's four horses, a brown mare named Dust, has been found dead on the road a half-day's walk toward Trazh. Her throat was cut. Castra Vull assumes Trazh did it. Trazh denies it. Nobody in Trazh would kill a horse, which is the one thing both villages actually agree on.
Something else happened on that road and neither village knows what. `

- Quarterly Compliance Report, Castra Vull, filed by Station Clerk Duscha Pell
The Mandate

Imperial Road Maintenance Protocol, Section 4, Subsection 11: "supply points shall be established at intervals not exceeding forty kilometers along any segment of the Imperial Path within three days' march of the Mire perimeter.

Each supply point shall maintain housing for no fewer than 250 support personnel, a granary of standard capacity, stabling for 30 horses, one public house of no fewer than twelve rooms, and road maintenance facilities sufficient to service the adjacent segment."
Castra Vull was built to this specification 400 years ago. It has been maintained to this specification since, and it currently holds 97 people.

The inn has twelve rooms because the protocol says twelve rooms. On a good night three of them are occupied. The innkeeper, Vesna Drol, keeps the place clean because it is her livelihood, not because she has read the protocol. She has not read the protocol.
Nobody in Castra Vull has read the protocol except Duscha Pell, the station clerk, who everyone treats as a nuisance they have to deal with so that the village receives its yearly budget.

Travelers, soldiers mostly, come off the Imperial Path, which is smooth white stone and in good repair, and step into a muddy clearing that passes for the village square. After rain, the yard is a thick brown mess.

A few benches along the edges hold the same old men every morning, with nut casings on the floor next to them, which have had years to accumulate. Three or four market stalls sell vegetables and candles and whatever came in on the last cart.
Outside the inn Vesna has set up tables under a wooden awning where the same five men play dice every afternoon.
The buildings beyond the yard are white stone foundations gone grey, laid out on an imperial grid, streets too wide for the foot traffic they carry and spaced for a population that did not arrive.

Not everyone in Castra Vull thinks about Castra Vull the way Castra Vull thinks about itself. The road crew, five men and two women who maintain the Imperial Path between markers 14 and 18, take genuine pride in their stretch.
The road is in better condition here than in most of the segments closer to Mirestead, and the crew knows it. They do not care about the protocol. They care about the road, which is different.

A few of the younger residents have plans to leave and a few of the older ones had plans that did not work out, and in between is a village of people getting on with things in a place that happens to be where they live.

The relationship with Trazh is worth mentioning, since it might just be the one interesting thing about the place. Trazh is a day's ride south, breeds horses, punches people for recreation, and has never filed a quarterly report in its life.
The two villages have been pulling at each other for as long as anyone can remember. Trazh has stolen Castra Vull's road sign twice and filled the village well with horse dung last spring.

Castra Vull has responded by letting the road surface near Trazh's end of the segment go just slightly to hell, overcharging Trazh riders at the stable, and on one occasion somebody loosened a paddock gate in the night and let three of Trazh's mares wander for a day and a half.
Nobody in Castra Vull has admitted to the gate. Trazh is bigger, louder, and better in a fight, which means Castra Vull's contributions tend toward the quiet and the deniable.

A road worker named Gresch went to Trazh to demand an apology for the well, came back two days later having lost a fistfight and acquired a friend named Kolev, and now rides down to visit every few weeks without discussing it at home.
Plot Hooks
The Rejected Report:

For the first time in 400 years, Castra Vull's quarterly compliance report has been returned from Mirestead with a notation: "Discrepancy in road segment 14-16. Clarify and refile." Duscha has never had a report returned. She does not know what the discrepancy is.
The road crew says the segment is fine. Duscha has walked it herself and it looks fine.

She is going to refile the report with the same numbers and a note saying she has inspected the segment personally, and if it comes back again she is going to have to go to Mirestead for the first time to ask in person.
Gresch's Favor:

Gresch's friend Kolev in Trazh has asked him for a quiet favor involving Castra Vull's granary. Kolev will not say what it is for, exactly, but it involves borrowing a quantity of grain that Gresch does not have the authority to lend, and returning it before the next quarterly count.
The Empty Stable:

One of Castra Vull's four horses, a brown mare named Dust, has been found dead on the road a half-day's walk toward Trazh. Her throat was cut. Castra Vull assumes Trazh did it. Trazh denies it. Nobody in Trazh would kill a horse, which is the one thing both villages actually agree on.
Something else happened on that road and neither village knows what. `

trazh.title: Trazh
trazh.text:
Trazh
"The mare threw a shoe on the south road and I walked her back. Took four hours. Kolev offered to lend me his, which was decent of him considering I broke his nose last week."
- Overheard in Trazh
The Pasture
Trazh grew up around good grass. A few families found pasture near the Imperial Path some time before anyone was keeping count, started breeding horses, and the village filled in around the work.
About two hundred people live here now in wood and fieldstone houses arranged without any particular plan, and on a clear day you see the horses before you see the rooftops.
The pasture runs south and east of the village, fenced with post and rail, and the animals are out in all weather except deep winter.
The horses are working stock. Road horses, cart horses, patrol horses. Animals that can take a week on the Imperial Path without going lame. They are not fine mounts, and the breeders do not pretend otherwise.
A Trazh horse costs a fraction of what a cavalry mount runs and outlasts it on bad road, and the reputation is old enough that buyers come to the village rather than the village going to find them.
The trade keeps everyone fed without making anyone rich, and most of the breeders prefer it that way. A woman named Dalla Madric handles the selling end, knows every military procurement officer on this stretch of the Path by name, and sets prices that do not negotiate downward.
The ring is behind the Madric house, which is the largest in the village. A circle of packed dirt, twenty paces across, low split-rail fence. Young men fight to ready themselves for conscription. Older men fight to settle things they could settle with words.
Soldiers passing through sometimes step in, and the local opinion is that no Trazh man has ever lost to one, which is probably wrong but sincerely believed.
The fights are bare-knuckle, the rules are unwritten, and the main ones are: no biting, no weapons, no kicking a man on the ground, stop when one walks out or stays down. Not every man in the village fights.
The breeders who value their hands tend not to, and Boz the farrier, who is the largest man in the village, has never set foot in the ring and considers the whole tradition a reliable source of business since somebody always needs something looked at afterward.
Trazh has a feud with Castra Vull, a day's ride north. The details are covered in Castra Vull's entry and do not need repeating here except to say that Trazh's version of the story involves considerably less guilt.
The sign-stealing and the well are remembered fondly by the young men who did them and with mild embarrassment by everyone else. Kolev, who was involved in most of it, has recently made a friend in Castra Vull and has been less involved since, though he would not put it that way.
The loosened paddock gate that let three mares wander is not remembered fondly by anyone, and the breeders' opinion of Castra Vull hardened after it in a way the pranks had not managed.
Notable Locations
•
The Ring:
Twenty paces of packed dirt behind the Madric house, slight bowl from decades of stamping, split-rail fence for leaning on. No schedule. Fights happen when two men agree to one and the village drifts over because there is not much else to watch on a given evening.
Someone rakes it flat afterward.
•
Anka's:
The front room of the Madric house, which Old Madric's wife has run as a public house for twenty years without a sign or anyone's permission. The beer is standard Remosan, the bread is good, soldiers who stay past dark are charged double.
Anka keeps a tally board behind the bar of every man she has thrown out. Her husband's name is a recurring one.
•
The Paddock:
Trazh's main pasture along the south side of the Imperial Path. Travelers coming up the road see the herd before they see the village, and the quality of the animals speaks for itself.
During foaling season the near paddock fills with mares and the breeders sleep in the field shed to keep watch.
•
Boz's Forge:
A small smithy on the east edge of the village. Boz shoes the horses and does the village ironwork and occasional emergency dentistry on fighters who did not keep their guard up.
He is a gentle man with enormous hands who has strong opinions about hoof care and no opinions about anything else.
Plot Hooks
•
The Dead Horse:
A brown mare belonging to Castra Vull was found dead on the road between the two villages with her throat cut. Castra Vull has accused Trazh. The accusation is wrong and the breeders are angry about it. Nobody in Trazh would kill a horse.
Kolev has told Gresch he will find out what happened, which is a promise he made after his third drink at Anka's and which he now has to keep sober.
•
The Conscription Rider:
A military courier arrived last week with updated conscription rolls. Trazh's quota has doubled. The village has always sent its share without complaint, but the new number would take nearly a third of the men under forty, including two of the better breeders.
Old Madric rode to Mirestead to argue the number four days ago. He has not come back.
•
The Buyer:
A well-dressed man from the interior arrived on the Imperial Path last month, looked at the horses, and offered to buy the entire spring foal crop at a price far above market. He would not say who he was buying for. He is coming back next week with a contract and a cart.
The breeders are split between wanting the money and wanting to know why someone needs thirty horses quickly and will not explain why.

the_hung_tree.title: The Hung Tree
the_hung_tree.text:
The Hung Tree
A solitary giant oak, standing in the middle of a clearing in the grove at the meeting point between Remosa, Haldrith and Rivhalde. Thirty to forty meters tall, and wide enough that six people linking arms could not close the circle.
Its name has been long forgotten by most, but the well informed know that it relates to the tree's grim history. During the Witch Wars, a Remosan military command ordered the mass execution of deserters at the site.
A large tree, big enough to hang dozens of bodies from at once, was the type of sight that deterred others who might consider following in the deserters' footsteps.
The tree served as a warning to all three regions, and was so effective, in fact, that it was joked to be a permanent signpost at the time. The excess nourishment has allowed it to grow even bigger than it was, resulting in the wonder that it is today.
